## D90 Two verdict rows measured the machine, not the data — one had a date in it, the other could not fail

`data/seed/quality.sql` raises unless all 216 of its checks pass, and D89 fixed the one row that reported how
fast the build host was. Two more were still reading the wall clock. Neither was hypothetical: both were
measured on the database D89's third gate run left behind (`nexus_gate_217782_1790380257`), on 2026-09-26,
before anything in this unit was written.

**The horizon row had an expiry date nobody wrote down.** Its second arm read
`(SELECT min(starts_at)::date FROM availability_slots) >= current_date - 7`. The seeded horizon is pinned to
`2026-09-22T11:00:00+08:00` (`data/seed/generate.py:1990`), so `min(starts_at)` is fixed at
2026-09-22 07:00+08 while `current_date - 7` walks forward one step a day. On 2026-09-26 the threshold read
2026-09-19 and the arm had 3 days of slack; on 2026-09-30 it reddens with the source tree unchanged and every
decision it encodes still true. A gate that fails on a Tuesday for no reason but Tuesday is not a gate; CI
running this file was scheduled to go red in its sleep.

**The TTL arm could not fail.** Its third arm read `stale AND expires_at > now()`. The generator sets the flag
only where the expiry already precedes its own instant — `stale = bool(exp and exp < self.now and ...)` at
`data/seed/generate.py:966` — so every stale row in the dataset expires before the base instant, and the
newest of the 72 stale rows read 2026-09-22 09:30:00+08, which is 90 minutes *before* the 11:00 base. Any
`now()` that has not been wound backwards reads later than that. The count it reports is 0 and, for a seed
loaded after the base instant, has to be: at the 11:41 reading it had been unable to fail for 4 days and
35 minutes. A predicate no input can satisfy is not checking the input; it is decoration around a `NOT EXISTS`.

Both rows ask the same question — *is this data self-consistent?* — so both now ask the data, and the answer
travels with the dataset.

**The anchor is published by the thing that knows it.** `data/seed/generate.py:1654` writes the resolved base
into `out/00_truncate.sql` as one comment line, `-- seed-base: 2026-09-22 11:00:00+08`, in the same
`write_outputs()` call that writes the CSVs beside it, in a file that call deletes before it starts. That
placement is the whole design: the carrier cannot outlive the data it describes, because the only way to have
data is to have run the call that rewrote the carrier. `data/seed/load.sh:65` reads the line back in
preflight — before the container check, before the connection, before the load — and refuses with
`SEED_ANCHOR=1 needs a '-- seed-base: <instant>' line` if the shape is wrong, so a dataset whose base cannot
be published is refused in the second it is noticed rather than after ten minutes of loading it.
`data/seed/load.sh:90` gates that read on the same `SEED_ANCHOR=1` that D89 introduced, and
`data/seed/load.sh:171` records it as `ALTER DATABASE … SET nexus.seed_base`, called beside the window bounds
at `data/seed/load.sh:190`. `scripts/db_gate_fresh.sh:173` turns all three on for the database it owns. One
flag, one carrier, one stamp, no new table: `tables=58` is unchanged.

**The gate reads it and refuses to guess.** `data/seed/quality.sql:72` defines `seed_now` — `known`, `ts`, and
a `shown` string that says `NO BASE STAMPED — re-run data/seed/load.sh with SEED_ANCHOR=1` — through the same
`nullif(current_setting(...), '')` form D89 used, with no fallback to `now()`. The TTL arm is now
`stale AND expires_at > (SELECT ts FROM seed_now)` (`data/seed/quality.sql:836`), and the horizon arm is a
window around the same instant (`data/seed/quality.sql:892`): the first slot may be no earlier than a day
before the dataset's own now and no later than 8 days after it. Both rows lead with `known`, which keeps `ok`
a boolean instead of a NULL the verdict's `WHERE NOT ok` would walk past, and the two-sided horizon bound is
what replaces the single `>=`: an arm that can be broken from either end is an arm that is watching.

Measured on the shipped bytes, against the database the run that ships them left behind:

| condition | `seed_now` reads | shipped TTL row | shipped horizon row | HEAD's TTL row | HEAD's horizon row |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| nothing touched | 2026-09-22 11:00+08 | pass, 0 | pass | pass, 0 | pass |
| same instant re-SET by the session | 2026-09-22 11:00+08 | pass, 0 | pass | pass, 0 | pass |
| one row marked stale while its TTL runs 31 min past the base | 2026-09-22 11:00+08 | **fail, 1** | pass | pass, 0 | pass |
| base moved 9 days later | 2026-10-01 11:00+08 | pass, 0 | **fail** | pass, 0 | pass |
| base moved 12 days earlier | 2026-09-10 11:00+08 | **fail, 72** | **fail** | pass, 0 | pass |
| database never stamped | NO BASE STAMPED | fail, names it | fail, names it | — | — |

The last column is the point of the exercise: HEAD's two rows did not move on any of the six states, including
the one where a fact is labelled stale while the data itself says it still had half an hour to live. That row
is `216fb47c-9e39-52f6-9a62-a02adba85739`, a price fact observed 05:30:39 and expiring 11:30:39 against an
11:00 base, planted inside a transaction the harness rolls back; the residue check after the run reads 72
stale rows and 0 offenders, which is what it read before. The re-anchored rows are sliced out of
`data/seed/quality.sql` at run time, and the two HEAD rows are sliced out of the same file at `HEAD` and
renamed — nothing in the table above is a hand-copy of a rule.

The margins are reported rather than assumed: the first slot sits 20 h above the lower bound and 196 h below
the upper one, and the newest stale expiry sits 90 min below the base. The bounds are not what makes these
rows pass, and the 20 h one is tight enough to be interesting.

**What this does not buy.** The TTL arm still cannot be tripped by any dataset `generate.py` writes, for the
same reason `now()` could not trip it: `data/seed/generate.py:966` forbids the combination at the source. What
changed is *which* producer the arm watches. `MerchantContentRepository.expireFacts` and the row's own
`stale` column are written by the platform at read time, and 4,484 of the seed's facts are past expiry while
4,412 of those carry `stale=false` — so the guard is real for a served database and the plant above is its
witness for the predicate. Recorded as a limitation here, and as task #70, rather than papered over: the same
census found `scripts/verify_consumer_slice.py:77` asserting that every past-expiry fact arrives marked
stale, which the seed refutes by construction and which nothing has ever swept
(`markExpiredStale` at `FactRepository.java:102` has no callers in the repo).

**Two claims corrected, named rather than quietly edited.** The horizon row's detail text used to end with
`(pinned base date, see README)`. There is no README to see: `data/seed` holds `generate.py`, `load.sh`,
`quality.sql`, `seed_pools.py`, `out/`, `out_smoke/` and `__pycache__`, and the only README under it is
`out/images/README.md`, about SVG placeholders. The sentence shipped in a committed file and pointed at
nothing; the text now names the chain it actually reads. Second, D89's block at `data/seed/quality.sql` said
"Nothing is measured against now() any more", which was true of the clock set and readable as a claim about
the file; it now reads "Nothing in this set…", and the file says which remaining `now()` is deliberate —
part A's `past_expiry` column is a report about the reading instant, and the reading instant is what it
reports on.

**Four things about the measuring.** (a) A validator's first execution must not be its first test: this one's
was, and it refused a *correct* carrier line on a real gate run — see the gate section, where that run is
named as the red it was. (b) A shape guard is about shape. The regex now takes an explicit alternation of the
three offset spellings `ts()` can produce; it does not validate the calendar, and that is the right division
of labour, because `::timestamptz` on the read side raises for an impossible date and says so in step 5. (c)
`SET x = (SELECT …)` is not SQL: psql's `SET` takes a literal, and a plant whose prelude errors still prints
green, because the failure is in a statement the verdict never reads. `ON_ERROR_STOP=1` in the plant driver is
not decoration — it is what makes a broken arm distinguishable from a passing one. (d) An arm that can only
move one way is worth auditing, and so is a table that only runs one way: the six states above include two
that must stay green, and the two HEAD columns exist to be *unable* to move.

**Gates.** The first official 8-step run of this unit's bytes FAILED, and it failed on the loader's new
preflight: `load.sh` refused `2026-09-22 11:00:00+08`, the exact string `generate.py` had just written,
because bash read `[0-9]{2}?` as "these two digits are optional" and so required a colon the generator never
emits. `gate-d90-official.log` keeps that run, ending `GATE_RC=2`, and the empty database it left behind was
dropped after the cause was read; the refusal was correct behaviour on incorrect input, and the input was the
generator's own output.
The guard was fixed, and then driven through the shipped `load.sh` over nine carrier shapes — four it must
accept (`+08`, `+0800`, `+08:00`, `-0500`) and five it must refuse (no offset, ISO `T` separator, a quote with
a `DROP DATABASE`, an empty value, a file written before carriers existed) — 9/9 as expected, exit codes read
as the classifier (2 = refused in preflight, 3 = accepted and gone on to look for a container).

The second official run passes end to end in about three minutes on a warm cache: migrations to `tables=58`,
`migrations=7`, generate's own self-check, the load stamped with all three anchors
(`nexus.seed_started=1790395434`, `nexus.seed_finished=1790395448`, a 14-second load, and
`nexus.seed_base=2026-09-22 11:00:00+08`, byte-identical to the carrier line on disk), `-> 216 quality checks
passed against a from-scratch schema`, the truncate probe's both-branches PASS, the jsonb read census, and
the ledgers' own citations resolved. That a run this short passed matters less than what it proves about
D89's row: the same predicate on a 14-second load and an 807-second load, both green, which is the claim that
unit bought. The 807 s load in run #3 and this 14 s one are the two ends of the width the row no longer
cares about. Every tracked file's mtime precedes the run's start, so the bytes the gate certified are the
bytes that ship.

D89's four clock arms were re-run over the new bytes on the stamped database: the two arms that inherit the
recorded window pass, and the two that override it with a 2020 window or a window around the pinned base date
fail, naming the generation-clock row — the separation still holds after the file changed under it.

**Next.** The unit's own residue: `nexus_gate_225101_1790395370` (stamped, full dataset) and
`nexus_gate_217782_1790380257` (D89's, stamped for the window only) are kept for the readings above; drop
them when the numbers have been re-derived. Task #70 carries the served-plane twin of this defect, which is
worse: it is already past its trip date rather than three days from it. Task #57 still owes a plant witness
for the two arms D90's census found dead in the same row — `expires_at <= observed_at` and the confidence
bounds — where the honest fix is a plant per arm, not a deletion.

**After the commit.** Step 8 then ran in its HEAD-strict default, over the committed text rather than a blob:
166 headings seen, 371 `name:number` tokens resolving to 55 distinct files, and the working copy's 157
citations in 165 sections read back with 0 offenders. Two of those headings are this unit's — D90 here and §87
in STATUS.md — so the citations this entry makes are the ones a later gate run will be able to check, not
merely the ones it will re-read. The numbers are printed by the checker, not transcribed from this run's
memory of an earlier one, which is the mistake class §86 (j) names: a count without the condition it was read
under is not a number. What step 8 still cannot see is stated in its own output: it proves a cited line
exists, never that the line says what the sentence claims.

## D91 The consumer verifier asserted a stamp no producer writes; the UI derives freshness from `expires_at` instead

D90's census did not stop at the data gate. The same shape — an assertion whose predicate no input can
satisfy — was sitting in `scripts/verify_consumer_slice.py`, one of the three lines that check the served
promise about fact freshness.

**Measured first.** On the database D90's passing gate run left behind, and again on the live demo database:
every one of the 520 `opening_hours` facts is past expiry and none of them carries `stale=true` — 0 of 520.
The price facts read 2,080 past expiry with 72 marked, the rating facts 1,727 with none. The reason is
arithmetic, not sloppiness: `stale` is set at the instant the row is written, and `data/seed/generate.py:966`
marks a row only where its expiry already precedes that instant. A TTL of 24 hours is never already-expired
when it is stamped, so no 24-hour fact can ever be marked at load; and 24 hours after the pinned base every
one of them is expired to a client while the column still says "no". Nothing re-stamps them either:
`markExpiredStale` (`FactRepository.java:102`) is defined and has no callers anywhere in the repository.

**What the arm claimed, and what it could see.** `expired facts arrive marked stale` compared each served
fact's `expires_at` against `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` and required `stale is True` on the ones past it. On
the live leg that has been unsatisfiable since 2026-09-23 11:00+08 — three days before D90 was even written —
and on the offline demo catalogue the same line is vacuously true, because that builder derives
`expires_at` from its own `now`, so nothing is ever past it. One assertion, both failure classes, and which
one you got depended on which backend happened to be up. §87's next (a) recorded the aggregate ratio
(4,412 of 4,484); the sharper number is this one, because `opening_hours` is exactly what the walk's cards
carry: 100 percent past, 0 percent marked.

**The promise is real; the column is not the promise.** The consumer's "may have changed" comes from
`packages/ui/src/trust/fact.ts:66` — `isStale()` is `fact.stale === true || isExpired(fact, now)` — so the
flag is one input and the client's own clock the other. That makes `expires_at` the only freshness signal a
served fact actually owes, and it rewrites the check as two properties that can both fail:

  * every served fact carries an `expires_at` the client can compare. A missing or unparseable one is the
    dangerous direction: `isExpired()` can never fire, the column says no, and an expired number is presented
    as live forever. `parse_instant` in the verifier names the assumption it makes to answer this — a naive
    stamp is read as UTC, because the alternative is a verdict that depends on where the script ran.
  * no fact is marked stale while its own TTL still runs. This is the milder direction (a live number
    presented as doubtful), and it is the one that keeps the flag honest as an input.

Neither is the old arm's question, and neither is empty: 24 of the 32 facts in the witness fixture are past
expiry, and the two verdicts disagree about which side of the derivation each of them is on.

**Falsifiers, offline, over the shipped text.** `d91_witness.py` reads `parse_instant` and
`freshness_defects` out of the verifier at run time rather than restating them, builds its fixture by querying
the loaded database (8 cards, 32 facts, `expires_at` rendered the way the API renders it), pins NOW to
2026-09-26 04:00Z so no plant is an accident of the clock, and runs five arms: the seed as served (0/0), one
`expires_at` removed (1 unageable), one unreadable (1), one live fact marked stale (1 early), and one naive
stamp (0/0 — it parses, and it is past). 5/5 as expected. The fixture asserts it contains both sides of NOW
before any arm runs: an arm that passes because its plant is impossible is D90's dead arm in a new costume,
and the witness would otherwise have printed a green table over it.

**The live leg is BLOCKED, not skipped.** With `:8090` down the two fact verdicts are now filed as BLOCKED
naming the HTTP status that starved them, and that path was run rather than described: the shipped script
against a stopped stack prints `FAIL directory listing -> HTTP 0` followed by the two BLOCKED lines.
Restarting the developer platform is not this lane's call, so the served payload itself remains unwitnessed
today — the predicates are witnessed, the wire is not, and the distinction is the entry, not a footnote.

**Left as a decision, not edited away.** Whether anything should ever set the column after load is a product
question with three answers: run the sweep the repository already has, drop the method so nothing looks like a
rule that is not one, or keep the column as a load-time opinion only — which is what the UI already assumes.
This unit changes what it owns and files the question; it does not wire a write into a read path to make a
tally go green.

## D92 The two arms D90 shipped without a falsifier get one each — and `facts` turns out to have no CHECK at all

D90 re-anchored a row and gave one of its three arms a working plant. The other two shipped in the same
statement with no witness that they can fail, which is the same hole D83's task line had been describing since
it was written: §88's next (c) carried them, attributing them to task #57 — imprecise, since #57 closed with
witnesses for its own census arms long before this row existed. They are named here as what they are: two arms
of `confidence within 0..1 and a TTL that runs forward` (`data/seed/quality.sql:830`) that nobody had broken.

**The plants.** Both go through the shipped text — the harness slices the row out of the working copy at run
time — inside a transaction that is rolled back, and both pick their victim with a subquery that can only
match a row the arm does not already count, so an UPDATE that changed nothing cannot print a green table.

| arm | planted row | detail text the shipped row then printed | verdict |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| none (control) | — | `0 bad confidence, 0 non-forward TTL, 0 marked stale…` | pass |
| `confidence = 1.5` | `00079ece-…d375`, a rating fact | `1 bad confidence, 0 non-forward TTL, 0 marked stale…` | **fail** |
| `expires_at = observed_at` | the same row, in a separate run | `0 bad confidence, 1 non-forward TTL, 0 marked stale…` | **fail** |
| both at once | the same row again | `1 bad confidence, 1 non-forward TTL, 0 marked stale…` | **fail** |

The last two rows are the point of doing the pair. A detail string that reported "1 problem" would be one flag
with three names on it; these three counts moved independently, including when the offender was a single row
carrying both defects. Residue after each arm: 0 out-of-range confidences, 0 backwards TTLs, the planted row
back at its seed value of 0.700.

**What the first plant found next to it.** The database accepted `confidence = 1.5` without complaint, because
nothing stops it: `facts.confidence` is `numeric(4,3)` — a type that can hold anything to 9.999 — and
`pg_constraint` reports **zero** CHECK constraints on `facts`. So this arm is not a restatement of something
the schema already guarantees, which is the criticism that makes most defensive range checks decoration: it is
the only thing between a stored 1.500 and a rendered claim, and D80's census shows the readers do trust that
column. The corresponding decision — add a CHECK in a V8 migration so the database refuses it, or keep the
gate as the only bound and say so — is filed rather than taken: a new migration changes the shared schema
plane, the `tables=`/`migrations=` figures every gate line quotes, and `docs/DATABASE.md`, which belongs to
another lane.

**A witness that reads `HEAD` starts reading itself, and this one did.** The D90 harness pulled the
superseded rule out of `HEAD:data/seed/quality.sql` so the old and new predicates could be scored against one
state without anything being retyped. That was correct until D90 was committed: `HEAD` then contained the *new*
row, the `stale-while-live` text it searched for was gone, and the next call failed — loudly, this time, on an
end-marker assert, having earlier come within one commit of quietly slicing the rule it was meant to compare
against. It is pinned to `989baca^` now, the last commit before that change, with two guards: the superseded
text must be present at the ref, and must be absent from the working copy. D90's arms were re-run after the
pin — control, the stale-while-live plant and the 9-day-late base all behave as first recorded.

**Gates.** Nothing shipped by this unit is a byte the database gate reads: the plants are transactions that
roll back, the harness is a witness script outside the tree, and `git diff 989baca..HEAD -- data/seed
scripts/db_gate_fresh.sh` is empty, which is the evidence that D90's passing 8-step run still certifies the
seed plane rather than a memory of it. Step 8 is re-run after this commit, as it was after D89's and D90's.

## D93 The comment plane carries 68 citations the ledger gate never reads — and all five offenders are the checkers' own examples

`scripts/check_ledger_citations.mjs` opens every `file:line` the ledgers claim, and it reads `docs/*.md`.
Source comments make the same kind of claim — `data/seed/quality.sql`'s own notes cite `load.sh` and
`generate.py` lines, the two scanners cite Java sites — and nothing reads them. Task #67 has carried that gap
since D87 with a remembered number ("5 offenders") and a remembered list. Both are now measured, and the list
is right in count and wrong in detail.

**The reader, built out of the gate rather than beside it.** `d93_census.py` slices the token grammar out of
`check_ledger_citations.mjs` at run time — it matches the one line containing `matchAll(`, asserts exactly one
such line exists, and compiles the literal it finds — then extracts the citation-shaped tokens from comment
lines of every `.sql`/`.sh`/`.py`/`.java`/`.mjs`/`.ts`/`.tsx`/`.yml` file in the tree, excluding `docs/` (step
8 already owns that plane) and the generated and vendored directories. It writes them into a markdown file —
one bullet per token — and runs the shipped checker over that file with `--text=`, which is the mode D88
already uses to score text that is not yet committed. So the resolution is done by step 8's resolver, over the
working tree, with no second implementation to drift. Writing the provenance as `file:2345` would have made
the checker score the census's own bookkeeping; provenance is spelled `at line 2345` for exactly that reason.

**Measured.** 68 citation-shaped tokens in the comment plane, across 18 files, naming 25 distinct files; the
shipped checker exits 1 with 5 offenders:

| offender | where it actually sits | what it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `File.java` line 12 | `scripts/check_jsonb_reads.mjs:311` | a JSDoc example of the grammar |
| `dir/File.java` lines 78-84 | `scripts/check_jsonb_reads.mjs:311` | the same sentence's second example |
| `services/platform/.../growth/EventRepository.java` line 39 | `scripts/check_ledger_citations.mjs:12` | an elided path, cited as a shape |
| `package.json` line 9 | `scripts/check_ledger_citations.mjs:66` | an example of an AMBIGUOUS cite |
| `.gitignore` line 5 | `scripts/run_platform_dev.sh:20` | an example of a dotfile held twice |

Task #67's note named the fourth one `package.json` line 66; measured, the cite inside that comment is
`package.json` line 9, and 66 is the *line the comment sits on*. A remembered cite conflated the two, which is the
reason this lane re-measures before it re-states.

**The finding is not "five false citations".** Every one of the five is an illustrative example inside the
sentence that explains the grammar — prose about what a bad citation looks like, written in citation shape. A
comment-plane gate wired up today would go red on the two files whose job is defining citation shape, which is
a gate that punishes honesty. So the missing piece is a convention, not a checker: a placeholder has to be
written in a form that reads as an example (`File.java line 12`, `File.java:NN`, or fenced so it is not
token-shaped), and the plane has to be scanned for it. The census reports 63 citations that resolve and 5 that
are examples pretending to be claims — the ratio is the argument for adding the gate, and the convention is
the precondition.

**One filter nearly lost an offender silently.** The first run found 67 tokens and 4 offenders: my
file-shaped-name guard required a `.suffix` of up to six characters, so `.gitignore` — extension `gitignore`,
nine characters — was dropped before the checker ever saw it, while the checker itself special-cases dotfiles
precisely because the ledgers cite them. Accepting the checker's two shapes (a suffixed name, or a leading dot)
moved the count to 68 and the offenders to 5. A filter written narrower than the thing it feeds does not report
a smaller number; it reports a wrong one, in the direction of green.

**Gates.** Nothing in the tree's shipped behaviour changed: the census is a new untracked witness script, and
step 8's committed behaviour is untouched. `scripts/` is not read by the database gate's steps 1-7 — but step 7
(`check_jsonb_reads.mjs`) and step 8 are executable files in that directory, and neither was edited, so
D90's passing 8-step run still certifies the tree. Step 8 is re-run after this commit and its numbers recorded.

**The convention proved itself on this entry.** The first draft of the table above wrote those five
placeholders in claim shape — a bare name, a colon, a line number — and the staging check refused to commit
it: "citations do not resolve over the exact committed bytes", naming all five as offenders in the
ledger's own text. Rewriting them as `File.java` line 12 kept the sentence true and stopped it reading
as a claim about a file that does not exist, which is the whole proposal in one edit. A section about a
gate that reddens honest prose was reddened by that gate, and the fix was the prose, not the gate.

## D94 Four grammar examples stop reading as claims: the placeholder convention is `:NN`, and it went into the plane that produced the offenders

D93 measured the comment plane at 68 citation-shaped tokens and 5 offenders, all five of them illustrative
examples written in claim shape inside the sentences that define claim shape. It filed the convention as task
#72 rather than inventing one in passing. This is the convention, chosen and applied, with the plane re-scored
after it.

**The rule.** A comment that *shows* the grammar writes digits as `NN`: `` `File.java:NN` ``,
`` `dir/File.java:NN-NN` ``, a bare `` `:NN` ``. The checker's token grammar requires digits after the colon,
so the placeholder stays readable as the shape it names and cannot be mistaken for an assertion about a file.
The alternative — spelling it as "`File.java` line 12", which is what D93's own ledger sections had to fall
back on under the staging check — loses the thing being illustrated: the colon is the point of the example.
So D93's prose and D94's code use different forms for different jobs, and the difference is worth naming: in a
census table you are quoting a string that exists, and in a grammar comment you are showing a shape that does
not.

**Applied.** `scripts/check_jsonb_reads.mjs`'s JSDoc line defining a citation token, and two examples in
`scripts/check_ledger_citations.mjs`'s header — one of an elided path, one of a name six files share. All line
counts were preserved, because a shifted line in a checker silently invalidates every `file:line` cite that
crosses it; the edits replace a line with a line.

**The fifth was not a placeholder, and treating it like one would have been a lie.**
`scripts/run_platform_dev.sh`'s `(gitignored at ` + a bare `.gitignore` with a colon and a line number) is a true claim about a real line in a real
file — the checker flagged it AMBIGUOUS because two `.gitignore` files exist, the root's and
`packages/sdk`'s. Rewriting the number to `NN` would have made the census clean by deleting the claim. It
became `./.gitignore:5` instead, the root-relative form `check_ledger_citations.mjs` documents as exactly the
disambiguation for a file the repo owns twice. That is also the third time this lane has met the same failure:
make a check pass by removing the thing it was checking. The fix for an ambiguous cite is the path that
resolves it.

**Measured after.** 64 tokens in 17 files, 0 offenders, the shipped checker exiting 0 on the same census file
D93 ran. The arithmetic is checkable: four placeholders retired (68 − 4 = 64), one disambiguated and still
counted, and the file count dropping 18 → 17 because `check_jsonb_reads.mjs`'s only two comment-plane tokens
were both grammar examples — that file now says nothing about any file's line, which is correct for it.

**Gates.** Both executable checkers still parse (`node --check`), and because the edited files are themselves
read by the gate, steps 7 and 8 were re-run over the changed bytes rather than argued about: step 7 exits 0,
step 8 in its HEAD-strict default reports 172 sections, 396 tokens, 56 files, 0 offenders. The database
gate's steps 1-6 are untouched — no seed file changed, and D90's passing 8-step run still covers them.
`scripts/check_contract_drift.mjs` also shows as modified in this working tree; it belongs to another lane, was
not read or written by this unit, and the commit is pathspec-limited so it stayed out.

**Next.** Task #72's second half is now unblocked in substance: a comment plane with 0 offenders can be made a
gate step, and the remaining cost is the step-number change — `db_gate_fresh.sh` and the ledgers quote "8
steps" and "step 7/8" in prose, so a ninth step is a coordinated edit with a blast radius, not a bolt-on.
Recorded there rather than started here.

## D95 The comment plane becomes a gate step: nine steps now, and the reader's first three verdicts were green, red-by-plant, green

D93 built a reader for the citations that live in source comments; D94 set the convention that made the plane
clean enough to enforce. Neither is worth much while running it is something a person remembers to do. This
unit ships `scripts/check_comment_citations.mjs` and makes it step 9 of `scripts/db_gate_fresh.sh`.

**One resolver, delegated.** The new script resolves nothing itself. It reads
`scripts/check_ledger_citations.mjs`, finds the single line where the token grammar lives — asserting exactly
one line matches, so a refactor that duplicates or moves the pattern stops the scan rather than silently
scoring a different grammar — compiles the literal out of it, and then hands the list it collected to that same
checker with `--text=`. The alternative, a second implementation of the same rules, is the failure D85 named
for hand lists and D93 named for filters: two readers of one plane disagree silently, and the disagreement is
always found in the direction that lets more through.

**What the step owes a verdict, and what it actually printed.** Three arms, in order, against the real tree:

| arm | tokens | files | step 8 exit | step 9 result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| the plane as it stands | 64 | 17 | 0 | PASS, rc 0 |
| one unresolvable cite planted in `scripts/.d95_plant.py` | 65 | 18 | 1 | FAIL, rc 1, naming a cite to `nothing_here.py`, a file that exists nowhere |
| plant removed | 64 | 17 | 0 | PASS, rc 0 |

The plant is an untracked scratch file with a comment, and it is gone: `ls` after the third arm reports
`No such file or directory`. A scan that never went red has not been shown to be reading anything.

**Two independent readers, agreeing.** D93's witness (`d93_census.py`, python, the temp-dir artifact this
section's numbers came from originally) and the shipped script now report the same census: 64 tokens, 17 files,
25 distinct cited files, 0 offenders. The shipped one is authoritative from here; the python stays where it is
as D93's evidence, and the agreement is the cross-check rather than a second opinion to maintain.

**The numbering, stated honestly.** Nine `step "n/…"` labels became `/9`, and step 8's rationale sentence —
"the other seven steps all read the working tree" — became eight, because after this unit it is false. The
ledgers' older sentences about "the official 8-step run" are left exactly as written: they describe runs made
before this one, and those had eight steps. A run on 2026-09-26 at 12:57 local — recorded here as
`gate-d95-official.log`, `GATE_RC=0` — is the first to execute nine, and it printed step 9's own block:
`tokens found 64 in 17 file(s)`, `RESULT: PASS … (step 8 exit 0)`.

**What this does not buy.** The scan's third exit code — 2, reserved for "the plane contains no tokens at all",
which is the shape of a broken scan pretending to be a clean one — has no witness. Every way to reach it needs
either a temporary edit to the shipped extension list or a parameter that does not exist yet, and inventing one
to test the other is the kind of seam that outlives its purpose. Recorded as untested rather than passed. The
step also still ignores anything in `docs/` (step 8's plane, deliberately excluded so a citation is attributed
to one reader and not two), and it reads comment markers by position, so a string literal containing `--` or
`//` can be scanned as prose; it over-reports, which is the direction that hides nothing.

**Three things the measuring gave back.** (a) A green claimed from wording is a green that gets renamed out
from under you: the first version of the verdict line tested the child's output for the phrase
`0 offender(s)`, which step 8 does not print in `--text` mode at all — so the clean tree reported FAIL with the
child exiting 0. The exit code is the verdict; a non-zero offender count is only a belt on it. (b) The
newest file in the tree nearly carried the defect the previous two units retired: its own header comment
illustrated a trailing cite as `x.py` with a colon and a digit, which is exactly a claim-shaped token, and it would have reddened the
step on its first run. D90's rule again — a guard's first execution must not be its first test. (c) The RESULT
block's two added lines printed as one run-on sentence, because they were written without their trailing
`\n`, and `bash -n` — which is what this lane reaches for to check a shell edit — passed anyway. A syntax check
is not a read of the output; the defect was found in the log, and the fix is certified by the re-run below
rather than asserted.

**Gates.** Run 1 (nine steps, before the newline fix): `GATE_RC=0`, 216 quality checks, `tables=58`,
`migrations=7`, truncate probe both branches, jsonb reads and sites reconciled, ledgers resolved, comment
plane censused at 64 tokens / 0 offenders. Run 2, over the fixed RESULT block, is what certifies the bytes that
ship; its verdict is recorded in §92 rather than predicted here.

## D96 Trying to witness one untested branch found a worse one: the comment gate called a crashed reader a false citation

D95 shipped its own exit code 2 — "the plane contains no tokens, so this scan read nothing" — and recorded it as
untested. This unit went to test it. It turned out the branch is unreachable with byte-identical copies of the
shipped scripts, and the attempt to reach it exposed something worth more than the original target: step 9
reported a reader that could not start as a citation that failed.

**The attempt.** A scratch tree (`Temp\d96tree\scripts`) holding copies of `check_comment_citations.mjs` and
`check_ledger_citations.mjs` plus one source file whose comments make no citation-shaped claim. The copies are
byte-identical — sha256 prefix `c4770675901e5a4b` and `51971a1b597b2b94`, matching the repo files — which is
what makes the run a witness rather than a rehearsal: the script derives its repository root from its own path,
so an isolated copy is the only way to point it at a smaller plane without touching the tree it gates.

**What it found instead.** The copied step-8 checker imports `source_index.mjs`, which the scratch tree did not
have. The child died on `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` — no report at all — and step 9 printed:

```
RESULT: FAIL — 3 comment-plane citation(s) across 1 file(s), at least one does not — see the report above
```

That sentence says a citation does not resolve. Nothing was examined: the reader never ran. The same category
error D91's verifier made about a `stale` stamp — a verdict phrased as a fact about the data when it is really
a fact about the machinery — in the tool that exists to catch such phrasing. It was found only because the
witness was attempted; a guard nobody has seen fire is not evidence the guard works, and here the attempt paid
for itself before reaching its target.

**The fix, and the arms that hold it.** Step 9 now asks whether the child produced a report before it claims
anything about citations, and separates the two outcomes:

| arm | plane | what step 8's child did | verdict line | exit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | the real tree, clean | reported, 0 offenders | `RESULT: PASS … 64 tokens / 17 files` | 0 |
| B | scratch tree, checker's import missing | crashed, no report | `RESULT: NOT RUN — step 8 produced no report … a reader that crashed is not a citation that failed` | 2 |
| C | same scratch tree, import supplied | reported, 3 tokens resolved | `RESULT: PASS … 3 comment-plane citation(s) across 1 file(s)` | 0 |
| D | real tree, one unresolvable cite planted | reported, 1 offender | `RESULT: FAIL … 65 tokens / 18 files, at least one does not` | 1 |
| E | plant removed | reported, 0 offenders | `RESULT: PASS` | 0 |

C is the arm that makes B mean something: the same tree, the same copy of the script, one file added to the
environment, and the verdict moves from "not run" to "pass". Without C, B is just another red. The plant for D
is an untracked scratch comment — a cite to `nothing_here.py`, a file that exists nowhere — and it is gone after
the run: `ls` reports `No such file or directory`.

**What is still untested, named exactly.** The zero-token trigger of exit 2 is not covered by any arm here.
B reaches the same exit code through a different condition — a reader that failed to start, not a plane that
held nothing — and the two print different messages. Reaching the empty-plane branch would mean stripping the
citation comments out of the copied checkers, at which point the copy is no longer the shipped bytes, or adding
a parameter that controls which extensions are scanned purely so a test can turn the scan off. Both trade a real
guard for a green row, so the branch stays recorded as untested: the category it belongs to (a scan that read
nothing must not report a clean plane) is now witnessed at B, and the specific line is not.

**Two numbers corrected, neither edited away.** D95's commit message states the ledger append as "DECISIONS
+62, STATUS +55". `git show --numstat 905d1f8` says `62 / 0` and `60 / 0`: the second figure was wrong and the
first was right. The committed §92 text carries no size claim, so no line in the tree needed changing — the
error lives in a commit message, which is history and stays as it is, corrected here rather than amended away.
Writing that down matters more than the digit: a remembered count is exactly what this lane has been
re-measuring all week, and it got me again.

**Gates.** Step 9's shipped bytes changed, so the whole gate was re-run rather than the changed step alone —
see §93 for the nine-step result and its `GATE_RC`, read from the log after the run rather than asserted here.

## D97 162 of the gate's 216 assertions are never named in this lane's ledgers — and the carry-on that said otherwise was three sections stale

Three consecutive STATUS sections — §89's next (b), §92's, §93's — told the next unit that two arms of
`data/seed/quality.sql:830` still needed a working falsifier. D92 supplied both, plus the pair-on-one-row arm
that proves the counts are independent. Nobody re-read the carry before writing it again, so the plan grew
work that was done and the ledger quoted a number nobody had looked at. That is the reason to measure coverage
rather than remember it.

**The denominator came from the gate, not from a reader of it.** Two attempts to get the list of assertions out
of the SQL text failed before the right way was found:

  * A regex over `quality.sql` returned 115 names of 216 and produced junk rows — tuples split in the wrong
    place, a fragment that began `|| (SELECT count(DISTINCT rating)`. This is the failure mode the lane keeps
    being shown: a hand transcription does not under-count honestly, it invents entries.
  * Running the whole shipped file and querying after it printed nothing at all. `quality.sql` sets
    `ON_ERROR_STOP` for itself at its top, so the hard gate's `RAISE` aborts the session before a trailing
    `SELECT` can run — the file's own directives outrank the flags on the psql command line, and an attempt
    that ignores them reports emptiness as a result.

What works is the pattern this lane already uses for witnesses: slice the assertions out of the shipped file up
to the verdict marker (line 3595), run that, and ask `qc` for its own rows. 216 rows read back, 216 unique, none
of them shorter than six characters — the last check being the one that says the tail slice is aligned with the
query rather than with part A's printed reports.

**The number, with its grammar.** For each of the 216 names: does the exact string, or a fragment of it at
least twelve characters long, appear anywhere in `HEAD:docs/DECISIONS.md` or `HEAD:docs/STATUS.md`.

| | count | share |
| --- | --- | --- |
| named exactly | 42 | 19% |
| named by fragment | 12 | 6% |
| **not named anywhere** | **162** | **75%** |

**What this does not say, stated first.** A mention is not a witness. The 54 named rows are an *upper bound* on
how many assertions have ever been shown able to fail, and the true count is smaller — of a size this script
cannot determine, because the ledgers record plants in prose and there is no machine-readable claim attached to
a row. So the finding is not "75% are untested" and never should be written that way: it is that three quarters
of the gate's assertions have not been *talked about* by eighteen units of witness-building, and that the
remaining quarter's status is asserted by sentences rather than by anything a script can check.

**The correction, named as one.** §89 next (b), §92 and §93 each carried the claim that the confidence and
forward-TTL arms of the TTL row wanted a falsifier. They were planted in D92, with the counts shown moving
independently. Nothing in the tree was wrong — the carry-on was — so the fix here is not an edit of those
sections, which record what was believed when they were written, but this sentence: the item was stale from
§92 onward and was copied twice more without being read.

**Gates.** No shipped byte changed in this unit: the census is a script in the temp dir, its input is the
committed `quality.sql` sliced at run time, and the only database it touches is the stamped one D90's gate run
left behind, read with `SELECT`s after the assertions. `d97_qc_names.txt`, `d97_unrecorded.txt` and
`d97_coverage.py` are the kept artifacts; the script prints the grammar above its own numbers, and re-running
it reproduces 216 / 42 / 12 / 162 from one command. Task #73 carries what follows, with the ordering constraint
written down before the work: a plant predicted from an assertion's wording rather than from a producer that
could violate it is D79's and D91's failure performed 162 times.

## D98 The coverage number held; the classification I went for worked on a third of it, and the reason is the gate's own design

D97 reported 42 named / 12 fragment / 162 un-named of the gate's 216 assertions. The number came out of a read
with two soft spots, so this unit set out to break it and then to classify the 162 by the producer that could
violate them — #73's ordering, no plants predicted from wording.

**The number held. The read was still wrong in two ways, and fixing them changed nothing.** Three check names
carry an embedded newline, which is why a line-oriented read counted 219 lines for 216 rows; the fix is to have
the database return the list in one row (`string_agg` on a tab) and to assert the count against `count(*)` from
`qc` in the same session. And `psql` without a pinned client encoding mangles § and em dash, which is what made
98 of D97's names unfindable in the file — a wrong answer that looks like a property of the data and is a
property of the terminal. Re-measured with both fixed: **42 / 12 / 162, identical**. A number that survives two
of its three derivations being corrected is worth keeping; a number that would not have survived being checked
at all is the thing to worry about.

**Then the classification failed on two thirds of the list, and that is the finding.** Of the 216 names, only
**111 occur exactly once as a string literal in `data/seed/quality.sql`**, **2 occur twice**, and **103 do not
appear as text at all**. Those 103 are built at run time: the FK sweep walks `pg_constraint` and files a row per
edge, so names like `orphan: facts.merchant_id` exist only in `qc` — D64's "one answer to which tables the seed
owns" and D72's widening past the suffix are precisely what makes them unsearchable in the source. So:

  * the producer classification landed on **51 seed-only, 0 runtime-watched, 0 empty-both** for the rows whose
    statement could be located, and **111 unclassified** — where "unclassified" means *this method could not
    reach them*, not that they read no table. Reporting the 111 as a class of assertions would be the same
    mistake as reporting an un-parseable row as a passing one.
  * the 0 for runtime-watched and empty-both is a real result for the locatable third: every assertion there
    reads tables the seed fills. The un-locatable remainder is where D79's "silence, not green" class lives —
    the FK sweep's edges point at tables that are empty by design in a fresh database — and it needs the sweep's
    own inputs to answer, which are in the catalog rather than in the text.

**What #73 should therefore do**, refined by measurement rather than by taste: split the 216 by how the name is
made. Literal-named rows (111) can be classified and planted by reading their statement out of the file, which
is what worked here. Catalogue-named rows (103) are one assertion with 103 instantiations — the FK sweep — so a
plant for them is a single act (orphan one child row in a table that has a foreign key) witnessed by the sweep
reddening on that one edge; enumerating 103 plants would be theatre. The 2 with embedded newlines need their
mentions checked across lines, or the coverage join under-reports them forever.

**Mistakes owned.** (a) D97's headline number was right for partly wrong reasons: the tail-line read happened to
land on 216, and it was the assertion-equality test — not the count — that exposed it. Counting is not checking.
(b) My first classifier pass reported 98 "unreadable" names as if the file were the problem; the mangling was in
my own invocation. (c) A "no-table-read" bucket of 111 was about my locator, not about the assertions, and the
honest fix was to say so rather than rename the bucket until it looked like a result.

**Gates.** No shipped byte changed: the reads are `SELECT`s against the stamped, kept gate database and the
live demo database (counts only), and the file is opened, not edited. Artifacts: `d98b.py`, `d98_qc_names.txt`,
`d98_unrecorded.txt`, `d98_seed_only.txt`, plus the earlier `d97_*` pair kept for the before-and-after of the
same measurement.

## D99 One plant, one edge, three reds — and the third red is D89's window catching a runtime write it was never tested against

D98 ended with the plan changed by the measurement: 103 of the gate's assertions have names built at run time by
the polymorphic reference sweeps, so they are one assertion instantiated per (table, subject type) the data
carries, and enumerating a plant for each would be theatre. What is worth doing is breaking one edge and
watching which rows move. This unit does exactly that, against the shipped text, twice, in transactions that roll
back.

**The arms.** The assertions are sliced out of `data/seed/quality.sql` at the hard-gate marker (the file sets
`ON_ERROR_STOP` for itself, and the verdict's `RAISE` would end the session and take the temp table with it, so
a read has to stop before that line). Both arms run the same 3,594 sliced lines in one session:

  * control — `BEGIN; <assertions>; report; ROLLBACK`: **216 rows filed, 0 failing**.
  * plant — the same, after `UPDATE facts SET subject_id = gen_random_uuid()` on one offering fact: **216 rows
    filed, 3 flipping from true to false**, no row appearing or disappearing between arms, and 0 orphan
    offering-facts left in the database afterwards.

**The three that moved, each explained to the mechanism rather than just named.**

  1. `orphan: facts.offering` — the intended one. The sweep pointed a name at a UUID no `offerings` row holds,
     and it reddened on the edge it names. The class is live; 103 instantiations need no individual theatre.
  2. `every column that cannot vary is answered for why it cannot` and
  3. `the columns stamped from the generation clock are exactly the ones answered so` — these two are the
     cascade, and the reason is arithmetic: `facts.updated_at` is maintained by the schema's
     `set_updated_at` trigger, so writing one row made the column **two-valued** (measured inside the same
     transaction: `distinct(updated_at) = 2` where the seed holds one value). A column that varies is no longer
     in the degenerate class the census answers for, so both census rows move with it.

Arm 3 carries the interesting part. The new stamp is not merely different, it is *outside the window*: the
recorded load bounds on this database are `1790395434..1790395448`, and the row the write produced reads
`1790400332` — 4,884 s after the load finished, or 4,284 s past the upper bound once D89's ±600 s widening is
applied. So the generation-clock row, re-anchored three units ago to stop measuring the host, has just refused a
runtime write to seeded data. That was never its stated purpose — D89 built it to separate a load-stamped
timestamp from a pinned one, and D90's docblock asserted in passing that the row watches rows the platform
writes — and here is a witness of that assertion, obtained by a plant aimed at something else. A guard that only
ever fires at the test built for it has not been shown to guard anything.

**What this does not buy.** Two of the three reds are the census reacting to a changed distinct-count, not the
sweep: a plant in `facts` is not a plant in `favorites` or `permission_grants` or `moderation_cases`, whose
sweeps have their own type vocabularies. This shows the sweep class is *capable of going red on a broken edge*
— which is the claim #73 needed — not that every instantiated edge has been individually falsified. Nor does it
cover the 111 literal-named rows #73 also lists: those need their own plants, one per assertion, where a producer
exists.

**Gates.** Nothing shipped changed: the witness scripts live in the temp dir, the only database touched is the
stamped one D90's gate run kept, every write was inside a transaction the harness rolled back, and the residue
query agrees (0 orphan offering-facts). The tree's certification remains D96's nine-step `GATE_RC=0` run; step 8
is re-run after this append because an append changes the plane it reads.

## D100 Each of the other three sweeps reddened on its own broken edge — and reddened twice, because each seam is guarded from both sides

D99 established that the polymorphic sweep class can go red, on `facts`. It also said, in its own
"what this does not buy" paragraph, that a plant in one table is not a plant in another: each sweep resolves its
own subject-type vocabulary through its own probe. This unit does the other three, one broken edge each.

**Method unchanged from D99, and deliberately so.** Four arms, one session each, the shipped assertions sliced at
the hard-gate marker, every write inside a transaction the harness rolls back: control, then `favorites`,
`permission_grants`, `moderation_cases`, each moving one row's `subject_id` to a freshly generated uuid no target
holds. Each arm filed 216 rows — the same 216, no row appearing or disappearing — and control filed 0 failures.

| arm | rows that flipped | the sweep | the companion that moved with it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| favorites | 2 | `orphan: favorites.merchant` | "favourites point at a renderable row" |
| permission_grants | 2 | `orphan: permission_grants.merchant_user` | "merchant_user grants reach a membership" |
| moderation_cases | 2 | `orphan: moderation_cases.review` | "every waiting review has exactly one open case" |

**The part worth more than the pass.** Each plant reddened *two* assertions, and the second is not an accident of
the census: it is the same seam read from the other direction. The sweep asks "does this reference resolve?"; the
companion asks the consumer-side question "does every row the UI would render point at something renderable?". One
broken edge answers both, and both answered. That is D67 and D79's "align the two directions" work turning out to
be load-bearing: until it was broken on purpose, the pairing was a claim in a comment.

Also unlike D99: no generation-clock or degenerate-column cascade appeared here, because none of these three
tables carries the `set_updated_at` trigger that made the `facts` plant change a column's distinct-count. The
absence is itself a confirmation of the mechanism D99 traced — the cascade was about a stamp, not about orphans,
and it did not follow the orphans here.

**Two false residue numbers, both from re-deriving a join by hand.** The witness script's own residue query
reported 14 orphan favourites. It counted the complement of what it named: the predicate filtered
`subject_type='offering'` *inside* the `NOT EXISTS`, so every favourite of another type satisfied it — 14 is
simply the number of non-offering favourites. Re-run with the type filter outside, it reported 0 for favourites and
cases but **36 for `permission_grants`** — all of them. That too was my join, not the gate: the shipped probe
resolves a `merchant_user` grant through `merchant_users JOIN users` onto the **user** id, so joining
`subject_id` to `merchant_users.id` directly is a different question with an alarming answer.

The lesson is the same one the file's assertion list taught two units ago, in the other direction: a hand-written
restatement of shipped logic reports on the restatement. The residue witness that survives is the shipped
assertions themselves, re-run after the rollbacks: **216 rows, 0 failing** — the database the plants touched is
the database the gate passed.

**Gates.** Nothing shipped changed: harnesses in the temp dir, one stamped database, rolled-back writes. D96's
nine-step `GATE_RC=0` run remains the tree's certification, and step 8 is re-run after this append because an
append changes the plane it reads. Artifacts: `d100_three_sweeps.py`, `d99_sweep_plant.py`.

**Where that leaves #73.** All four polymorphic sweeps have now been broken on purpose and named themselves, so
the 103 run-time-built rows are no longer a coverage debt — they are one assertion per sweep, each with a witness.
What remains there is the 111 literal-named assertions (plants where a producer exists; a changed detail text
where none does), the two names carrying newlines, and #71/#72 beside them.

## D101 The "read nothing" guard becomes reachable: a real `--plane`, and the flag shipped with two silent failures of its own

D96 recorded one branch of step 9 as untested — exit 2 when the comment plane yields no tokens — and said why
reaching it honestly looked impossible: either the copied scripts stopped being byte-identical, or a switch
existed only so a test could turn the scan off. Both are the same trade. This unit supplies the third shape:
`--plane <dir>`, which scans another tree while the resolver stays the checker the file slices its grammar from.
That is an option someone would want for a real reason — a worktree, a subproject — and it happens to make the
empty case reachable without touching a shipped byte.

**Armed, not trusted.** Five arms, and the first pass produced two false results that the flag itself caused:

  * The first implementation read only `--plane <dir>` and quietly ignored `--plane=<dir>`. Three arms then
    reported `64 tokens / 17 files / PASS`, naming the repository, while the operator believed them were looking
    at an empty directory. A silently-unread option is not a missing feature; it is a false witness with good
    manners. Parsing now accepts both spellings and exits 2 on any option it does not recognise — arm 5 shows
    `--plan` refusing rather than reading as clean.
  * Re-pointed at an off-repo plane, the tool returns `RESULT: NOT RUN`: the child checker cannot produce a
    report about citations outside the tree it indexes. That is D96's classification doing its job on its first
    outing — a unit ago this arm would have printed "at least one citation does not resolve", which is a claim
    about citations nobody examined.

With the parsing fixed, the branch is witnessed: `--plane` at an empty directory gives
`0 tokens found in the comment plane of <dir>. A scan that reads nothing is not a green scan …` and exit 2, in
both spellings; the default plane still reads 64 tokens across 17 files and passes; and the message names the
plane it read, so no arm can be mistaken for another.

**Scope, stated.** `--plane` is for trees the resolver can index — directories inside this repository, or a
worktree sharing it. It is not a way to audit some unrelated directory: there the reader will say NOT RUN, and
that answer is correct rather than inconvenient. The guard's other half — a plane that holds files but no
citations — is the same code path as the empty directory and is witnessed by it, not separately.

**Gates.** The nine-step gate was re-run over these bytes and passed: all nine step markers present, 216 quality
checks on a from-scratch schema (tables=58, migrations=7), step 9 reading
`plane censised D:\获客平台 · tokens found 64 in 17 file(s) · RESULT: PASS`, `GATE_RC=0`. That run, not the
earlier D96 one, is the certification this unit's tree carries; the ledger append that follows re-runs step 8,
which is the step the append touches.

## D102 A wrong claim survived four units because its symptoms were on screen and read as noise: no check name has a newline, and the coverage number depends on the join

D98 reported two things this unit has to take back. Both were plausible, both were used, and one of them is now
an item of work in #73 that should never have existed.

**The refuted claim.** D98 said the line-oriented read counted 219 lines for 216 rows "because two check names
carry an embedded newline", and §95 repeated it. Re-read with the names fetched as one tab-separated row and
written to a `.tsv`, the count is exactly 216 and **no name contains a newline at all**. The three extra lines
are identified by set difference against the 216: they are part A's printed report rows — `(1 row)` twice and
`string_agg` once — leaking into the tail of the slice, which is where a reader of a `psql` transcript should
expect the informational section's own noise. The arithmetic was the tell and I did not use it: three extra
lines is not two names, and a claim that does not fit its own numbers was on the page.

Worse, `string_agg` and `(1 row)` had already appeared in D98's output under "0 occurrences in the file" — a
line that should have been the alarm, since no real check name is a function call. They were read as artefacts of
the locator, which is what I called them in the ledger, and the deeper cause was the read itself. That is how a
measurement becomes a story: the anomaly is named, and naming it feels like handling it.

**What that costs elsewhere.** §96's method note and D99/D100's harnesses were built on the aggregated-row read,
which is the correct one, so no plant or verdict in those units is affected — they were computed from 216
genuine names. What is affected is a claim about the file and a task item.

**The coverage number is grammar-dependent, and must be quoted that way.** Same 216 names, same corpus (HEAD's
two ledgers, 954,043 characters), two joins:

| join | checks seen as named | un-named |
| --- | --- | --- |
| unfolded exact string, or a fragment of 18/20/30 characters | 57 | 159 |
| whitespace folded on both sides, then whole name or a 24-character prefix | 53 | 163 |

So the honest statement is not "162 of 216 are un-named" — that was one grammar's answer against an older HEAD,
which is also why it differs from D98's 54 seen (my own ledgers since D98 have named more checks). It is: **under
every grammar tried, at least 159 of the 216 assertions are never named in the ledgers**, and the exact count
moves by 4 either way — an 8% swing from a knob nobody had looked at. The floor is the claim; the point estimate
needs its grammar and its corpus beside it, which is the same rule the seed census has been repeating since D73,
applied to my own matcher.

**And the caveat got sharper, not softer.** A mention is an upper bound on being witnessed. Folding whitespace
made the question answerable; it did not convert one mention into one plant. The distance between "named at
least 57 times" and "shown able to fail some number of times that nobody has written down" is the actual work in
#73, and it is not narrowed by a cleverer join.

**Gates.** Nothing shipped changed: the reads are one `SELECT string_agg(...)` against the stamped, kept gate
database and `git show` of two committed documents. The fix is to how this lane asks a question of its own
artifacts, so the artifacts are named — `d102_qc_names.tsv`, `d102_unnamed.tsv` — and the lossy
`d98_qc_names.txt` stays where it is, beside the entry that says what it was wrong about.

scripts/check_falsifier_registry.mjs` with no `--db` prints `RESULT: NOT CHECKED -- no --db given` and
