## D152 Gate steps 8 and 9 get the same reachability arm steps 10 and 11 already had, and both are shown able to stop the run — 2026-09-28

**Why this unit.** D151 answered the question for step 11 — the guard's exit code can end the gate — and named
the two steps still without an answer. Both checkers had long carried an aiming flag: step 8's checker has read
a `--text=<file>` option since it was written, so a plant can be shown to it without touching the ledgers
another lane is appending to, and step 9's grew `--plane` in D101 for exactly the reason D96 states — the guard
that refuses a scan which read nothing has to be reachable without editing shipped bytes. What neither had was
a path from the gate. Every witness for those two steps was therefore a hand-run, and a hand-run measures an
invocation nobody else makes: the thing that protects the tree is step 8 as the gate calls it, not step 8 as I
call it from a shell.

**What landed.** Two environment knobs in `scripts/db_gate_fresh.sh`, documented in its overrides block and used
on the two invocation lines — `db_gate_fresh.sh:279` and `db_gate_fresh.sh:302`: `GATE_LEDGER_TEXT` becomes the
text-aiming flag and `GATE_COMMENT_PLANE` becomes the plane-aiming flag. Both use the same shell shape the two
existing arms use rather than a bash array, because steps 10 and 11 already set that shape, and the shape was
measured before it was written: with the variable unset the expansion adds zero argv elements even under the
strict-mode flags, with it set to a path containing a space it arrives as exactly one element with the space
intact, and a failing node call behind the step's filter returns its code because the pipefail option is set at
`db_gate_fresh.sh:33`.

**Measured.** Three full runs of the twelve-step gate, driven in sequence by a scratch script, each log read to
its own echoed return code:

- **Neutral, both knobs unset** — `gate rc=0`, ending in the run's own `RESULT: PASS` line for 216 quality
  checks on a from-scratch schema (tables=58, migrations=7). Step 8 censised 594 name-number tokens, 366 of them
  citation-shaped, resolving to 69 distinct files; step 9 found 73 comment-plane citations across 21 files.
  Those are the same figures the same two checkers printed by hand on this tree before the knobs existed, which
  is what makes the unset case inert rather than merely green.
- **Armed at step 8** — the text knob pointed at a one-paragraph plant holding one citation that resolves and
  one that names line 99999 of the gate script, which has 287. Step 8 printed its false-citation table with one
  row, kind PAST EOF, and the gate exited 1. The log carries step headers 1/12 through 8/12 and nothing after
  them: steps 9, 10, 11 and 12 never started.
- **Armed at step 9** — the plane knob pointed at an empty directory. Step 8 ran first and printed its full
  green census of the real ledgers, then step 9 refused: zero tokens found in that plane, with its own words
  that a scan which reads nothing is not a green scan. The gate exited 2 and headers 10/12 through 12/12 never
  appear.

The prediction sheet was written before the runs and lives in the driver's own comments (file on disk at
03:51:17, first run started 03:51:33). It predicted the third run would exit 1. It exited 2, and the difference
is the checker's own vocabulary rather than the gate's: 1 means a citation is false, 2 means this run cannot
certify anything, and the gate forwards whichever the step returns. Whether that distinction reaches anybody
was measured rather than assumed: the gate's file name appears on 18 lines across 9 code or config files at
HEAD, and of the 11 that sit outside the gate script itself every one is a comment, a docstring or a printed
hint — none is an invocation. The committed `Makefile` holds 23 targets and none of them mentions the gate, and
the CI workflow never names it. No automation consumes the gate's exit code at all, so 2 versus 1 breaks nothing
and also protects nothing. That is D151's finding about the falsifier scripts, now measured against the gate
itself; the CI workflow's own weakness is filed separately as task 100.

All three run databases are gone. The container holds four gate database names and none of the three this
driver created is among them, which is the cleanup trap at `db_gate_fresh.sh:109` and `db_gate_fresh.sh:162`
dropping a run that died at step 8 or step 9 as reliably as one that finished.

**What this does not buy.** Neither arm is evidence that a real ledger citation ever drifted; the plants are
planted, and step 8's green census over 366 genuine citations is the separate claim, unchanged here. The two
arms are not even the same kind of red: the step 8 arm is the checker finding a false citation, while the step
9 arm is the checker refusing to certify, and the comment plane's false-citation path has witnesses in D93 and
D94 that were not re-shown. And an environment knob is only as good as someone's willingness to set it — no CI
job, Makefile target or script in the repository runs the gate, so these arms serve whoever runs it by hand,
which is the audience the ledgers already describe.

**Gates.** `bash -n` clean on the edited file. Steps 8, 9, 10 and 12 on this entry's final bytes are reported
in the commit that carries it, and the two hand falsifiers — 6 arms for the spelled citation plane and 8 arms
for the ledger heading plane — were re-run after the append, because this entry adds sections to the plane they
read.

## D153 The heading harness resolved its fixtures through one developer's home directory, and the fix is shown by making the environment hostile — 2026-09-28

**Why this unit.** §156 (e) counted the paths in shipped bytes that name one account rather than a platform,
and found exactly one code site: the heading falsifier built its fixture root as an environment variable
defaulting to a literal under `C:\Users\18414\…`. The sibling harness in the same family already used the
documented resolver from `node:os`, so the two harnesses for the same gate family wrote their fixtures under two
different conventions, and only one of them could be steered by the environment at all. Nothing was broken on
this machine, which is the whole problem with a literal of that shape: it works precisely where it was written
and says nothing about anywhere else.

**What landed.** `scripts/falsify_ledger_sections.mjs` resolves its fixture root through `tmpdir()` from
`node:os`, the way its sibling does, and prints the root it resolved on the summary line — because a harness
that writes 8 fixture directories somewhere is a harness whose claims cannot be checked without knowing where,
and because the next reader should not have to re-derive it from a comment. The line it replaces is quoted in
the ledgers already — D116's own entry and the census in §156 that found it — so the old shape is on the record
rather than deleted silently.

**Measured.** Five cases, the mutants being the shipped file with its ROOT pinned to this repository and only
the fixture line swapped back, so an arm's verdict differs from the shipped one by that line alone:

| case | fixture root resolved | arms | rc |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| shipped, plain environment | the account's Temp directory | 8 held · 0 missed | 0 |
| shipped, `TMPDIR` set to a drive that does not exist | same as above | 8 held · 0 missed | 0 |
| mutant with the old line, same hostile `TMPDIR` | — | no arm printed | 1 |
| shipped, `TEMP` set to a scratch directory | that scratch directory | 8 held · 0 missed | 0 |
| mutant with the old line, its fallback home renamed to an absent account | — | no arm printed | 1 |

The third case dies before the table exists: `Error: ENOENT: no such file or directory, mkdir
'Q:\nope\nexus-d116-falsify\a_committed_section_deleted_from_the_wor\docs'`. That is the old code honouring an
environment variable the platform resolver ignores, and it is the worse kind of failure for a harness — not a
missed prediction but an OS crash with no prediction in it, which reads as "the harness is broken" rather than
"the guard is wrong". The fifth dies the same way with `EPERM` on
`C:\Users\nobody-on-this-machine\AppData\Local\Temp\…`; it is a stand-in for the real defect and is named here
as one, because this machine has one account and the claim is about the others.

**The prediction that missed.** The fourth case was first written as a `TMP` override and it printed the usual
root, which looked like the fix not working. Measuring `tmpdir()` directly under each variable answered it:
overriding `TMP` alone does not move it, overriding `TEMP` does, and `TMPDIR` does not either — so the probe
used the wrong variable, not the wrong code, and the re-run with `TEMP` moved the fixtures to the scratch
directory named on the summary line while all 8 arms held. The lesson is the census lesson again: an
environment claim has to name the variable that platform's resolver actually reads.

**What this does not buy.** It does not make the harness portable by testing it on another account — no such
account exists here, and the EPERM case is a simulation of that machine, not the machine. It also does not
remove the literal from the repository: the mentions that remain are prose about the defect, which is where
they belong, and the claim is only that no code or config file resolves a path through one user's home any
more. And a printed root is a printed root, not a guarantee: the harness still writes into a shared temporary
directory, so two runs of it on one account collide by name, exactly as they did before.

**Gates.** Both harnesses re-run after the append for the same reason as D152: this entry adds sections to the
plane the heading arms read. The twelve-step gate itself was not re-run, because no step of it executes either
harness — the finding D151 census named and D152 measured against the gate.

**Amendment, same day, forced by a wider pattern.** The sentence above that §156 found exactly one code site is
wrong, and it was wrong because that census searched one spelling of a path separator. Re-measured at the
revision this entry was committed as, with a pattern tolerating both separators, the account path appears in 6
tracked files: three code and three prose. The three code sites are archived witness scripts under
`data/seed/falsifier_witnesses/` — a sweep plant and two drivers, each opening its own result file at a Temp
path under one account — and they are named by 17 rows of the falsifier registry, so they are live witnesses
rather than dead artifacts. They were not touched here, and that is a decision rather than an oversight: an
archived run's output path is part of what that run did, and editing a witness to make a census read clean is
the same mistake in a new costume. Task 101 owns the question of what should happen to them. What survives of
this entry's claim is narrower and still measured: no file under `scripts/`, no build file and no workflow
resolves a path through a user's home any more, and the one that did is fixed.

**Amendment two, same day: the sentence about concurrent runs was a hazard statement wearing a measurement's
clothes.** The paragraph above says two runs of this harness on one account "collide by name". Attacked as
claimed — eight pairs fired simultaneously, sixteen runs sharing the fixture root — it produced 0 red pairs,
0 non-zero exits and 0 missed arms, so the collision was never demonstrated and the wording is withdrawn. What
is true is narrower and read off the code rather than measured: the harness removes the whole fixture root once,
at its own start, and every arm re-creates its own directory immediately before running the checker on it, so a
second run can take a first run's fixture only inside the gap between one arm's write and that arm's subprocess —
a per-arm window, not a per-run certainty, and sixteen shared-root runs found it shut every time. Whether it can
be forced open is a question for whoever owns the next visit to this file, and the answer needs a rate from a
loop, not a single try — the standard the paragraph above now holds itself to.

## D154 — The last citation step gets an in-gate arm, and the knob that exposed a flag nobody parsed

**Context.** D152 gave gate steps 8 and 9 an env-supplied arm so a reader could see the step stop the run from
inside the gate rather than from a hand-run of a different invocation. Step 12 — `check_status_citations.mjs`,
the spelled `STATUS §NN` reader added at D144 — was the remaining citation step with no such seam: its gate
line is a bare `node scripts/check_status_citations.mjs`, and the proof it cites
(`scripts/falsify_status_citations.mjs`, 6 of 6 held at D117) runs the checker as *its own* subprocess. That
proves the reader reddens. It does not prove this step can halt this gate — the same gap D150 and D151 closed
for step 11.

**Decision.** Add `GATE_STATUS_DIR`, documented beside the other three knobs in the header, and forward it as
`${GATE_STATUS_DIR:+--dir="$GATE_STATUS_DIR"}`. Then, before claiming the arm works, run the checker by hand on
the spelling the shell makes easiest.

**What that found.** `--dir=<path>` was not parsed at all. The reader had one shape,
`const arg = (name, dflt) => { const i = process.argv.indexOf(`--${name}`); return i < 0 ? dflt : process.argv[i + 1]; }`,
so `--dir=C:\...\d154_fixture` was an argument it never looked at: the run printed
"files scanned 568 of 568 candidates under D:\获客平台" and `RESULT: PASS`, while the operator believed they were
scoring a two-file fixture. `--head-rev=435d388` was the same story. An option that fails to fail, in D96's
vocabulary — worse than a missing option, because the green line is real output from a plane nobody aimed at.
The saving grace, and the reason this was catchable at all: the reader prints which revision and which root it
scored, so the wrong plane is visible in the report rather than only inferable from a suspiciously large count.

**The fix.** Both spellings parse now, an empty value is refused, and a flag this file does not read is a
`RESULT: NOT CHECKED` with exit 2 — the file's existing refusal vocabulary, not a new one. The usage block says
so. The gate forwards the `=` form, which dogfoods the shape that used to be silently dropped.

**Measured.** (1) bare: 568 files, 11 spelled citations, 11 resolve, 31 mentions of which 15 would resolve,
exit 0. (2) `--dir <fixture>`: 2 files, one BAD plant at line 1 of the fixture (`STATUS §1700`), exit 1 — unchanged,
which is the regression half of the fix. (3) `--dir=<fixture>`: the same 2-file plane and the same exit 1, where it used to
read the repository and pass. (4) `--head-rev=435d388`: 116 headings (max §148) and 1 BAD,
`docs/DECISIONS.md:9097: STATUS §155`, exit 1. (5) `--verbose`: `unknown option --verbose — flags this reader
parses: dir, head-rev`, exit 2. (6) `scripts/falsify_status_citations.mjs` still holds 6 arms / 6 / 0, exit 0 —
it passes the space form, so no arm of D117 was ever faked by this defect; read off `falsify_status_citations.mjs:70-71`
rather than assumed.

**The in-gate half.** Two legs, back to back in about twenty minutes, on the same working tree (which holds
other lanes' uncommitted files — the comparison is between the two legs, not against a clean checkout).
Neutral, no knob: 12 step headers and 7 `RESULT: PASS` lines — step 6's truncate probe, step 9's comment census,
step 10's two-plane reader, step 11's two (anchor self-test, then the registry), step 12, and the gate's own
closing `RESULT: PASS — 216 quality checks on a from-scratch schema (tables=58, migrations=7)`; exit 0. (Steps 7
and 8 report in their own words, not with a `RESULT: PASS`, so the count is six inner plus the closing line.)
Armed, `GATE_STATUS_DIR` at the two-file fixture: the same 12 headers and the same five inner PASSes, then step
12 printing "files scanned 2 of 2 candidates under the fixture root", one BAD pointer and `RESULT: FAIL` —
exit 1, with the gate's closing PASS line printed 0 times. Both runs' databases were dropped; the four
`nexus_gate_*` names that predate this session are untouched. So the step's reachability is now shown the way
steps 8 through 11 show theirs: from inside the gate, through a variable the operator can set.

**Limits, stated.** Step 12 still scores disk files against HEAD's headings — that is §126's grammar, and it
means an untracked file from another lane citing a section only it has written reddens this gate for everyone;
that is the step's job, not a defect to smooth over. `scripts/check_ledger_sections.mjs:34` has the identical
bare-`indexOf` shape and is step 10's reader, so a hand-typed `--dir=<checkout>` there also reads the repository
and prints PASS; it is not fixed in this commit because the gate is running and must not have its checker
changed under it — the rule D153 wrote for the fixture root applies to the reader too. The wider finding, that
this repository has two flag dialects (`check_jsonb_reads.mjs:52` parses only `--quality=`) and no gate enforces
one, is #102. And the probe script written for the expansion check printed `rc=0` on the armed case: its
`|| true` clobbered `PIPESTATUS`, so that number is the probe's bug, not the checker's — case (3) above is where
exit 1 was measured.

## D155 — The flag D154 fixed was not a one-off: step 10's reader had the same blind half, and now neither does

**Context.** D154 found `check_status_citations.mjs` parsing `--dir <x>` but not `--dir=<x>`, and the search for
other copies of that shape came back with the `arg` helper in `scripts/check_ledger_sections.mjs` —
`const arg = (n, d) => { const i = process.argv.indexOf(n); return i >= 0 ? process.argv[i + 1] : d; }`, the
reader gate step 10 runs. (Its line number is not cited because this patch moved it, and a pointer that only
the pre-patch file satisfies is the kind of claim step 8 exists to catch.) It was left alone in that commit on
purpose: the gate was mid-flight and a checker must not change under the run that is certifying it. That
constraint lifted when the two legs finished.

**Measured first, on the unpatched file.** `node scripts/check_ledger_sections.mjs --dir=<fixture>` — a fixture
holding two STATUS sections and two DECISIONS entries — printed
"docs/STATUS.md HEAD 127 sections · on disk 127 · missing 0 · duplicate numbers 0" and `RESULT: PASS`, exit 0.
That is the repository being censused while the operator reads a fixture's result. The same fixture through the
spelling the file does parse (`--dir <fixture>`) prints "on disk 2 · missing 127" and `RESULT: FAIL`, exit 1.
The equals form was not a rarer typo either: `check_jsonb_reads.mjs` documents only `--quality=<x>`, so both
dialects are live in one gate, and `--report` — a real flag of steps 7 and 8 — was silently accepted here too.

**Fix.** Same shape as D154: both spellings parse, an empty value is refused, and a flag this reader does not
know is a `RESULT: NOT CHECKED` exit 2 rather than a silence. One helper now, defined above its first use, which
removed a duplicate `notChecked` definition that the patch would otherwise have had to shadow.

**Measured after.** Bare: HEAD 127 · disk 127 · PASS · exit 0. `--dir <fixture>`: missing 127 · FAIL · exit 1
(unchanged — the regression half). `--dir=<fixture>`: the same fixture plane, missing 127 · FAIL · exit 1.
`--report`: `unknown option --report — flags this reader parses: --head-rev, --dir` · exit 2. `--dir=`: `--dir=
was given no value` · exit 2. Its harness `scripts/falsify_ledger_sections.mjs` still holds 8 arms / 8 / 0
missed, exit 0, and it passes the space form, so — as with D117's arms — no existing arm was faked by this.

**What is left of #102.** The dialect itself is still a convention, not a gate: nothing reddens a checker that
accepts only one spelling, and `check_contract_drift.mjs:29` and the `verify_*.mjs` readers parse only the bare
form. The rule this lane now follows when writing a checker is in both files' usage blocks; promoting it to a
gate needs a shared argument parser, which is a larger seam than a two-line fix and is not invented here.
## D156 — Step 7's `--quality` seam really does reach the site census, so the step got the arm steps 8-12 already had

**Context.** `scripts/check_jsonb_reads.mjs` has carried `--quality=<path>` since D87 with the sentence "Nothing
in the gate itself passes the flag", and that sentence was true: steps 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12 each got an in-gate
knob in D150-D154 so that a witness no longer has to be a hand-run of an invocation nobody else makes, and step
7 was the last census step still in that position. Before giving it one, the claim had to be executed — the seam
might have reached only the declared-reads half, leaving the `site` column (the thing D87 added, and the thing
D86 shipped three false instances of) unverifiable through it.

**Measured first, and the first measurement measured nothing.** The initial probe replaced six occurrences of one
citation in a Temp copy of `data/seed/quality.sql` and passed that copy through the seam: `ANSWER SITES` printed
22 rows / 31 locations / 12 files / 38 lines before and after, with exit 0. The reason is not a hole in
the seam, it is where the census looks: the site reader walks only the rows inside the two
`INSERT INTO read_answer VALUES` / `INSERT INTO shape_answer VALUES` blocks, and five of the six occurrences were
comment lines while the sixth sat in a tuple of a third table. Re-aimed at a row the census does parse, four
plants each reddened the run and an unmutated copy through the same flag left every number where the tracked file
put it — which is what makes the four plants evidence rather than a coincidence of counts.

**The two fixes.** (1) The reader parsed one spelling: `--quality=<path>` only, via a `find` on the `=` prefix, so
`--quality <path>` was silently ignored and the run censused the tracked file and printed a PASS — D154's defect
in a fourth reader, and the third inside this gate. Both spellings now parse, an empty value is refused, and an
unknown flag is a `RESULT: NOT CHECKED` exit 2 naming the flags the file does read, which is the shape
`check_comment_citations.mjs` already had. (2) `scripts/falsify_quality_seam.mjs` — 8 of 8 arms over Temp
copies, no database, ~8s — now runs inside step 7, and `GATE_QUALITY_SQL` forwards the seam into the step, inert
when unset. The knob moves only the census reader: steps 3-5 load the tracked seed file, so an armed leg is a red
on the text plane while the dataset stays the shipped one.

**Measured after.** `scripts/falsify_quality_seam.mjs`: 8 arms / 8 held / exit 0, and its control arm pins
the tracked plane's own numbers (22 rows citing 31 locations in 12 files, 38 distinct lines, 41 spans
across 31 tokens) so a plant's delta is a prediction, not a recollection. On the pre-patch checker at HEAD,
over a Temp copy: the space spelling of the same plant exited 0 with the tracked numbers (38 lines), the equals
spelling exited 1 with `FALSE SITES (1)` and one line fewer — the defect and its fix measured on one invocation.
`--qualit=<plant>` on the pre-patch file printed the whole report and exited 0; on the patched file it exits 2.

**GATE_LEG_TOKENS**

**Two legs, one working tree.** Neutral (`GATE_QUALITY_SQL` unset): 12 step headers, 8 `RESULT: PASS`
lines including the closing one, exit 0 — with step 7's seam harness reporting 8 of 8 arms held
while the census itself stayed green. Armed (the same variable set to a Temp copy whose cited line runs past the
end of the source file): step 7's census printed `FALSE SITES (1)` — `the file has 453 lines` — and
37 distinct lines instead of 38, the drive stopped after 7 of 12 step headers, exit 1. The
harness still reported 8 of 8 held inside that red leg, which is the shape worth having: the step that
proves the guard reachable is not the step being reddened. One driver defect is recorded because the invocation is
part of the measurement — the first armed attempt took the plant path from `$TEMP` as the shell wrote it, node
resolved it against the repository's drive, and the leg died of ENOENT at step 7 rather than of a false site; leg
2b re-ran the same plant with the spelling node reads.

**What is left.** The step's arm now covers the census half of the seed answers; the payload-shape answers that
D86 filed live in the same file's other blocks, and #102 keeps the dialect's remaining half: step 8's reader
`check_ledger_citations.mjs` is the fourth instance of the equals-only shape — measured for the first time here,
`--text=<fixture>` printed 1 heading and `FALSE LEDGER CITATIONS (1)` · exit 1 while `--text <fixture>` printed
295 headings of the real ledgers and exit 0 — and three readers take the space form only, because they find
`--name` with `indexOf` and fall back to a default when the value is glued on (`verify_contract_runtime.mjs`,
`verify_served_reads.mjs`, and step 11's `check_falsifier_registry.mjs`, which is another lane's file and is
reported rather than edited here). The real fix is one shared parser, not a fifth two-line patch.

## D157 — Step 8's `--text` seam was claimed by D152 and never tested: the space spelling censused the two real ledgers and exited 0

CONTEXT. D152 gave gate step 8 the `GATE_LEDGER_TEXT` knob and recorded that it "aims the step at one file
instead of the two ledgers". D156 gave step 7 the same shape and, unlike D152, put a harness inside the gate so
the claim is re-asked on every run instead of trusted. Step 8 had no harness: the paragraph was the evidence.
Reading the reader in order to write one found the same class of defect, on the half of the sentence D156 had
just fixed.

MEASURED FIRST, ON THE BYTES AT HEAD (which equalled the working copy for this file, `cmp` before the probe).
The parser was one `process.argv.find` over a `--text=` prefix, so the two spellings of the same request were
not two ways of asking the same question:

  * `--text=<plant>`, the spelling gate step 8 passes, printed `headings seen 1 section(s)`,
    `citation-shaped 1` and `FALSE LEDGER CITATIONS (1)`, and exited 1;
  * `--text <plant>`, the spelling the USAGE line invites a person to type, printed `headings seen
    297 section(s)`, `citation-shaped 377`, `every citation-shaped token resolves to one file, by name, within
    its bounds`, and exited 0. It had censused the two real ledgers.
  * `--tex=<plant>` — a mistyped flag — did exactly the same.

Every one of those lines is true about the plane it read; none of them read the plane the operator named. That
is what makes this a defect rather than a cosmetic one: a green that is a silent re-aim is indistinguishable, in
the log, from a green that is a result. The same `find` also kept the first of two `--text` arguments and let
`--text=` with nothing after the sign fall through to `join(ROOT, '')`, which exited 2 for the wrong reason
(`EISDIR` on the repository directory, not "you gave me no file").

SECOND DEFECT, SAME FILE. The four non-vacuity guards were `throw new Error`. A fixture holding no `## ` heading
— the exact case a guard exists for — printed a stack trace (which included the guard's own source line) and
exited 1, and exit 1 is this step's code for "a ledger names a file that is not there". A census that had
certified nothing was reporting a finding about the ledgers.

THE TWO FIXES. `scripts/check_ledger_citations.mjs` now takes its flags from one table and parses both
spellings of `--text`: an unknown option, a bare positional, a missing value, an empty value, a value that reads
as another flag, a switch given a value, and `--text` given twice each print `RESULT: NOT CHECKED` and exit 2 —
refused rather than dropped. The four guards refuse in that same vocabulary. The fourth guard's
`head.citations > 0` conjunct is gone, because the guard above it already exits when the citation count is 0: a
condition that can never be false is not a guard.

WHAT THE HARNESS CAUGHT WAS THIS LANE'S OWN TEXT. `scripts/falsify_ledger_text.mjs` runs inside step 8 before
the reader, over Temp fixtures, and its first draft carried a literal past-the-end example inside a comment
explaining the plant. Gate step 9, which scores source comments through step 8's own grammar sliced out of the
checker rather than copied, reddened on that line inside the minute — correctly. The number is now read out of
the checker's own length instead of written down, which also means the plant cannot drift back inside the file
it cites. D94's placeholder convention with a fresh case: a plant may hold a false citation; a comment about a
plant may not.

TWO MISSED PREDICTIONS, KEPT AS ARMS. (a) A plant whose only citation names a file the index does not hold does
not print `FILE NOT FOUND`. It exits 2 saying the census found citations and resolved none of them, because the
vacuity guard cannot tell "every cite in this file is broken" from "the index is broken", and it refuses rather
than guessing. So the `FILE NOT FOUND` arm is only observable next to a cite that resolves — the fixture now
cites `scripts/source_index.mjs:1` beside the plant, and the refusal is pinned as its own arm. (b) A cite that
names only the basename `package.json`, with a line number after it, is AMBIGUOUS: six files in this
repository hold that name, so a citation that looks precise names none of them in particular. That is a third
refusal, now reached too. The sentence is written without the citation grammar on purpose — this lane's own
first draft wrote the shape, and step 8 reddened on the ledger for describing it.

MEASURED AFTER. The harness reports 18 arms · 18 held · 0 missed, and the two spellings of the same
plant now print verdict lines that are identical, which the harness checks as text rather than as
two independent reds. On the bytes of this entry: step 8 --worktree sees 299 headings · 608
name:number tokens · 378 citation-shaped · 73 distinct files · exit 0; HEAD-strict 297 headings ·
377 citation-shaped, working copy 378 citations · 0 offenders · exit 0; step 9 74 comment-plane
citations across 21 files · exit 0; step 10 8 arms · exit 0; step 12 11 spelled citations · exit 0;
and the three sibling harnesses 0/0/0. The ledgers at HEAD hold 143 decisions and 129 sections
against 144 and 130 on disk, which is this entry and the next one being written, not a fork.

TWO LEGS, ONE WORKING TREE. Leg 1 is the full neutral gate — generate, migrate, seed and all twelve
steps — exit 0 with 12 step headers, carrying this harness's 18 arms inside step 8. Leg 2 runs with
`GATE_LEDGER_TEXT` aimed at a Temp plant whose one citation is past the end of the checker, and
exits 1 after 8 step headers, printing `FALSE LEDGER CITATIONS (1)` and naming the file, the section
and the line that wrote it — so the claim D152 made about this step is now measurable from inside
the gate, on the plane the gate runs. Leg 2 was started with --skip-generate because generation is
not the seam under test and leg 1 had re-verified it minutes earlier on the same tree; the
twelve-step header count of leg 1 is what covers generation, the seed and steps 1-7.

WHAT IS LEFT. #102's other half: two readers now parse both spellings, but they are two parsers, and only this
one refuses a value that reads as a flag; one shared argument parser, plus a gate arm that feeds every checker an
unknown flag and requires exit 2, is the real fix and will not be invented inside a two-line commit. #100 stays
report-only: CI's `required` job asserts the e2e result alone, and its census steps run through `| tee` without
`pipefail`, so a checker that exited 1 would have to be read out of the log rather than out of the job status.


## D158 — D157's shared-parser residue landed, aimed first at the two readers that talk to a live service: one character of `--tenant=` had been answering a different tenant

CONTEXT. D157 closed by naming its own residue: two readers then parsed both spellings, but they were *two
parsers*, and only one of them refused a value that reads as a flag. "One shared argument parser, plus a gate arm
that feeds every checker an unknown flag and requires exit 2, is the real fix and will not be invented inside a
two-line commit." This entry is that parser. It went into the two readers that had not been fixed at all, because
those two sit on the plane that speaks to a running service, where a silently-dropped flag does not re-aim a
census at another file — it re-aims the whole run at another tenant and another port, and the output cannot say
so.

MEASURED FIRST, AGAINST A SERVICE THIS LANE FOUND LIVE. `verify_served_reads.mjs` and
`verify_contract_runtime.mjs` looked every flag up with `argv.indexOf('--name')`, which is the spaced spelling
and nothing else:

  * `--tenant d158-not-a-tenant` → 1 check, HTTP 404, exit 1. The flag was read.
  * `--tenant=d158-not-a-tenant` → 626 checks, `RESULT: PASS`. The flag was dropped, another tenant answered
    every one of those 626 checks, and not one printed line named the tenant that had been asked for.
  * `--base http://127.0.0.1:1` → `fetch failed`, exit 1. Read.
  * `--base=http://127.0.0.1:1` → the same 626-check PASS. Dropped.
  * `--bes <url>` and `--tesnant <id>` → exit 0 with the full report printed. An option the reader does not
    implement is not a refusal here either; it is an ignore.
  * `verify_contract_runtime.mjs --base=<dead port>` printed the identical report — 123 documented, 117 served,
    6 gaps — as the run aimed at the live service, because the report describes the *contract* it reads from disk
    and the address it believed it was probing was the default one all along.

A PASS that cannot say which service answered, and which tenant it posed as, is not attributable to a plane.
Then the live service went down — it belongs to another lane — so the equivalence proof below does not rest on
`:8090`; it runs against a stub this harness owns.

THE PARSER. `scripts/cli_args.mjs` exports `parseFlags(argv, spec)` and a `flagHelp(spec)` that prints the table
rather than a hand-counted line range (D157 found a `--help` that had fallen three knobs behind its own header).
A spec declares each knob as a value or a switch, with the unit named in prose so the refusal is about the
operator's request: "was given without a path", "was given without a service URL". Both spellings of a value
knob parse; both spellings of a switch parse; and a request that cannot be aimed is refused rather than dropped —
unknown option, a switch given a value, a missing value, an empty value, a value that reads as another flag, the
same knob twice, and a bare positional are seven separate refusals. The module prints nothing and never exits:
each reader owns its own verdict vocabulary, because these files already disagree about what `RESULT: PASS` means
and a shared parser must not silently harmonise that.

THREE READERS MOVED ONTO IT. `verify_served_reads.mjs:30` and `verify_contract_runtime.mjs:37` lost their
`indexOf` helpers. `check_ledger_citations.mjs:90` — step 8's reader, whose inline table D157 wrote — lost the
table too and now imports the module. That move is only safe if the 18 arms D157 pinned still hold, and they do:
`falsify_ledger_text.mjs` runs the shipped checker as a subprocess on every arm, both spellings of the same plant
still print identical verdict lines, and all seven refusals still arrive in the wording those arms match on. The
refactor is behaviour-preserving because a harness written the day before it says so, not because the diff looked
equal.

VERDICTS NAME THE PLANE THEY MEASURED. `verify_served_reads.mjs` now ends either
`N of M served-read checks FAILED (against <base> as tenant <tenant>)` or
`RESULT: PASS — M served-read checks passed against <base> as tenant <tenant>`;
`verify_contract_runtime.mjs` prints `service answering : <base> (the document describes the build it came
from)` in its report header. Its `RESULT:` sentences are deliberately untouched — other planes quote them.

THE ARM, INSIDE THE RUNNER. `scripts/e2e_fresh.sh` gained a preflight step before container discovery, running
`scripts/falsify_flag_dialect.mjs`, and a knob `E2E_FLAG_PLANT` that aims that harness at a planted reader file —
the same shape as `GATE_LEDGER_TEXT` (D157), `GATE_QUALITY_SQL` (D156) and the rest: a seam is not wired until a
run can be shown to stop *from inside the thing that wires it*. The harness owns its stub server and its fixtures,
so the preflight costs seconds and touches no database, no Java process and no other lane's port. Its `--help`
is now derived from the header block instead of a counted `sed` range.

WHY THE READERS ARE AWAITED, NOT WAITED ON. The first draft called them with `spawnSync`, and every arm hung
until its 120-second kill. `spawnSync` parks the parent's event loop, and the parent's event loop is the thing
that answers the stub: the witness could not service the world it planted. Children are `execFile` promises now,
and the request log fills while they run.

HOW IT IS WITNESSED WITHOUT A SERVER. Every arm runs the SHIPPED reader as a subprocess against an in-process
HTTP stub on an ephemeral port; the stub logs `{host, tenant, path}`. Which plane a run touched is therefore
out-of-band evidence, not the run's own claim. One arm rebuilds the old one-dialect parser as a mutant copy of the
reader in the OS temp dir and re-runs this harness against the mutant, predicting exit 1 — and it reddens with
stub-derived reasons ("the glued spelling … the run addressed 0 host(s) and tenant(s) []", "a refused run still
sent 2 request(s) to the stub"), which is the proof that the fifteen green arms above it are measuring something.

THE CENSUS, AND ITS TWO FALSE STARTS. The last arm enumerates `scripts/*.mjs` rather than describing it. The
first version counted any file whose *text* mentioned `process.argv`, which put `cli_args.mjs` — a parser that
takes argv as a parameter, and whose header quotes the broken shape — in the population of readers. Keying on code
use fixed that; the predicate then went too far the other way and matched only `= process.argv.slice(`, so the
files that pass argv inline (`parseFlags(process.argv.slice(2), SPEC)`) vanished from the count — including two of
the three this entry moves onto the shared parser. It reported 5 readers with 1 shared, and the arm that requires
the shared-parser readers to be named reddened: the census had lost its own subjects. Comment lines are stripped
first now, then any `process.argv.` use counts. On this tree that is 11 readers · 4 on the shared parser · 7
hand-written.

MEASURED AFTER. `falsify_flag_dialect.mjs` 20 arms · 20 held · 0 missed, then twice more on the bytes of this
entry. Two legs of the runner's preflight on one working tree, both with docker kept out of the `PATH` so the run
stops at the container guard and creates nothing: neutral `NEXUS_PG_CONTAINER=nosuchcontainer` printed the
preflight, 20/20 held, `RESULT: PASS`, then the pre-existing `no running Postgres container among: …` and exit 2;
armed `E2E_FLAG_PLANT=<the temp mutant>` printed 19 arms · 7 held · 12 missed, `RESULT: FAIL`, and exited 1 after
exactly one step header — before any container is opened. The gate plane re-certified on these bytes: step 8
HEAD-strict 299 headings · 608 name:number tokens · 378 citation-shaped · 73 distinct files, working copy 388
citations in 301 sections · 0 offenders · exit 0, and the same reader on the working tree 301 headings · 622
tokens · exit 0; step 9 80 comment-plane citations across 22 files · exit 0; step 10 HEAD 144 decisions and 130
STATUS sections against 145 and 131 on disk, missing 0 · duplicates 0 · uncommitted 1 each, which is this entry
and its neighbour; step 12 11 spelled citations · 11 resolve, against 130 headings at HEAD with max §162; and the
four sibling falsifiers 18 · 8 · 8 · 6 arms, all held. The full neutral gate ran on these bytes to their final
shape: generate, migrate, seed and all twelve steps, exit 0, 12 step headers, `216 quality checks on a
from-scratch schema (tables=58, migrations=7)`, carrying step 7's 8 arms, step 8's 18 and step 11's registry
reconciliation inside it, and closing with the databases dropped.

WHAT IS LEFT, AND WHY IT IS NOT QUIETLY NARROWED. Seven readers still hand-write their argument handling, and
they are not one problem. Four accept both spellings from their own tables and are pinned by their own harnesses
(`check_jsonb_reads.mjs`, `check_comment_citations.mjs`, `check_ledger_sections.mjs`, `check_status_citations.mjs`)
— migrating them is a behaviour-preserving change each harness can prove, and it is the next unit, not this one.
Two decide behaviour by presence alone (`check_contract_drift.mjs:29` reads `argv.includes('--report')`, and
the untracked `verify_payload_conformance.mjs` in this working copy keeps a `Set` of `--report` and `--json`),
so `--report=1` is not "report mode with a value" but a token nothing matches. In the drift checker that
switch is the difference between a report and a failed build — its line 248 exits 1 only when `reportOnly` is
false — so a caller who typed the glued form asked for tolerance and would have got a red. That is the
opposite direction from a false green, and it is why the finding is filed as a severity defect rather than a
truthfulness one. Measured on this tree the two spellings are INDISTINGUISHABLE: the drift set is empty, both
printed the same 5-line report and both exited 0. So what is on offer is a hazard read off the code plus the
one plane where it cannot yet show, not a demonstration — answering it needs a planted drift row and a rate. One
reader takes a value in the spaced form only, `check_falsifier_registry.mjs:38`, gate step 11's reader — another
lane's file, so it is reported, not edited.
And #100 stays open for the same reason as before: CI's `required` job asserts only the e2e result, and its census
steps run through `| tee` without `pipefail`.

## D159 — Step 9 got the arm its four siblings already had, and the last four both-dialect readers moved onto the shared parser: a swallowed flag is a refusal, not a stack trace

**What was measured before any of it moved.** Four checkers each read their own argv, and each one's
failure had a different shape, which is what a shared parser is for:

* `node scripts/check_jsonb_reads.mjs --quality --report` died with `path: 'D:\获客平台\--report'` and
  exited 1 — and in that file exit 1 means "a site is false", so a mistyped request printed the verdict
  of a check that never ran. `check_comment_citations.mjs --plane --verbose` had the identical shape at
  the identical exit code, with `--verbose` taken for a directory name.
* `--report=1` and `--verbose=1` each exited 0 with output byte-identical to a bare run of 25 lines; a
  real `--verbose` prints 46. A glued value was not "the switch with a value", it was a token nothing
  matched, so the run answered a different question than the one asked.
* `check_status_citations.mjs` and `check_ledger_sections.mjs` already refused all seven cases (D154 and
  D155 fixed their dialect) but each in its own sentence, and one of them named its flags bare —
  `dir, head-rev` — while the other dashed them. An operator reading a refusal learned one of two
  formats depending on which step reddened.

**What landed.** Those four readers now call `parseFlags(argv, spec)` from `scripts/cli_args.mjs`, which
accepts both spellings of every knob and refuses seven shapes: unknown option, a switch given a value, a
missing value, an empty value, a value that reads as another flag, the same knob twice, a bare
positional. What stays per-file is the verdict: each reader owns its own `RESULT:` vocabulary and its own
exit codes (0 green · 1 a red verdict · 2 NOT CHECKED), because a shared parser that harmonised those
silently would be a worse defect than the one it fixed. `check_comment_citations.mjs` needed its refusal
helper moved above the parse so the sentence is printed in that file's voice, and it stopped reading argv
a second time for the switch it had already parsed.

**Step 9's arm, which had never existed.** `scripts/falsify_comment_plane.mjs` — 13 arms, all held — now
runs inside gate step 9 before the reader does, forwarding `GATE_COMMENT_PLANE` the way steps 7, 8, 10, 11
and 12 forward theirs. Its past-EOF line is derived from the cited file's own length at run time rather
than written down, so it cannot rot into a green that means "no offence". Two of its arms read the gate
text and the gate's own `--help`, which is what makes unwiring the step red without touching a database.

**A missed prediction, and the two-layer hole behind it.** The arm expecting an unresolvable file to print
`FILE NOT FOUND` at exit 1 got exit 2 and no explanation. Reading it rather than retrying it found two
causes stacked: step 8 refuses a census in which `0 file(s) resolved` — its own non-vacuity guard, already
pinned elsewhere — and step 9 filtered the child's output through a word list that dropped the line saying
so. The filter now passes `NOT CHECKED` and `RESULT:` through, and the arm became two: an all-phantom
plane that must exit 2 with its reason visible, and a mixed plane of one resolvable citation plus one
phantom that must exit 1 and report `tokens found 2 in 1 file(s)`. A green run had been swallowing a
child's refusal for as long as the filter existed.

**My own patch produced the class this unit exists to close.** The first control run of the migrated
`check_status_citations.mjs` died with `ReferenceError: parseFlags is not defined` at exit 1 — a crash
where a refusal belongs, in the file that carries a comment explaining that a crash is not a refusal. The
import was simply missing; that file's control arm caught it before anything downstream was believed.

**A citation this patch broke, and the step that could not see it.** `check_ledger_citations.mjs`'s D157
note named `check_comment_citations.mjs:135` as the site that passes `--text=` to step 8; the parse
migration moved that statement to `check_comment_citations.mjs:142`. Step 8 kept resolving the old number,
because it checks that a named file has the cited line and not that the line says what the sentence claims
— its own documented blind spot, demonstrated by its own author's edit. Repaired here. Three committed
rows name lines this change moved, and they stay as history corrected by this paragraph rather than
rewritten: `check_comment_citations.mjs:35` was the `--plane` accept site and is a blank line at HEAD (the accept
sits at `check_comment_citations.mjs:44` and `check_comment_citations.mjs:51`); `check_ledger_sections.mjs:34`
named the line beside a bare-`indexOf` parse that no longer exists in that file; and the two
`check_jsonb_reads.mjs:311` rows were already 32 lines off at HEAD, where the JSDoc grammar examples they
refer to sit at `check_jsonb_reads.mjs:343` — `check_jsonb_reads.mjs:338` in the working copy.

**Measured on the bytes this entry describes.** Two legs of the fresh-database gate: neutral rc=0 with 12
step headers and `216 quality checks on a from-scratch schema (tables=58, migrations=7)`; armed rc=1,
stopped after 9 headers, step 9 censusing a 2-token plant outside the repository and reporting one PAST EOF
offence against a file of 86 lines. Both run databases were dropped; the two product databases and the four

quality seam 8 of 8, ledger text 18 of 18, comment plane 13 of 13, ledger sections 8 of 8, status
citations 6 of 6. The readers after the citation repair: 622 citation-shaped tokens over 301 sections with
0 offenders, 80 comment-plane citations across 22 files, HEAD 145 decisions against 145 on disk with
missing 0 and duplicates 0, and every spelled section citation resolving. Both spellings reach one plane,
printed rather than claimed: step 9's reader at a non-repository directory returned byte-identical output
at rc=2 either way, and step 10's reader returned byte-identical output at rc=0 either way.

**The population, printed not guessed.** 11 files in `scripts/` use `process.argv` in code: 8 on the
shared parser, 3 still hand-written — `check_contract_drift.mjs` deciding by presence alone,
`check_falsifier_registry.mjs:38` taking a value in the spaced form only, and the untracked
`verify_payload_conformance.mjs`. D158 left that split at 4 shared, 7 hand-written.

**Limits, stated.** This unit witnesses four readers and one gate seam. The drift checker's glued-value

## D160 — The blank line a citation lands on: measured the content predicate this arc kept hinting at, shipped the half that has signal, and refused the half that does not

**The question, asked with numbers instead of adjectives.** Step 8 checks that a cited file has the cited
line. It has never checked what that line holds, and D159 gave two reasons to suspect the gap is paid for: a
note inside `check_ledger_citations.mjs` pointed at `check_comment_citations.mjs:135` while the statement it
describes had moved to `check_comment_citations.mjs:142`, and three older rows name lines that moved years
of edits ago. So the pre-measurement asked, for every citation in the two ledgers that resolves to a real
file and a real line, whether the identifier the citing sentence backticks actually appears on that line.

**It does not, often enough to be useless as a gate.** Of 64 citations whose sentence names a backticked
identifier, the identifier sits on the cited line 18 times, within three lines of it 21 times, anywhere in
the file 43 times. A predicate with 18 hits and 46 misses over a population nobody disputes would spend its
first run drowning two real findings under four dozen sentences that mean "the code around here". The
reason is structural, not sloppy authorship: a ledger row cites a *region* — a SQL string literal, the body
of a function, a line inside the sentence's paragraph — and the sentence's noun names the thing the region
does. `check_jsonb_reads.mjs:311` is the same defect in miniature that D87 named for answer sites, and the
fix for that one was a per-kind predicate, not a stricter global one. So the content check is refused here,
in writing, with its measurements, rather than shipped as noise and renamed a guard later.

**What does have signal: the line is empty.** Of 149 resolvable citations, exactly 6 land on a blank line,
and a citation to a blank line cannot be what its sentence says it is — there is nothing there to hold a
claim. They are not one cause but three:

* `docs/DATABASE.md:88` from two rows (`docs/DECISIONS.md:5170` and `docs/DECISIONS.md:5230`) — that file is
  dirty in this working copy with another lane's uncommitted 10-line append, which moved the line under the
  citation. Reported, not edited: the row is mine to note and the file is not mine to touch.
* the cite of `scripts/db_gate_fresh.sh` at line 144, from two rows (`docs/DECISIONS.md:5415` and `docs/STATUS.md:4647`) — D159's
  step 9 wiring added 8 lines above that number, so this lane's own change is what blanked it.
* `scripts/check_ledger_sections.mjs:34` from two rows (`docs/DECISIONS.md:9352` and the D159 row that
  corrects it, `docs/DECISIONS.md:9698`) — the parse migration deleted a line there, and the correcting
  sentence inherited the staleness of the statement it was writing off. That is the second time this arc has
  found its own record drift while describing a drift, which is the argument for a class of check rather than
  a one-off repair.

**Why the class is not armed as a refusal today.** A `BLANK LINE` offender would red the gate on six rows,
four of which sit in committed history that this project's rules forbid rewriting — the correction channel is
an append, and an append does not move the number the old row printed. So arming the predicate needs a
stale-row policy first, and a hand-typed allowlist of `file:line` pairs is the shape this repo has already
rejected: an exemption keyed on a line number is an exemption that expires on the next edit, silently. The
predicate therefore ships as a measurement with a re-measure command, not as a verdict, and the follow-up is
filed with its design constraint spelled out: count blanks in the plane a run is *writing* (the `--text`
mode the harnesses already use), where every row is new, rather than in the plane it is *reading*.

**Measured on the bytes this entry describes.** Readers before the append: step 8 resolved 635
citation-shaped tokens over 303 sections with 0 offenders and 401 working-copy citations; step 9 printed 80
comment-plane citations across 22 files; step 10 printed HEAD 146 decisions and 132 STATUS sections against
disk 146 and 132, missing 0, uncommitted 0, duplicates 0; step 12 resolved every spelled section citation.
The two gate legs of D159 are unchanged by this entry, which adds prose to the two ledgers and touches no
reader, no harness and no gate step.

**Limits, stated.** The probe's population is its own definition: 149 resolvable citations here against 200
in the first pass, because the first pass counted tokens whose line number runs past the end of the file and
this one does not — the 51-token difference is the past-EOF and unresolvable-name class step 8 already
scores, not a hidden set. The blank-line census reads the working copy, so another lane's uncommitted append
can change it between two runs of this same script; every figure above names the tree it was taken from.

## D161 — The blank-line class is armed where a row is new, and the first thing it caught was a false citation in the file that hosts the convention against false citations

**The predicate.** Step 8 has scored `FILE NOT FOUND`, `AMBIGUOUS`, `BACKWARDS`, `ZERO` and `PAST EOF` since
D88, and every one of them asks a question of the *name*, never of the line. D160 measured the gap and found
one class inside it with signal: a citation whose span starts on a line holding nothing. That is now an
offender kind, `BLANK LINE`, with the detail line naming the emptiness rather than the expected content — the
reader already knows what it meant, and this checker has never claimed to know what a line should say.

**Where it judges, and why that is not a loophole.** The class offends in `--text` mode and is counted-only on
the reading plane, and the split was chosen from D160's own numbers: the ledgers hold 14 span starts on blank
lines today, and a committed row can only be corrected by appending, which leaves the old number standing. The
plane where every row is new by construction is `--text` — what the falsifier plants use, and what gate step 9
funnels the whole comment plane through. So the comment plane is judged from this commit forward and the ledger
plane is not, which is the asymmetry D160 said the design needed; the backlog to close it is #108, and the
count is printed on the reading plane every run so the exemption cannot be forgotten.

**What it caught first was in `scripts/check_ledger_citations.mjs` itself.** Step 9 went red the moment the
class was armed: one comment-plane citation landing on an empty line, attributed to the census file's own
section. The site was this checker's header comment, listing example cites of the shapes it accepts — written
with real line numbers rather than under the placeholder convention D94 established for exactly that mistake,
which is "an example of the grammar written inside the sentence explaining the grammar". One of the two
examples pointed at a blank line, and the blank line was blank at HEAD too, so this was not another lane's
drift: it was a false claim in a source comment that had been passing because nothing had ever asked what the
cited line contains. The examples are now written the way D94 prescribes, which takes the comment plane from 80
citations to 78 and the blank count on that plane to zero.

**Armed from both ends.** `scripts/falsify_ledger_text.mjs` grew two arms and holds 20 of 20. The red arm
plants two citations, one onto a blank line and one onto a line of text in the same file, and requires exit 1
with `BLANK LINE (1)` naming the blank one — so the arm cannot pass by flagging both, and cannot pass by
flagging neither. The line numbers are derived from the cited file at run time, the way D157's past-EOF number
is, because a fixture written with a hand-counted line number proves the checker is reading a stale file rather
than reading correctly. The green arm runs the real ledgers and requires the count to print with no offence,
which is the sentence that stops someone from quietly turning the exemption into an amnesty: it can only stay
green while the count is reported.

**Measured on the bytes this entry describes.** Reading plane: 650 citation-shaped tokens over 305 sections,
416 working-copy citations, 0 offenders, 14 blank starts counted. Comment plane: 78 citations across 22 files,
0 blank, `RESULT: PASS`. Steps 10 and 12 PASS. Sibling harnesses on the same bytes: flag dialect 20 of 20,
quality seam 8 of 8, ledger sections 8 of 8, status citations 6 of 6, comment plane 13 of 13.

**Limits, stated.** The predicate asks only whether the span's first line is empty, so a citation onto a line
of `}` or a stray `else` still passes — this closes "nothing is there", not "what is there is wrong". The
counted-but-not-judged split means a fresh false citation can still be written into either ledger and stay
unpunished until #108 lands, and #108 has to answer the self-reference D160 documented first: this census's
population includes the sentences written about it.

## D162 — The blank-line class now judges the sections a run is writing, and the append that shipped the rule is the thing that proved it can redden

**The rule.** Step 8's `BLANK LINE` class offends under `--text` (D161) and, from here, on the reading plane
too — but only inside a section that does not exist at HEAD. That subset is derived from the two planes the
census already reads, so it is not an allow list and cannot go stale the way one would: the committed headings
are the ones `git show` prints, and a `## ` heading on disk that is absent from them is, by construction,
being written now. The 14 span starts D161 counted all live inside committed sections, which is exactly why
arming them there would have been an amnesty dressed as a check, and why the count stays printed on every run.

**It has teeth.** A judged blank now affects the exit code, printed under its own heading
(`FALSE LEDGER CITATIONS — BLANK LINE IN A NEW SECTION`) rather than folded into the strict HEAD list, because
the two planes mean different things: one is "what the ledgers claim today", the other "what this paragraph
claims, before anyone has reviewed it". The other working-copy offenders keep their old non-strict status and
say so in a paragraph that now names the exception instead of covering it up. Two details that only matter when
they go wrong: the text before the first heading is registered as a title in both planes, so a preamble cannot
read as "new" on the disk side alone; and `--worktree` remains counted-only, which is what its own arm pins.

**The red side was demonstrated by this entry's own first draft.** It cited line 88 of docs/DATABASE.md in prose, on purpose as a live citation, and
that line is blank on both planes (D160's list), inside a section that exists only on disk. Step 8 exited 1
naming this section, the line, and the file — the first time in this arc that the record's own draft was
stopped by the reader the record is about. The committed version of this paragraph carries that citation in
the placeholder form D94 prescribes, so what is on offer here is one observed event described in prose, not a
re-runnable arm: reaching the same red from a harness needs step 8 to grow the `--dir`/`--head-rev` pair that
steps 10 and 12 already have, and that is #110.

**Arms, and what they pin.** `scripts/falsify_ledger_text.mjs` holds 21 of 21. The old reading-plane arm became
two: `--worktree` must print the counted-only half and no verdict; the default plane must print both halves —
the committed count, and the new-section count with the sentence saying a blank there offends — and exit 0
while it holds none. A `--text` plant still reddens on one blank cite out of two, with the numbers derived from
the cited file at run time. The wording the arms match is now load-bearing in a new way: the printed halves are
the only visible sign that a limit exists, so renaming them reddens this harness, which is the point of pinning
a sentence rather than a count.

**Measured on the bytes this entry describes.** Default plane at the moment of the red demonstration: 14 blank
starts inside committed sections, counted; 1 inside a new section, judged, exit 1. After the placeholder repair:
14 counted, 0 judged, 0 offenders over 416 working-copy citations in 309 sections, exit 0. Comment plane: 78 citations
across 22 files, PASS. Steps 10 and 12 PASS. Sibling harnesses 13 · 20 · 8 · 8 · 6 arms, all held.

**Limits, stated.** An append *into* an existing committed section is still unjudged by this rule — the
pattern this ledger almost never uses (an entry is a new `## ` heading), but nothing here proves that claim
except D160/D161's own history, so treat it as measured-by-example. A new section written by another lane in
a shared working tree reddens this gate for everyone; step 12 has carried that bargain in writing since D154
and this checker now carries it too. A citation onto `}` or a lone `else` still passes, since the predicate
reads emptiness and not correctness — D160's refused anchor-on-line predicate (18 hits in 64) stays refused.
And the exemption this unit shrinks is not gone: the 14 committed blanks remain, each needing an appending row
that names it, which is what a later unit can spend its turns on instead of adding another predicate.

## D163 — Step 8's two planes became addressable, which is what turns D162's one-off red into an arm that can be re-run, and the mutant says so

**The seam.** `scripts/check_ledger_citations.mjs` now takes `--dir <checkout>` for the plane it reads as the
working copy and `--head-dir <checkout>` for the plane it reads as committed, both as ordinary files instead of
`git show`. That is all of it: the source index and the cited files stay in the repository the script is
installed in, because the thing a fixture claims about is real code (`scripts/cli_args.mjs` and its line
numbers), and a witness that moved the cited world too would be reading its own invention. Both spellings parse
through the shared parser, an empty value is refused naming its unit, and a value that reads as another flag is
refused rather than guessed — which is the same defect class D154 through D159 kept finding in other readers,
now closed here before this file ever had a hand-written argument loop to grow.

**Why it needed to exist.** D162 armed the blank-line class for "a section this run is writing" and could only
report one observed red: this lane's own ledger draft cited a blank line and step 8 stopped it. A rule whose red
side has been seen once, in prose, is a rule nobody downstream can re-check — and the next person to edit the
predicate has no test that fails. Four arms now cover the seam: the red (a head plane with one section, a disk
plane adding a second that cites a blank line, requiring the offence to be attributed to the new section and the
run to exit 1), the control (the same head plane for both, green, which is what makes the claim about *newness*
rather than about fixtures), and the two refusals. `scripts/falsify_ledger_text.mjs` holds 25 of 25.

**The mutant, which is the part that says the arms are about the rule.** A Temp copy of the shipped reader with
one predicate replaced by D162's — blanks judged only where `--text` was given — was run on the red arm's own
command. It prints `0 blank(s) among 1 section(s) this run is writing, and a blank there offends` and exits 0:
it still sees that the section is new, and refuses to judge it, which is exactly the difference the arm exists
to catch. The shipped reader on the same command exits 1 and names the section. Two notes on how that was
measured, because the first attempt got both wrong: the copy has to live inside `scripts/`, since the reader
imports its siblings by relative path and a copy in a temp directory dies of `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` at exit 1 — a
red from a crash, which is evidence about nothing; and this harness takes no `--reader` argument, so
`node scripts/falsify_ledger_text.mjs --reader=<copy>` ran the SHIPPED checker and reported 25 of 25 held
against a mutant it never touched. That flag is not a seam, it is an ignored word, and the fact that it looked
like a result is the defect D154 through D159 have been closing one reader at a time. Giving this harness a
real reader seam is #112.

**A numbering finding, because it nearly became a false statement in this record.** While choosing a blank line
for the plant, a python probe reported a line in `check_jsonb_reads.mjs` as empty and the checker disagreed —
`str.splitlines()` cuts on form-feed and a handful of other separators that the census's own splitter
(`/\r?\n/`) does not, so the two disagree on any file carrying one. The plant's number was derived from the
shipped file with the checker's splitter after that, and every blank number in this lane's harnesses is derived
that way. The general form is a question this lane has not answered yet: `.sh` files here are CRLF and `.mjs`
files are LF, and a lone CR would shift a python-side line number out from under any cite a script files — so
the next reader that counts lines should say which splitter it used, and a census that mixes languages should
re-derive through the shipped reader rather than trusting a hand count from another runtime.

**Measured on the bytes this entry describes.** Default plane unchanged: 650 citation-shaped tokens over 305
committed sections, 416 working-copy citations, 0 offenders, 14 blank starts counted and 0 judged, exit 0. The
seam's fixture: exit 1 with one offender named in the new section, exit 0 with none when no section is new.
Against the mutant copy of the reader: the same request exits 0 and counts the new section without judging it. Step 9's reader stays at 78
comment-plane citations across 22 files, PASS; step 10 reports HEAD 149 decisions and 135 STATUS sections
against the same on disk, missing 0, duplicates 0; step 12 resolves every spelled section citation. Harnesses
after the change: 25 ledger-text · 13 comment-plane · 20 flag-dialect · 8 quality-seam · 8 ledger-sections · 6
status-citations, 80 arms, none missed.

**Limits, stated.** `--dir` and `--head-dir` have no environment knob in `scripts/db_gate_fresh.sh`: the arms
run inside gate step 8 through the harness, but an operator cannot point the gate's step 8 at another checkout
the way steps 7 through 12 can point at theirs, so this seam is a witness interface, not a drive interface —
naming it as the next unit's job (#111). The committed plane is supplied as files, so there is no `--head-rev`
spelling here and a fixture cannot ask what three revisions ago said. And the source index stays at the
repository, which means the seam cannot test index questions at all; that is deliberate, and the reason is in
the paragraph above rather than in a comment in the code.

## D164 — Step 8's two planes became drivable from the gate, its harness learned to take a reader, and the first armed attempt was caught by the guard rather than by me

**What landed, in two halves.** `scripts/db_gate_fresh.sh` forwards `GATE_LEDGER_DIR` and
`GATE_LEDGER_HEAD_DIR` into step 8, and `scripts/falsify_ledger_text.mjs` now parses `--reader` and `--help`
through the same shared parser the readers use — so a flag this harness does not read is refused at exit 2 with
the flags it does take named, instead of being ignored. D163 had made the planes addressable from the command
line, and its own record said the harness could not be aimed at a planted reader; that gap was not cosmetic.
The run that believed it had tested a mutant had tested the shipped checker and printed a green tally about a
file nobody opened.

**Step 8 keeps two branches, and the branch itself is what the arm reads.** With either knob set the step runs
in comparison mode — `--dir` and `--head-dir`, no `--worktree`; otherwise it runs the old line, which is
byte-for-byte what it was before this unit, so an unset environment reaches the reader exactly as it always
did. That separation is not decoration: `--worktree` reads one plane and calls it strict, so a run that passed
a supplied plane alongside it would compare nothing, judge nothing, and still print a verdict that looks
configured. The wiring arm now requires both branches to be present in the shipped text, together with the
harness call and all three knob forwardings, which is what makes silently unwiring one red without opening a
database.

**The drive, stopped by a plant.** With both knobs aimed at a temp fixture — a head plane holding one committed
section, a disk plane adding a second whose citation lands on a blank line — step 8 printed `FALSE LEDGER
CITATIONS — BLANK LINE IN A NEW SECTION (1)` naming the section, the line and the emptiness, and the gate came
back exit 1 after 8 headers with 3 passes before it. The run database was dropped; the four pre-existing gate
names and the two product databases were not opened. The neutral leg on the same bytes printed 12 step headers,
12 `RESULT: PASS` lines and `216 quality checks on a from-scratch schema (tables=58, migrations=7)` at exit 0.
So the state D162 reached once by accident is now reachable on demand from the script everyone runs.

**The first armed attempt failed, and the guard is what said so.** Its fixture was built by a shell here-string
whose template literals the shell had already interpolated away, so the census read a plant with no citation
tokens in it at all — and step 8 answered `RESULT: NOT CHECKED — no citation-shaped token in 0 name:number
tokens` and the gate stopped with exit 2 rather than reporting a clean sweep of a plane that held nothing. That
is the non-vacuity guard earning its keep on a drive path, at the exact moment a driver defect was on the other
side of the camera: it distinguished "the plant is empty" from "the plant is clean", which is the distinction
D79 has been enforcing since it was written. Nothing about the predicate was wrong, so nothing in this unit was
changed because of it; the fixture moved to a file written outside the shell.

**The mutant arm, and the two wrong predictions that came before it.** The arm rebuilds the reader in a temp
directory with D162's predicate — blanks judged only under `--text` — copies the two modules it imports
relatively, and runs this harness against it, predicting the child comes back red. Its first version put that
copy inside the harness's own fixture root, which every harness run clears at startup: the child deleted the
file it had been told to read and reported an `ENOENT` about its own subject. Its second version predicted the
child's seam arm would print `exit 1 expected, 0 printed`, having read the child's exit code as the reader's
verdict — but the child exits 1 because IT has a missed arm, which is a different 1 one level up. The arm now
predicts the child's own line, `MISSED … a new section citing a blank line reddens`, with the missing-heading
diagnostic and the skip notice that a planted run does not plant inside itself.

**Measured on the bytes this entry describes.** Readers before the append: 650 citation-shaped tokens over 311
committed sections, 416 working-copy citations, 0 offenders, 12 blank span starts counted on the committed plane
and 0 judged, exit 0; step 9 at 78 comment-plane citations across 22 files, PASS; step 10 at HEAD 150 decisions
and 136 STATUS sections against the same on disk, missing 0, uncommitted 0, duplicates 0; step 12 resolving

flag-dialect · 8 quality-seam · 8 ledger-sections · 6 status-citations, 82 arms, none missed. The committed
blank count is 12 where D161 and D162 recorded 14 — the ledgers are this census's own population, so a
paragraph that re-wraps a citation moves the number, which is why every figure above names its plane and its
moment.

**Limits, stated.** Giving one knob without its pair is not refused: `--dir` alone compares the supplied working
copy against the real `git HEAD`, which is a coherent question and one no arm asks yet, so either the refusal
