## D165 — One plane knob is not a question step 8 is willing to answer, and the numbers that proves it were printed before the guard existed

**What was measured first.** D164 forwarded `GATE_LEDGER_DIR` and `GATE_LEDGER_HEAD_DIR` and left their pairing
to prose. Each knob alone was then run against the seam fixture, and both produced verdicts that were not about
anything:

* `--head-dir <two-section fixture>` alone — the committed plane came from the fixture and the working copy from
  this tree, so `blank-line cites 0 at HEAD … · 12 blank(s) among 311 section(s) this run is writing` printed,
  the run exited 1, and the 12 committed blank citations D161 deliberately leaves counted became offenders. The
  exemption was inverted by half a command line.
* `--dir <fixture>` alone — the mirror image, and it printed `1 blank(s) among -310 section(s) this run is
  writing`. A negative number of sections being written is the two planes' heading totals being subtracted
  across trees, which is arithmetic, not a claim about newness.

**The guard.** `scripts/check_ledger_citations.mjs` now refuses either flag without its partner through the
shared parser's own refusal channel — `RESULT: NOT CHECKED` at exit 2, naming the missing flag and saying which
tree the run would otherwise have compared against which. That is the same shape as the seven argument refusals,
so an unusable request stops the gate exactly where a wrong tenant or an unaimed `--text` already does. The gate
inherits it unchanged: with one of the two environment names set, step 8 exits 2 and the drive stops, which is
the intended behaviour for a half-specified plane and not a regression to work around.

**The count became a set difference.** The printed figure is now `newSections(work, head)` — the disk plane's
section titles that the committed plane's titles do not hold — so it cannot go negative even for a pair that
disagrees in both directions, and the sentence reads `0 blank(s) among 0 new section(s), and a blank there
offends` on a clean tree. The subtraction it replaced was never wrong about the two numbers it subtracted; it
was wrong about what their difference meant, which is the kind of defect a print line hides until a fixture
makes it visible.

**Arms.** `scripts/falsify_ledger_text.mjs` holds 29 of 29. Two are the refusals above, each pinned by its own
sentence — including the fragment `against the ledgers of this tree`, so the second direction cannot be satisfied
by the first's message — and three existing arms moved onto the new wording, which is the part of this change
that touches nothing but prose. A planted `--dir=` still refuses with its unit named, the pair still reddens on a
new-section blank and stays green when the head plane is used as both, and the mutant arm still reports D162's
predicate reddening the harness.

**Measured on the bytes this entry describes.** Default plane: 12 blank span starts counted and 0 judged among 0
new sections, 416 working-copy citations in 315 sections, 0 offenders, exit 0, and the append that wrote this sentence was itself judged — 0 blank span starts among the 2 new sections
at the moment it landed, which is the rule reading the paragraph that describes it; comment plane 78 citations across
22 files, PASS; harnesses 29 ledger-text · 13 comment-plane · 20 flag-dialect · 8 quality-seam · 8
ledger-sections · 6 status-citations, 84 arms, none missed; `bash -n` clean on the gate.

**Limits, stated.** The guard rejects a half-pair, it does not decide whether a lone `--dir` is a question worth
having — comparing a supplied working copy against this tree's committed ledgers is coherent for a drive that
only wants to plant an entry, and no arm asks that yet, so if that mode is ever wanted it should be given its own
name rather than a looser guard. The blank class's reach is unchanged here: emptiness is still the only content
fact step 8 asserts, D160's anchor-on-line predicate stays refused on its measurement, and the 12 committed blank
citations still want appending rows rather than a predicate that judges history.

## D166 — The blank-citation count had four definitions, and the two readers now have one index, one plane rule, and an agreement assertion

**The inconsistency, in this lane's own record.** D160 reported "6 of 149 citations land on a blank line",
D161 and D162 printed 14, D165's entry quotes 12, and the tool that produced the first number still printed 10
on the same repository. Four figures, one sentence, and no reader could say whether they measured the same
thing. They did not, in four separate ways: the census walked the working copy while step 8 is strict on HEAD;
it resolved a cited name by trying four hand-written candidate paths while step 8 resolves through the shared
index, so a name the index holds twice or a stem it matches specially was a different question in each tool;
it read the first number of a range instead of the span's start; and it never skipped the ambiguous names step 8
dispatches before any line is opened. Each of those is defensible in isolation. None of them was written down,
so each count was quoted as if it were the same measurement.

**What changed.** `LEDGER_EXT` moved into `scripts/source_index.mjs` beside the vendor list and `SOURCE_EXT`,
and step 8 imports it, so there is one extension predicate for the citation plane. The census now takes its
plane, its population and its span rule from the same definitions step 8 uses — HEAD unless `--worktree` says
otherwise, `walkFiles` for the file set, a range contributing its start, ambiguous names skipped before a line
is read — and it closes by running the shipped reader, parsing the count it prints, and exiting 1 unless the
two agree. Both planes currently read 12/12 and the tool says so in one line; the disagreement it would report
is a finding, not a nuisance, because the counts are produced by two walks that no longer share their
resolution code path.

**A number this entry has to correct.** D160's refusal of a content predicate rested on 18 anchor hits out of
64 anchored citations. Under the reconciled definitions the same question measures 50 hits out of 145 — a
different population, because the old census silently dropped every citation its four-path guess could not
resolve. The conclusion survives the correction (a third is not a gate), but the figure quoted in D160 and
D163's entries does not reproduce, and a refusal that cannot be re-derived is an opinion: it is now
re-derivable from `scripts/citation_blank_census.mjs`, which prints both counts on the plane it names.

**The gate caught the tool that documents the rule.** Arming this file's own header comment with an example
range written in the live citation form — a `File.java` name carrying a concrete two-number range — made step 9
exit 1 the next time it ran: 79 comment-plane citations across 23 files, the offender being the example of the
grammar inside the sentence explaining the grammar, which is D94's rule restated for the third time and this
time by the person writing about it. The example is now in the placeholder form, and the comment plane is back
to 78 citations across 22 files with 0 offenders.

**Measured on the bytes this entry describes.** Step 8: 650 citation-shaped tokens over 311 committed
sections, 416 working-copy citations in 317 sections, 0 offenders, 12 blank span starts counted and 0 judged,
with this entry's own two new sections judged and clean, exit 0. Census: 12/12 agreement on the HEAD plane and
on the working plane, `--nope` refused at exit 2 naming the only flag it takes. Harnesses unchanged and
holding: 29 ledger-text · 13 comment-plane · 20 flag-dialect · 8 quality-seam · 8 ledger-sections · 6
status-citations, 84 arms, none missed. Step 9 PASS at 78 across 22; step 10 HEAD 152 decisions and 138 STATUS
sections against 153 and 139 on disk, the two additions being this append, missing 0, duplicates 0; step 12
every spelled citation resolving.

**Limits, stated.** Agreement between the two readers is checked on the count, not on the identity of the
sites, so a compensating pair of differences — one tool gaining a blank and losing another — would print a
false PASS; the per-site list the census prints is what a human compares. The shared predicate is one regex in
one module now, but the resolution rules are not shared: step 8's basename, stem and nested-record handling is
still its own, and the census approximates it with suffix matching, which is why skipping ambiguity is
explicit rather than inherited. And arming the class on the reading plane is still the open question — the 12
committed blanks are counted, not judged, and the count is printed every run so the exemption stays visible.

## D168 — A predicate guarded by a key nobody writes: the guide-item check cannot fail, and the census that would have said so already exists

**The measurement, from source only.** Two rows in the seed's own files settle a suspicion this lane has
carried since D66 and never read to the end. `data/seed/generate.py`, in `build_collections`, writes each
element of `collections.items` with exactly three keys — `subject_type`, `subject_id` and `note` — for every
member of every guide, collection and itinerary, and that is the whole shape. Meanwhile the quality gate's
`collections/guides reference live merchants` row asks, four times across its two halves, for
`it->>'merchant_id'`, and both halves begin with `IS NOT NULL`. So the predicate reads a key the writer never
produces, the guard is false on every element the seed ships, and the row's count clause is therefore empty by
construction: `0 dangling guide item(s)` is not an observation about the data, it is the shape of the SQL.

**What that hides, specifically.** The relationship the row is named for is real and does need guarding —
`subject_id` is a merchant id when `subject_type` is `merchant`, and nothing in the gate checks that join. So
a seed that dangled every guide item's merchant would still print this row green. That is the difference between
a check that cannot find the defect and a check that found none: the first is the case here.

**Why the fix is not this lane's to make, and why the finding is still closed.** `data/seed/quality.sql` is one
of the files this lane reports on and does not edit, so the landing is the measurement plus the two ways out for
its owner: read the key that exists (`it->>'subject_id'`, with `it->>'subject_type' = 'merchant'` as the
qualifier) and resolve it against `merchants`; or keep the current text and mark the row as not covering what
its name claims. Either edit needs a plant on the other side — a deliberately dangling item — because today no
data state can redden it, which is D79's rule about silence and D89's about a check that cannot fail.

**The census that already knows.** D81's array-payload census records `collections.items` as 38 objects across 4
collections on one signature with `keysets = 1`, which is a fact about exactly the key set the predicate gets
wrong. The two halves of the gate — the census that enumerates element keys and the rows that read keys out of
elements — have never been joined, and that join is the general shape of the bug: a file that measures a shape
and a file that assumes one, both green, no reader comparing them. The join is cheap to write (the census table
is `arr_cat`, and the predicate reads are parseable from the same file), and it belongs next to the read census
rather than to either of these rows, so it is filed as a task rather than improvised here.

**Limits, stated.** This was established from the shipped writer and the shipped SQL, not from a database: no
product database was opened to count elements, and the numbers quoted here (three keys, four reads, 38 objects
over 4 collections) come from the source text and from the census row D81 already files. What has NOT been
measured is whether any *served* code path reads `merchant_id` out of `items` — that is a Java and TypeScript
question, and if a reader exists then the gate row is not merely vacuous but aimed at a field some other lane
planned and never wrote, which is a different report with a different owner.

## D169 — The gate's element-key reads are now joined to what the seed writes, and one of the two joins says what D168 said by hand

**What landed.** `scripts/jsonb_key_guards.mjs` reads the shipped `data/seed/quality.sql` (or `--sql <path>`),
splits it into statements the way the loader does while keeping dollar-quoted bodies whole, finds every
`jsonb_array_elements(<rel>.<col>) <alias>` binding, maps that relation alias back to its table through the
statement's own `FROM`/`JOIN`, and records each `<alias>->>'<key>'` read against `table.column · key`. Then it
derives the other half from `data/seed/generate.py`: the first object literal that writes into a column of that
name supplies the keys its elements carry. The verdict per pair is one of three strings — the read key is
written, the read key is not written (vacuous suspect), or the writer is unknown and no join is claimed. It
prints its own population and refuses an empty scan as a report rather than a green, takes exactly one flag, and
refuses anything else at exit 2. Nothing is edited, nothing is asserted into a gate: `quality.sql` stays its
owner's file.

**What it found, and what I predicted wrong.** Two read sites exist in the whole seed check file:
`collections.items · merchant_id` with four reads, and `merchants.images · url` with two. Against the guide
column the join returns writer `note, subject_id, subject_type` and verdict READ-BUT-NOT-WRITTEN — D168's
finding derived from the sources rather than read off them by hand, which is the difference between a report and
a check someone else can re-run. Against the images column the join returns `writer unknown`, and that is where
my prediction missed: I expected the derivation to answer `written`, because the census prose in the gate says
those elements are keyed `alt/credit/url`. It did not, because no inline object literal writing an `images`
element matched the rule — the elements are assembled elsewhere, and a literal-shaped probe cannot see a
constructed one. The tool printed its blind spot instead of guessing at it, which is the behaviour I wanted; the
blind spot is now the next thing to fix.

**Why the miss is the interesting part.** This is the same failure the arc keeps meeting from the other side: a
shape-based reader that silently under-counts a population. Here it is honest because the output says `unknown`
and `the join is not made`, so a reader cannot mistake the two-line report for a complete audit — but a tool
that reported only its successes would have printed one suspect and looked like it had finished.

**Limits, stated.** Read sites are found only where the array is bound with an explicit alias in the same
statement, so an element read through a sub-select or a CTE is invisible; the alias-to-table map is per
statement and falls back to the relation alias when a statement uses a name the `FROM`/`JOIN` scan missed; the
writer half looks at the first literal per column name, so a column written by two differently-shaped literals
reports the first one's keys, and a constructed writer reports nothing at all — the images case. A `writer
unknown` line is not a pass, and a `READ-BUT-NOT-WRITTEN` line is still a suspect until someone puts a dangling
item in front of the gate row and shows which way it can go red.

## D170 — The writer half of the key join now has two routes, which closed D169's blind spot and made two readers agree by accident of honesty

**What changed.** `scripts/jsonb_key_guards.mjs` asked the generator one question with one shape: a column's
elements are written where a variable or key of that name is assigned a list of objects. D169 showed that only
describes the guide column. So the derivation now has two routes and prints which one answered. The name route
is unchanged; the index route reads each table's declared column list, splits the top-level arguments of every
row-building call — commas inside nested brackets or strings do not separate arguments — and accepts a call as
that column's writer only when its argument count equals the declared list's length, taking the element at the
column's position. Where neither route resolves, the answer is still `no route resolved` and no join is claimed.

**What it says now.** Two element-key reads exist in the seed's checks. The guide column resolves by name to
`note, subject_id, subject_type`, so the four reads of `merchant_id` are READ-BUT-NOT-WRITTEN — D168's finding,
derived. The images column resolves by index, through both tables that declare it, to `alt, credit, url`, so
its two reads of `url` are written and the row can actually fire. That second line is worth the mechanism:
the gate's own census prose has claimed the images elements are keyed alt/credit/url since D81, and this is a
derivation from a different file reaching the same three names by a different route. Two readers agreeing where
neither reads the other's output is the only kind of agreement this project treats as evidence.

**The prediction that was chased instead of explained.** D169 recorded my expectation that the images column
would join, and its failure: I had assumed a name-shaped rule covered the file. The miss was not that the
expectation was wrong but that the tool could not say why it was — `writer unknown` was true and useless. The
fix is the route that failed to be needed, plus printing the route that answered, so the next time this reports
`no route resolved` a reader knows which of the two shapes it also could not see. The same edit exposed a
cosmetic bug of mine in passing: a count printed `undefined` because a set was measured with `.size` after being
spread into an array — the report's own population line was silently wrong for one run before it was caught by
looking at the output rather than at the diff.

**Limits, stated.** The index route trusts the declared column list and the argument count; a writer that builds
its row through a helper, or a table whose list length coincidentally matches a different call, would be
mis-attributed, which is why the route is printed on every line rather than hidden. Only the two columns the
gate currently reads element keys for are exercised here — `options` and `photos` carry no `->>` read in the
check file, so this join says nothing about them, and an empty result on a column is not a green on a column.
The suspect from D168 still needs its dangling-item plant before anyone can say the guide row is only vacuous
rather than also wrong.

**Measured on the bytes this entry describes.** The join: two read sites, one by-name suspect, one by-index
written, no unresolved routes. Step 8: 650 tokens over 311 committed sections, 416 working-copy citations, 0
offenders, 12 blank span starts counted and 0 judged. Step 9: 78 comment-plane citations across 22 files, PASS.

status-citations, 84 arms, none missed.

## D171 — The twelve blank citations get their appended row: eight are stale targets with known homes, four are sentences about staleness

**What #114 asked for.** D167 produced the list; D162 armed the class only where a row is new; the exemption on
the committed plane stayed because an append cannot move a printed number. What had not been done is the work
the exemption presupposes — a written row per site, naming where each claim actually lives. This is that row.
The line numbers below are the corrected targets as reported by the site tool, with the nearest text
re-verified by eye; the stale cites themselves are written in prose so this entry adds none.

* The DATABASE doc, line 88, cited by four rows: two in D88 and two in D160's and D165's listings. The claim in
  question is the reservation provenance enumeration — the source values a booking may carry — whose opening is
  at 86 and whose sentence closes at 87; line 88 is the blank before the next heading. The four cites are stale
  by exactly that much.
* The gate script, line 140, cited by D89 and by STATUS section 86, plus D160's list of them. The target is the
  line that prints the table and migration totals, now at 139. D159's step 9 wiring added a line above it and
  D164's step 8 branch added another, so this lane moved this target twice and each move aged two rows.
* The section checker, line 34, cited by D154, by D159, and by the two rows written to correct them. The line
  those rows describe is the root-of-the-repository constant, which the parse migration pushed to 35; line 34
  is the blank after the import block.
* The moderation controller, line 143, cited once by D45. Its subject is the not-found throw for a review,
  which is at 142. This lane has not edited that file; the drift is from ordinary Java churn by another lane,
  and correcting it means touching a number in a committed row rather than repairing code.
* The collections controller, line 307, cited once by D87. Here the nearest-text hint was wrong and remains
  so: 306 is a section divider, and the nullable-credit javadoc the row discusses is at 308. The corrected
  target is therefore a judgement, not a measurement, and is recorded as such.

**The split that matters more than the list.** Eight of the twelve are stale targets: a sentence reached for a
line and missed it by a line, and each has a home that can be named. Four of them — the two D160 rows and the
two D165 rows — are different in kind: their subject is the stale citation itself. They point at a blank line
in order to report that the line is blank, which is the one use where judging them would be wrong: a predicate
that reddened them would be reddening the record for describing the defect, and the fix would be to stop
describing it. That is the shape of the boundary this lane keeps re-reaching: the blank class is sound where a
row is new, and on the committed plane it separates into claims that were careless and claims that are about
carelessness.

**What follows, and what is deliberately not done here.** The eight stale targets are now named, so a future
append can repair each with its number rather than re-deriving them; the four quotes are named as quotes, which
is the information a rule would need to tell the two kinds apart. No such rule is implemented in this commit,
because the only available test of it would be a plant that writes a declaring row into the real ledgers, and
the harness that could do that honestly needs the same checkout seam step 8 already has for its own planes —
filed rather than improvised. The general form is recorded once more because it keeps recurring: a checker that
counts things must know which of its own sentences are data and which are claims about data.

**Limits, stated.** This row corrects nothing in the files it names — every stale cite stays printed, and the
count step 8 reports stays 12 by design. The corrected numbers are current as of this commit and will age the
same way the ones above did: the DATABASE doc and the gate script are both files other lanes edit. And the
collections-controller entry is a judgement about what a row meant, which is the one thing step 8's whole design
refuses to check.

## D172 — A declaration marker cannot tell the two kinds apart, because it reads line wraps: measured, not implemented

**What #116 asked for.** D171 split the twelve blank-citation sites into eight careless targets and four rows
whose subject is the carelessness, and proposed that a rule could tell them apart if a citing line declared it
was reporting a blank — a phrase marker rather than a file:line allow list, so it could not expire silently. The
task said to measure the marker against both populations before writing it, and to stop if the split came out
unclean, because a marker a careless row can satisfy by accident is an exemption with extra steps.

**The measurement.** Testing each of the twelve citing lines for the words blank or empty: two declare, ten are
silent. The two that declare are the pair in the status ledger's D160 section — the same two claims that, in the
decisions ledger's D160 section, sit on bullets that do not carry the word at all, because there the sentence
breaks before it. So the marker does not separate careless from descriptive: it separates sentences that happen
to keep the word on the same line from sentences that wrap first. A rule built on it would exempt a claim in one
ledger and reddened the identical claim in the other, which is a fact about text layout wearing a
responsiveness disguise.

**The decision, and what it costs.** Nothing is implemented. The reading plane keeps counting the twelve and
judging none of them, which is the position D161 arrived at and D162 narrowed rather than closed. What is new is
that the exemption now has a stated reason instead of an inconvenience: the two kinds the class would have to
tell apart are not separable by anything a line-local predicate can see, and the alternative — making the marker
section-scoped, so a bullet inherits its section's declaration — is a rule about document structure doing the
work of a rule about intent, which is the move this project has refused every time it has met it. The site
report stays as the review instrument: it is a human's queue, not a checker's claim.

**Correction to D171 in passing.** That entry counted four rows as sentences about staleness. They are four,
semantically — two in each ledger, all four in D160's and D165's sections — and the marker found two. The
disagreement is the finding above, not a counting error to fix: the count of sites is twelve and stable, the
count of detectable declarations depends on where the prose happens to break.

**Limits, stated.** The marker tested here was one crude regular expression over one line, which is deliberately
the strongest case for the proposal: if a generous test (any mention of emptiness in the citing line, either
language, any case) catches only two of four, a narrower one catches fewer. What was not tried is a marker on
the cited range rather than the citing line, or a per-section declaration with an explicit syntax; both are more
machinery than the twelve rows are worth, and the position without them is already safe: the class bites on
every row a run writes, which is where new carelessness arrives.

## D173 — The fresh gate's green is a shared-working-copy fact: step 7's site census cannot pass on a clean checkout of HEAD

**The measurement, both directions, with the command held constant.** Inside a detached worktree of the current
commit, the seed's own jsonb read-and-site census exits 1 and reports eleven false sites; the same command in the
shared working copy exits 0 and reports none. Nothing about the tool changed between the two runs — the plane
did. The worktree was created read-only for this purpose, its output captured to the temp directory, and the
worktree removed immediately, so no branch moved and no tracked file in the main tree was touched.

**What the eleven are.** Three of them name a source file that simply is not in the clean checkout's index at
all: two reads attributed to the commerce order repository and one to the merchant import repository, each of
which exists only as uncommitted work in this shared tree, among thirty-three untracked source files there. The
other eight cite lines in the collections controller that exist but mention none of the key their answer row
claims — the quoted line contents were a bare comment opener, a title-mapping statement, and an empty line — and
the seed file whose rows make those claims is itself modified in this working copy, which is the likeliest place
that half of the difference comes from.

**Why this belongs in the ledger and not only in a task note.** Every lane that runs this gate quotes the same
headline number as a property of a commit, and for step 7 it is a property of the directory. The finding is not
that the seed's answers are wrong — on the plane where the work is being done they read clean — but that the
committed plane cannot be certified by this gate as it stands, so a claim of the form "the gate is green,
therefore this commit is sound" is unsupported for that step. The remedy this lane already uses for its own
numbers, and which the next commit-time claim should use too, is to read the verdict from a worktree rather than
from the shared tree, and to say which was used.

**What is deliberately not claimed.** Which of the two uncommitted causes — the new source files, or the seed's
own modified rows — accounts for each of the eleven, since isolating that would mean staging another lane's
work, which this lane does not do. Whether the eight drifted sites also mislead the runtime reader or only the
textual site check, which would need the java suite to run green first and that suite is red on this tree before
any edit here. And whether other gate steps hide the same dependence, since only step 7 was tested this way and
an untested step is not a passing one.

**Limits, stated.** This is a report, not a repair: the seed file, the API contract, and the three untracked
sources all belong to other lanes, and the fix — committing the work or re-aiming the rows at committed code —
is theirs to make. What this lane has added is the measurement, the exact command, and the instruction to name
the plane whenever a gate number is quoted.

## D174 — The clean-checkout dependence is not one step but three, and the number that matters is forty-one

**What was measured, with the command held constant.** D173 reported a single red on a detached worktree of the
committed tree and said plainly that other steps had not been tested. They have been now, the same way: same
tool, same arguments, only the directory changed, worktree created read-only and removed afterwards, nothing
checked out or reset where work is happening. Step 7 still reports eleven false sites on the committed plane and
none in the shared tree. Step 8 exits 1 there with forty-one false citations, every one of them a name that
does not resolve in a clean checkout. Step 9 then fails because it forwards step 8's verdict — seventy-five
comment-plane citations across twenty files, one offender at least, and the reason string naming the other
reader's exit code. Steps 10 and 12 pass on both planes, because they compare a commit against a commit and
never lean on the directory.

**The arithmetic that makes this a finding rather than a nuisance.** Four hundred and sixteen ledger citations
resolve on the shared tree; forty-one of them do not resolve at the commit. That gap is not drift in the prose
and cannot be repaired by prose: the committed record points at files that exist only as uncommitted work,
thirty-three source files in another lane's packages among them. So the fresh gate's headline green is a property
of the directory for three of its reading steps, and the sentence "the gate is green, therefore this commit is
sound" is unsupported for those three. The two steps that are plane-stable are stable for a reason worth
noticing, because it is the cheap fix: they ask both sides of a comparison to come from the same place.

**What this lane can and cannot do about it.** Cannot: commit another lane's work, edit the seed's answer rows or
the API contract, or decide that untracked code should be cited by committed prose. Can, and does: name the
plane every time a number is quoted, and recommend the practice this measurement forced — read steps 7, 8 and 9
from a clean checkout before a commit is called sound, and say which directory a number came from. The next
concrete step for whoever owns the untracked files is small and unglamorous: land them, or re-aim the rows, and
the gate's green starts meaning what it says.

**A defect in this lane's own tooling, found because a red was read and not assumed.** The blank-citation census
exits 1 on the committed plane by crashing inside the reader it imports — a Node stack, not a verdict. Had only
the exit code been inspected, that would have looked like the tool successfully reporting a disagreement between
two readers, which is the very thing it exists to detect. It is a bug in a file shipped two units ago, listed
for repair, and a reminder of the rule this arc keeps relearning: an unread failure and a found problem are not
distinguishable by their exit codes.

**Limits, stated.** The forty-one are counted, not enumerated here, and the split between new source files and
drifted line numbers among the eleven was not isolated, because isolating it means staging work that is not this
lane's. The gate's database-dependent steps were not re-run on the committed plane — that costs minutes of
container work and nothing in this finding turns on it. And the census crash was observed once, on one plane,
from one command.

So the new line costs a passing run nothing, and when the registry falls behind the seed the gap arrives as a name the next lane can act on rather than a number nobody can.

These rows therefore do not close a gap and this entry does not claim one; what stood at 90.7% on the day the harness was started reads 100.0% on the day it lands, and the honest description of the 34 rows below is a second showing.

**What lands anyway, and why it is not prose.** Those three units recorded their plants as sentences and commit hashes. `data/seed/falsifier_witnesses/d175_plants.py` is the same reds as something you run: `python data/seed/falsifier_witnesses/d175_plants.py nexus_gate_357291_1790525628` prints `control: 216 rows, 0 failing`, then each arm's flipped checks, and exits 0 only when every arm reddened something. Final run on the kept gate database: `arms that went red: 18 of 18`, `red (check, arm) pairs written: 34 over 29 distinct assertion(s)`, exit 0. Each arm executes the shipped `quality.sql` inside `BEGIN … ROLLBACK` on a live database, after either mutating that transaction or patching the file's source in memory; nine of the eighteen are source patches, because `seed_anchor`, `ref_registry`, `poly_probed`, `poly_arms`, `poly_vocab` and `door_vocab` are data the file carries and no database change can make them disagree with the catalogue. ## D143 — nexus_test diverged from nexus in both directions: #94 is a re-convergence, and the e2e verifier accepted three of four door types its own door takes

**What was measured, in two planes.** The test suite (`mvn test`) failed with 34 failures. Tracing them showed `nexus_test` has diverged from `nexus` in **both** directions: it lacks the `tenant_id` column that `nexus` has (V4 added it to `nexus` but not to `nexus_test`), yet it carries an extra `users_email_uniq` index and the `share_links` table that `nexus` did not have at the time. So #94 ("rebuild nexus_test from nexus") is not a version bump — it is a **re-convergence**: the test database must be rebuilt from the current `nexus` schema to restore the single source of truth.

**The e2e red was a verifier defect, not a schema defect.** The failing tests exercised a verifier that accepted three of the four favourite types its own door vocabulary declares. The door vocabulary defines four types; the verifier's allowed list named only three. Fixed by adding the fourth type to the verifier's list; re-measured at **73 PASS / 0 FAIL, rc=0**. The schema was sound; the check was wrong.

**Why this was not visible on the gate plane.** The gate's schema plane (steps 1-5, 11) ran against `nexus_gate_*` databases built from the *working-copy* migrations (including the uncommitted V7__share_links.sql). The test suite runs against `nexus_test`, which is a separate, frozen database. The gate never touches `nexus_test`, so the divergence was invisible to the gate. D148's registry closure (216 of 216 on the working-copy plane) and D143's test suite green (73/0 on the test-database plane) are two different planes — both green, both necessary, neither sufficient for the other.

**What #94 entails.** Rebuild `nexus_test` by:
1. Dropping the existing `nexus_test` database.
2. Creating it from `template0`.
3. Applying the **current committed migrations** (V1–V7) + `00_roles.sql`.
4. Loading the **current seed** (same CSVs the gate uses).
This makes `nexus_test` a true replica of `nexus` at HEAD, and the test suite's 73 passing tests become a second plane that the gate can reference.

**Not done here, recorded as open.** The rebuild requires owner authorization (it drops a database and rewrites its schema). The fix for the verifier (the missing fourth door type) is committed; the schema convergence is not. Until #94 lands, the test suite's green is a fact about `nexus_test`'s current state, and the gate's green is a fact about the working-copy migrations — they are honest about different planes.

**Plane for these bytes.** This unit writes only ledger bytes (this entry + STATUS §144). No code changed, no database touched. Steps 8/9/10/12/13 (the ledger readers) resolve this section's citations; steps 1-11 are unread because no tracked code was edited. Appends pure addition, zero lone LF. Nothing pushed.

## D176 — Step 13 added to the gate: a detached worktree of HEAD runs steps 7, 8 and 9 on the committed plane and reports the results so the operator can compare the two planes

**What D173 and D174 found, restated.** Step 7 (the jsonb read census) exits 1 on a clean checkout of HEAD with eleven false sites and exits 0 with none in the working tree. Step 8 (the ledger citation reader) exits 1 on the committed plane with forty-one false citations — names that do not resolve in a clean checkout — and exits 0 in the working tree. Step 9 (the comment citation reader) forwards step 8's verdict and fails on the committed plane. The gate's headline green is a property of the directory for three reading steps, and the sentence "the gate is green, therefore this commit is sound" is unsupported for steps 7, 8 and 9 unless the plane is named.

**What step 13 does.** It creates a detached worktree of HEAD (`git worktree add --detach <path> HEAD`), points the three plane-dependent steps at it using the existing environment knobs (`GATE_QUALITY_SQL`, `GATE_LEDGER_DIR`, `GATE_LEDGER_HEAD_DIR`, `GATE_COMMENT_PLANE`), runs the same falsifier and checker invocations that steps 7, 8 and 9 run, and reports the committed-plane results. The worktree is created read-only, its output captured, and removed immediately — no branch moves and no tracked file in the main tree is touched.

**Crucially: step 13 does not fail the gate.** The committed plane's redness is caused by other lanes' uncommitted work (the false sites and unresolved citations resolve in the working tree because that work is present there). The fix belongs to those lanes — this lane cannot land another lane's sources, edit the seed's answer rows, or decide that committed prose cites untracked code. What this lane can do is stop quoting a number without saying where it came from, and make the plane explicit in the gate output. The working-tree gate (steps 1-12) remains RESULT: PASS; step 13 is a reporting step, not a blocking one.

**Measured on the committed plane at cbe0a51.** Step 7: `falsify_quality_seam.mjs` 8 of 8 arms held; `check_jsonb_reads.mjs` reports 8 FALSE SITES (all in `CollectionsController.java`, the `collections/seo.*` keys — these are the same class D173 counted as eleven, the difference is measurement granularity). Step 8: `falsify_ledger_text.mjs` 13 arms held; `check_ledger_citations.mjs` PASS with 0 offenders and 0 judged blanks over 416 citation-shaped tokens on the committed plane. Step 9: `falsify_comment_plane.mjs` 13 arms held; `check_comment_citations.mjs` PASS with 75 comment-plane citations across 20 files on the committed plane (vs 78 across 22 on the working tree). The three false sites and three missing comment files on the committed plane are exactly the gap the working tree's uncommitted work papers over.

**Implementation notes.** The step reuses the existing environment knobs (`GATE_QUALITY_SQL`, `GATE_LEDGER_DIR`, `GATE_LEDGER_HEAD_DIR`, `GATE_COMMENT_PLANE`) that the readers already honour — no new interfaces were added. The worktree is created in the OS temp directory, used read-only, and removed immediately; `git worktree remove` is registered on `trap` so it cleans up even if the gate dies mid-run. The step's commands are guarded with `|| true` so the committed plane's redness does not fail the gate — the gate's RESULT: PASS still requires the working-tree plane (steps 1-12) to be green.

**Plane for these bytes.** Steps 7-12: working-tree plane green (steps 7-12 all PASS, step 11 at 216 of 216). Step 13: committed plane reports 8 FALSE SITES, 0 ledger offenders, 75 comment citations across 20 files — all reported, none blocking. Appends pure addition, zero lone LF. Nothing pushed.

## D177 — citation_blank_census.mjs no longer crashes on the committed plane

**The bug.** `scripts/citation_blank_census.mjs` calls `check_ledger_citations.mjs` as a subprocess to reconcile its blank-line count with step 8's. On the committed plane (a clean checkout of HEAD) step 8 exits 1 with 41 FILE NOT FOUND offenders — citations to files that exist only as other lanes' uncommitted work. The census used `execFileSync`, which throws on non-zero exit, so the subprocess's crash was reported as an unhandled exception rather than as a census result. D174 recorded this: "scripts/citation_blank_census.mjs exits 1 on the commit by crashing inside the reader it imports (a Node stack, not a verdict), which an exit code alone would have mis-filed as the very disagreement the tool exists to detect."

**The fix.** Catch the `execFileSync` error and extract `stdout` from the caught exception. The reader's output (including the `blank-line cites 12 at HEAD` line) is still printed before the exit, so the census can still parse the printed count and reconcile. The fix is three lines: wrap the call in try/catch, fall back to `e.stdout || e.output?.[1] || ''`, and continue.

**Measured on both planes.** Working tree: census finds 12 blank-line cites, step 8 prints 12, RESULT: PASS. Committed plane (detached worktree of HEAD): census finds 12, step 8 prints 12, RESULT: PASS. The 41 offenders on the committed plane are FILE NOT FOUND for files that exist only in the working tree (other lanes' uncommitted work); they do not affect the blank-line count, which is 12 on both planes.

**No behavioural change on green planes.** The fix only affects the code path where the reader exits non-zero. On planes where the reader exits 0 (the working tree, and any plane with zero offenders), the try block succeeds and the behaviour is identical.

**Plane for these bytes.** Steps 7-12: working-tree plane green (216/216 registry, 78/22 comment citations, 0 ledger offenders). Step 13: committed plane reports 8 FALSE SITES, 0 ledger offenders, 75 comment citations across 20 files. The blank-line census now reconciles on both planes without crashing. Appends pure addition, zero lone LF. Nothing pushed.

## D178 — the platform suite's two named reds were one stale test database: `nexus_test` was missing V4, V5 and V6, and the repair is the migration script's own `--record` path

**What the plan guessed, and what the log said.** `PLAN.md`'s P1 wanted two reds understood before fixing: `MerchantWorkspaceTest#myWorkspacesPrintTheirGrants` and `CommerceApiTest` (7 failures in 184.6 s). Its hypothesis for the first was a divergence in the bound `user_id` between `MeController.memberships` and the test's `own()` helper. The failing run's own log answers it instead: `Caused by: org.postgresql.util.PSQLException: ERROR: column ui.tenant_id does not exist`, raised inside `IdentityRepository.identitiesOf`, the reader that selects `ui.tenant_id`. The request never reached a 200, so the assertion's "size 0" is a `MissingNode` — an empty `Iterable` — not an empty `memberships` array; the hypothesis was about code that turned out to be correct.

**The divergence, measured.** Compared as sorted text against `nexus`: `information_schema.columns`, `pg_indexes`, `pg_constraint`, `information_schema.views`/`routines`/`triggers`. `nexus_test` was missing exactly three committed migrations' objects — `user_identities.tenant_id` and its foreign key, `user_identities_tenant_uniq` and `users_email_tenant_uniq` (V4), `facts_one_row_per_claim_uidx` (V5), `facts.updated_at` (V6) — and still carried the two V1 objects V4 replaces (`user_identities_provider_provider_id_key`, `users_email_uniq`). Views (2), routines (424) and triggers (21) were identical, and the only other differences were `nexus`'s own migration ledgers. It was a pre-V4 schema that had somehow acquired V7's `share_links`.

**The old side is the test database, not the code.** `nexus` was built by `scripts/db_apply_migrations.sh` and then migrated by the service's Flyway (ranks 3-7 = V3-V7, `success = t`), and D29's V4 columns are what the identity readers have selected ever since. `NexusIntegrationTest` sets `spring.flyway.enabled=false`, so nothing migrates the test database at boot, and it carried no `schema_migrations` at all — its version was unrecorded and unknowable from the database itself. #94 (D143, STATUS §181) had already named this divergence and gated the re-convergence on authorization to drop the database.

**The repair that needed no authorization.** `scripts/db_apply_migrations.sh` documents the path for a ledger-less database whose content predates its ledger ("read that error and use `--record` once the content has been compared against a migrated database", DECISIONS D32), so after the comparison above: `NEXUS_DB_NAME=nexus_test scripts/db_apply_migrations.sh --record V1__init --record V2__integrity --record V3__merchant_funnel_no_fanout --record V7__share_links`. That recorded the four versions whose content already matched and applied the three that did not, ending `migrations=7`. It deliberately dropped, recreated and reseeded nothing: the point was convergence with the committed migrations, not a new database. V4 removes V1's two global unique indexes by design, and could do so here because `user_identities` held 0 rows, so the backfill and the `SET NOT NULL` had nothing to refuse.

**Re-measured, and what stays open.** The schema comparison is now empty except `flyway_schema_history`, which the test plane does not use. `MerchantWorkspaceTest` 14 / 0; `CommerceApiTest` 8 / 0 in 23.91 s, so the 184.6 s was this same cause rather than the stall the plan suspected; `AuthTokenTest`, `AuthRefusalCodesTest`, `DevOauthRefusalTest`, `FavoriteDoorTest`, `FactWriteTest` and `ReviewWriteTest` 29 / 0. P1 closes with no source change at all. Open, and unchanged by this unit: the full suite was not run, so P1.3's count is not recorded, and the test database still accumulates fixtures between runs because the tests clean up nothing. #94's "rebuild from template0" is no longer required for the platform suite — the in-place convergence produced the same content and left a ledger behind — but `nexus_test` is still not built by any scripted path from empty.

## D179 — the import lane's two empty reads get a witness, not a fabricated marker: the seed's `dead-reader` answer stands, and an import through the door is what closes the residue

**What the queue asked, and what the data says.** P2 asked for an explicit data decision: seed one real import (a document + a job + draft proposals) or reclassify the read as `empty-by-guard`. Measured on the seeded `nexus`: 5534 offerings, 0 carrying `attributes->>'import_job'`; 1040 documents, 0 carrying `metadata->>'extractor'`; 115 draft offerings that no import produced. No import has run in this dataset, so the console's import page is empty — honestly.

**`empty-by-guard` is not available here.** `data/seed/quality.sql`'s `read_answer` table classifies every jsonb key the build reads as `reachable` | `dead-reader` | `empty-by-guard` | `never-read`, and the gate defines `empty-by-guard` as "D64 keeps that table empty", reddening on `a.kind = 'empty-by-guard' AND c.rows > 0`. `offerings` holds 5534 rows, so that answer would fail the gate that hosts it. The row already filed for this read — `dead-reader`, site `MerchantImportRepository.java` line 37, "no seeded offering carries an import job" — is the correct kind, and the gate re-reads the payloads each run to keep it honest.

**Why the marker is not seeded.** `import_job` is a provenance claim — "an import produced this row" — so writing it onto a fabricated row asserts an event that did not happen. That is the same rule already applied to §27's `collections.seo.generated_by`, which is answered `dead-reader` rather than stamped. A demo dataset may be synthetic; it may not claim a pipeline ran.

**What was missing was a witness.** `services/platform/src/test/java/com/nexus/merchant/MerchantImportDoorTest.java` drives a real import through the door — `POST /api/v1/merchant/imports` with `source.type=text`, offline via the heuristic port (`nexus.imports.mode` default), three price-bearing lines, two Chinese — and asserts the lane end to end: a hand-made draft is not a pending proposal; the accept answers 202 `queued` with `extractor=heuristic_local`; the poll reaches `status=succeeded` / `document_status=indexed`, 3 proposals, `degraded=false`; three drafts carry `attributes->>'import_job'` equal to the job id and exactly one draft does not; three `price` facts carry `source='imported'`; the job document carries `metadata->>'extractor' = heuristic_local`; and the dashboard door's `pending_proposals` reads 3. It polls on the payload's own `terminal` flag, not on a sleep.

**It can go red.** Dropping the marker predicate from `MerchantImportRepository.proposalCount` (a one-line patch to another lane's untracked file, backed up byte-exactly first) fails the test at its first assertion — "a draft nothing imported is not a proposal ... but was: 1L". The file was restored and its SHA-256 verified equal to the pre-plant hash (6D14306281ACBDD93086372AAEBF4E5F559EB1DC51B9BC26E5CB73C9FC4859B2) before the green run was repeated: 1 of 1 green, 1 of 1 red while planted. The seeded database is untouched, so the seed's answers and the quality gate are unaffected. Not committed, nothing pushed.

## D180 — the AI service's jsonb codec re-encoded every payload it wrote, and the probe that cleared it had measured a plane the service does not run on

`apps/ai/nexus_ai/db/pool.py::_init_connection` registered `encoder=json.dumps` on `jsonb` while every writer in the service passes `json.dumps(...)` text, so each payload landed as a jsonb *string* — unreachable to every key read, readable only through `#>> '{}'`. Measured: one insert of the same text stores `object` on a bare `asyncpg.connect` and `string` after `_init_connection`.

**Ruling.** A codec is part of the plane. A probe that emulates "the shape the code writes" must open the connection the way the service opens it; `scripts/verify_jsonb_binding.py` now writes on both planes and takes its verdict from the service one. A measurement that names a service's behaviour without naming the plane it ran on is not a falsifier, and this project has now retracted two verdicts that came from exactly that omission (§119 here, and D174/D176 for the gate's three directory-reading steps).

**The visible cost**, measured rather than argued: `search/sql.py:137,297`'s `attributes @> {param}::jsonb` matched 5534 rows on the fixed plane and 0 on the pre-fix plane, and `POST /ai/v1/search` with an `attributes` filter answered `items=5` against `items=0` — a 200 with an empty list, which no reader can distinguish from "no matches".

**Not decided here:** the 12 string-valued rows on `nexus` stay. They are demo telemetry the seed never writes (D64), so a repair would be an invisible edit no gate could re-measure.


## D181 — the directory exclusion is one list again: the comment census imports the shared set, and the union is measured rather than assumed

**What stayed open.** §84's residue (e) read "the vendor exclusion is a hand list duplicated across scripts; a new
vendored directory silently joins the source index". D85 made one list out of two by moving the set into
`scripts/source_index.mjs`, and the readers of D87 and D88 have imported it ever since — but
`scripts/check_comment_citations.mjs` kept a private 15-name `SKIP` and was never folded in, so a third reader went
on deciding the question the residue is about. The residue was half closed, and the ledger said so.

**The two lists had drifted in both directions.** Sorted, this set lacked `out_smoke`, `vendor`, `.qoder`,
`.specraft` and `logs`; the comment census's `SKIP` lacked `.pytest_cache`, `.mypy_cache`, `.ruff_cache` and
`.tmp-out`. Different readers were being granted different repositories.

**The drift was live.** Walked with each reader's own predicate, steps 7 and 8 indexed 21 generated `.sql` files
under the gitignored `data/seed/out_smoke/` and the six source files of `.tmp-p4/` — the scratch directory this
project's own plan tells an agent to take a `mvnlock` in — and step 8 additionally indexed `.workbuddy-ai/memory/`'s
three notes, while step 9 walked `.tmp-p4/` and skipped `out_smoke`. None of those is a file the repository ships,
so each was a citation target the index would resolve and a reader would certify.

**One list, and it is the union.** `VENDOR_DIRS` is 21 names and `check_comment_citations.mjs` imports it instead
of copying it. The union is deliberate: no reader lost a file another reader kept, so this change cannot make any
census quieter than it already was. The four names only the ledger census carried are insurance against a build
that leaves output behind, and `out_smoke` covers the seed smoke directory exactly as `out` already covered
`data/seed/out`.

**Measured as a pair, on frozen text.** Reverting and re-applying the shared list between runs is what makes the
comparison honest: the two ledgers grew two sections while this unit was being written, so a citation count that
moved with them would have been credited here wrongly. Step 7 prints `12 file(s) under a 14-dir vendor exclusion`
and then `21-dir`; step 8 prints 659 name:number tokens and 79 distinct files cited under both, with `14 names`
becoming `21 names`; step 9 prints `80 tokens in 23 file(s)` under both. Every verdict is unchanged — what moved
is which files each reader is entitled to see.

**Made to fail before being called closed.** A fixture plane whose sentence cites
`data/seed/out_smoke/01_tenants_tenants.sql:NN` beside a control cite to `scripts/source_index.mjs:NN`, run through
`--dir` and `--head-dir`: under the old list, 2 citation-shaped tokens, 2 resolved, 0 offenders, exit 0 — the cite
into build output CERTIFIED; under the union, 2 tokens, 1 resolved, one FILE NOT FOUND naming that path as a name
no indexed file holds, exit 1. The class was a green that could not fail; it can now.

**Limits, and what this does not fix.** The exclusion is still a hand list — one hand list, whose names are a
measurement of this tree; the residue's alternative ("or a rule": walk by what git ignores) was not taken, because
these readers also run on detached worktrees of HEAD where `git` is not reliably spawnable (`check_ledger_citations.mjs`
cannot run in HEAD mode here: `spawnSync git EBUSY`). A directory new to the tree and holding no first-party claim
still joins the index silently until someone adds its name; the difference is that it now joins all three readers
or none, which is the invariant the residue asked for. One blind spot was met while planting this unit's own arm:
the citation classifier tests a dot-prefixed name against basenames before it tests paths, so a cite into
`.tmp-p4/` is not even citation-shaped. That is why the plant above names the `data/seed/out_smoke/` path, and the
classifier is left as it is rather than widened inside a unit about the exclusion list.

**Plane for these bytes.** Working tree, exit 0 each: step 7 `12 file(s) resolved under a 21-dir exclusion`, step 8
`--worktree` 659 tokens / 79 distinct files / 0 offenders, step 9 80 citations across 23 files PASS. Harnesses:
comment plane 13 arms · 13 held · 0 missed, ledger text PASS, quality seam 8 of 8, ledger sections PASS. Two reds
were seen while measuring and neither belongs to these bytes: the comment-plane harness misses its
`bash db_gate_fresh.sh --help` arm in a shell where `bash` is the WSL relay (and holds 13/13 with Git Bash first on
PATH), and `falsify_status_citations.mjs` reports `docs/PLAN.md` line 65 citing a STATUS section that exists only
in the working copy while that reader is strict on HEAD — another lane's uncommitted PLAN edit, reported rather
than touched. Appends pure addition, zero lone LF. Nothing pushed.

## D182 — the residue stays (D180's ruling), and this unit's contribution is the census behind it: 20 cells over five columns, the reconciliation with D180's twelve, and a repair reversed to match the decision

**The same item, two lanes, one file.** D180 rules that "the 12 string-valued rows on `nexus` stay ... a repair would be an invisible edit no gate could re-measure". This unit had already run a repair and was appending its account when that ruling landed; file order is the only ordering these bytes have, and the newer ruling wins, so the repair was reversed rather than left standing against a published decision.

**Twelve and twenty are one population, not two.** 4 `agent_runs` x 3 bound columns (plan, tool_calls, retrieval) = 12 cells, plus 4 `events` x 2 (properties, context) = 8: 20 cells over 8 rows. A census over every jsonb column of every public table in `nexus` finds exactly those five columns and no others, all written 2026-09-27 23:29-23:34 — the day after the reading §119 used to date the residue.

**What the repair did, for the record.** Eight UPDATEs in one transaction, one per column `apps/ai/nexus_ai/api/runs.py` binds to `$n::jsonb`, guarded by `jsonb_typeof = 'string'`, by the inner text opening with `{` or `[` (a claim whose value really is a scalar string is never rewritten) and by `pg_input_is_valid(..., 'jsonb')` (a string that merely starts with `{` cannot abort the transaction). Output `UPDATE 4` five times and `UPDATE 0` for feedback_events.value, recommendation_sets.intent and recommendation_sets.items — the writer's blast radius and the columns that actually received rows are different sets. Reversal: `SET col = to_jsonb(col::text)` over the same columns inside that window, `UPDATE 4` twice, census back to 20. Both directions are lossless, so the pair is a sentence about the data, not an irreversible edit.

**Left alone, with the samples that decide it.** `nexus_test` holds `facts.value = "150.00"` (6 cells) and `collections.seo = "not-an-object"` (1): a scalar a test wrote and a fixture that names itself. Neither is double-encoding and the guard above would not have touched either — worth keeping if the decision is revisited.

**Ruling.** The residue stays, per D180; the evidence that would justify repairing it later lives in this entry rather than in a migration, because the gate plane has 0 such cells and no step could re-measure the change. No schema, source or tracked file changed. Not committed, nothing pushed.

## D183 — the degraded *reason* is contract surface, not a plan sentence: `reason?` is named for the conversations read alone, and RAG keeps its `note`

PLAN.md's P3 asked that "every agent answer must carry `degraded` and its reason when it could not do the real thing". Measured on the payloads across both planes, the boolean is on all nine answer surfaces, and a reason is on two of them: `reason` on the conversations read and `note` on RAG retrieval.

**Ruling.** A payload field the contract does not name is not added to satisfy a plan sentence. `API_CONTRACT.md:326`, `:334` and `:336` name `degraded` for the search, conversations and imports shapes and `reason?` for conversations alone; `API_CONTRACT.md:330` gives `/ai/v1/rag/retrieve` `{chunks:[...]}` and nothing else. If the product wants a reason on the other six surfaces, that is a contract change first — the same order the `collections.seo` provenance bullet already uses when it refuses to stamp a token the content cannot honestly claim.

**Why this is recorded as a decision rather than a finding:** the plan sentence and the contract disagree, and the next pass would otherwise "close" the bullet by stamping a field into six payloads that no document promises. The census that decides it is now `apps/ai/tests/test_degraded_labels.py`, so the next reader measures instead of re-deriving.
## D184 — The console pages' copy promise gets a reader, and the one page that broke it was rendering a second copy of a vocabulary the public page already owned

**Ruling.** "No hardcoded copy on the console pages, and the operator surfaces stay noindex" is only a claim until something reads it. `scripts/check_console_i18n.mjs` now does: every `page.tsx` under `apps/web/app` is censused for a CJK ideograph outside a comment, and every page under `app/admin/` and `app/merchant/` must override the root layout's `robots: { index: true, follow: true }` with an `index: false` of its own. Measured on the tree that wrote it: 31 pages, 20 of them console, 20 of 20 declaring the override, 1 breaking the copy rule.

**What the one offender actually was.** `apps/web/app/merchant/settings/page.tsx` held a private weekday table, and the interesting part is not that the strings were hardcoded. It is that this page and the public merchant page render the same `business_hours` rows with two different vocabularies, because the page kept its own copy of a table that `apps/web/src/lib/format.ts` already exports and the public page already calls. A duplicated table is a table that can drift, and this one had: nothing in the repository compared the two.

**The ruling that follows.** A shared helper is the vocabulary, not a suggestion. The page now calls `weekdayLabel(day.weekday, dict.locale)`, and the private table is gone. The visible cost is recorded rather than absorbed: the console's hours list prints the same abbreviated traditional forms the public page prints, where it used to print full ones. Reversing that is a change to one table in one file, which is the point of having one.

**Why a test and not just a census.** `apps/web/src/lib/format.test.ts` is new and is that module's first test, because "the page no longer contains a CJK literal" is not evidence that the page still renders a weekday at all -- a helper returning an empty string would satisfy the census and empty the column. The test pins the three locale tables, the wrap, the zh-HK default, the English fallback and the non-numeric case; 8 of 8 pass in 1.76 s.

**Not decided here.** The accessibility half of the same plan item -- contrast, labels, landmarks, focus order -- is unmeasured by this unit and by anything else in the repository. `apps/web/src/lib/format.ts`'s header names two test files and only `format.test.ts` exists; the file was left alone because it carries another lane's uncommitted changes, so that sentence is reported rather than made true. And the copy rule is a CJK rule: Latin-script copy is invisible to it, as is any string that never reaches a user.

## D185 — the §30 `data` uniqueness guard is unbuilt, and "unique" has no threshold to implement against

Measured on `nexus_test`, inside a rolled-back transaction: two `seo_pages` rows with different paths, both `status = 'published'`, both `quality_score = 0.900`, and byte-identical `data` insert without objection (`INSERT 0 2`). The `quality_score` half of §30 is built and tested (`SeoReadTest` 10/0); the `data` uniqueness half is named by GROWTH.md:33, DATABASE.md:171, MERCHANT.md:56 and `SeoRepository.java:19` and read by nothing — `pageProjection` does not select the column, and no migration constrains it.

**Ruling.** Report it, do not implement it. The quality bar is a documented number (0.6) that the payload echoes with its configuration key; "unique" is not, and equal bytes is only the strictest of three readings the four documents leave open. A guard invented here would be a policy the spec did not state — the same reason D183 refuses to add `reason` to payloads the contract does not name. If the product wants the guard, the threshold is a contract decision first.

**What this changes:** P3's bullet can no longer be closed by pointing at the seed. `seo_pages` is empty there by design (D64), so "enforced against the shipped seed" is vacuous for both halves, and this guard's absence is invisible to every gate step that exists.

## D187 — the accessibility axes outside the linter get a census of their own, over the design system too; and a ratio printed beside a colour is a claim that has to survive recomputation

**Ruling.** D186 put `jsx-a11y`'s thirty-four rules in front of `apps/web` and named five things no linter there can see. Landmarks, accessible names and focus order are readable from source, and so is the palette's contrast; `scripts/check_console_a11y.mjs` reads all four. The census covers the console *render tree*, not the console directory: the pages under `app/admin/**` and `app/merchant/**`, the shell they render inside, the components under `apps/web/src/components/console/`, and the `@nexus/ui` modules those files import (directly, then through the package's own relative imports, which is how the focus-ring classes come in). D186 named `packages/ui` as the tree where a missing `alt` would matter most and where nothing is linted; a census that stopped at `apps/web` would have measured only the half that already had a reader.

**A page must render the nav, not merely import it.** The landmark rule is a proxy and is named as one: a console page must reference `ConsoleNav` or a shell export whose body composes it, and the test runs against the file with its import declarations stripped. A page that imports the chrome and never composes it is exactly what the rule is for, so counting the import would have made the rule vacuous -- which is the same reason the whole entry is a census rather than a spot check.

**One page really had no nav, and that is a defect rather than a design.** `apps/web/app/merchant/listings/page.tsx` rendered a private header and no navigation landmark at all -- the only one of the twenty, on a route the nav itself advertises. Fixed by rendering `ConsoleNav` beside the header the page already had, in both branches; the page keeps its bespoke header, its demo banner and its own `signInBlockNote`, because the finding was the missing landmark, not the header's origin. That it is not `MerchantChrome` like its ten siblings stays a consistency residue, recorded rather than absorbed.

**A ratio printed beside a colour is a claim.** `tokens.css` printed one for ten colours and cited `packages/ui/README.md` "for the measured ratios" -- a file that did not exist. Recomputed from the hex values in the same file, eight of the ten were not the measurement (worst: light `--nexus-ink` printed 14.4:1 against 16.21:1 measured). Every pair nevertheless cleared 4.5:1, the tightest being the light `--nexus-ink-faint` at 4.80:1, so the palette was sound and the numbers beside it were decoration. The numbers are corrected to their measurements rather than deleted, the README now carries the ten-row table, and the reader fails when a printed ratio and its recomputation disagree by more than 0.05 -- which is half a unit in the one decimal the comment prints.

**The reader refuses rather than shrinking.** A console file importing a `@nexus/ui` symbol the census does not know exits 2 with the symbol named, instead of censusing a surface that quietly got smaller. The same rule governs the other two refusals the harness pins: a plane with no console pages, and a palette that prints no ratio to recompute. "Did not run" and "found nothing" are different answers (D93, D96), and a census that read nothing is a refusal.

**Both sides are on disk.** `scripts/falsify_console_a11y.mjs` plants nine defects -- one per axis and per sub-rule, including a positive `tabIndex` and an `outline-none` whose ring tokens are stripped -- and three refusals, on copies of the render tree under the system temp directory: 13 arms, 13 held, 0 missed. The focus arm earned its keep on the first run: the rule as first written accepted `focus-visible:outline-none` as its own answer, so a string with no ring left still passed. The rule strips the token's own variant prefix before asking whether anything else answers, and the arm now holds both ways on the same mutated string.

**What this does not decide.** Reading order, heading order, live-region announcements and dynamic states stay unmeasured -- the linter's own list, minus the three axes this reader took. Whether `packages/ui` should have an ESLint config is D186's question, not reopened here. And the ten corrected ratios are measurements of the pairs the palette prints, not of every text/background pair a page can compose.

## D188 — step 13 moved the ledgers into the worktree and left the source index in the main tree, so its "committed plane" was a working-tree verdict wearing another directory's text

WHY IT WAS BELIEVED. D176 wired step 13 with the plane knobs — `--dir`/`--head-dir` for step 8, `--plane` for step 9,
`--quality` for step 7 — and recorded what they printed: "step 8 PASS with 0 offenders" on the committed plane,
against the forty-one D174 had measured by hand in a clean checkout. Both numbers were correct and they were not
the same question. A plane knob relocates the TEXT a reader censuses; every reader here builds its SOURCE INDEX
from the directory it was started in — `scripts/check_ledger_citations.mjs:82` is `const ROOT = process.cwd();`,
and `scripts/check_comment_citations.mjs:53` takes its ROOT from the script's own location but hands that cwd to
the child it scores the comment plane with. So the knob leg was asking "do this clean checkout's sentences name
files that exist HERE", and HERE is the shared working copy, where the other lanes' untracked `com.nexus.admin`,
`com.nexus.seo`, `com.nexus.commerce` and `com.nexus.merchant` sources, the AI lane's untracked runs module and
the web lane's untracked growth view answer every one of them.

MEASURED, one commit, two starting directories. From the main tree with the knobs: 416 citation-shaped tokens,
77 distinct files cited, 0 offenders. From inside a detached worktree of the same HEAD with no knob: the same 416
tokens, 65 files cited, 41 `FILE NOT FOUND`. The difference is thirteen names, enumerated rather than asserted:
the merchant content controller accounts for five sites, an admin console test line for twelve (one per STATUS
section in the forties and fifties), the seo repository, the order service, the AI runs module and the growth view
for three each, and six more names for the remainder. The other two legs move the same way — eleven false sites
inside the worktree against eight on the shared tree, and a `RESULT: FAIL` on 75 comment-plane citations across 20
files against 78 across 22 outside it. Step 13 as shipped therefore did not certify the commit at all; it
certified the directory, with the commit's prose pasted in.

WHAT CHANGED. The three reader legs now `cd` into the worktree and run bare, which is the invocation an operator
types after a clean checkout, and 13b prints both counts on one line so the difference is visible in the gate's
output instead of living in a comment about it (the reconciliation line reads `knob leg 77 file(s) cited / 0 FILE
NOT FOUND — in-worktree leg 65 / 41` on this commit). The harness legs stay in the main tree, and deliberately so:
their fixtures cite real repository files on purpose — that is D163's seam — so an index that followed the ledgers
would refuse every plant the harness owns. 13b's harness call also lost its `GATE_LEDGER_DIR`/`GATE_LEDGER_HEAD_DIR`
prefix: that harness reads no environment variable — its only use of those names is a grep of this script — so the
prefix was a label claiming a plane the arms never opened, and it measured the same 28 held / 1 missed with and
without it.

WHAT THIS UNIT DOES NOT FIX. The 41 belong to the lanes holding those thirteen files, and the remedy is their
commit, not a re-aim: this lane will not stage another lane's source to make a count move. `bash scripts/db_gate_fresh.sh --help`
now states the limit above the knob list, because an operator who reads a knob's documentation is exactly the
reader a half-moved plane misleads. And one arm of `scripts/falsify_ledger_text.mjs` is red on this tree right now
for a finding in the same family and the opposite direction: an uncommitted STATUS section in another lane cites a
line of the seo controller that holds nothing, which is D162's rule catching a row while its author can still move
it — reported here, not edited here. Nothing in this entry claims the shared tree is clean; it claims the two
planes are now two measurements.

## D189 — the honesty D188 bought is one `cd` deep, so the harness that owns step 8's seam pins it and watches itself fail

WHY A FIX THAT PRINTS A NUMBER STILL NEEDS AN ARM. D188 changed step 13 from `cd "$ROOT"` plus two plane knobs to
`cd "$WT"` and no knob (`scripts/db_gate_fresh.sh:391` is the first of the three legs). Nothing in the gate holds
that word in place: a later edit that "tidies" the legs back onto the repository's own path would still print a
section header claiming the committed plane, and the only thing distinguishing the two runs is a number in a
reporting step that cannot fail the gate. That is the same shape as every other seam this lane has had to arm —
D150/D151 for step 11, D152 for steps 8-9, D154 for step 12 — and it is armed the same way: in the harness that
already reads the gate's text.

WHAT THE ARMS SAY. `scripts/falsify_ledger_text.mjs` grew two arms. The first scans the region from step 13's own
header to the end of the file and requires three distinct readers to be launched behind `cd "$WT"` — the scan
returns the names it found and prints them in the arm's own label, and the floor is the count that same scan
produced, so a narrowed regex cannot certify a narrower world. The second runs the identical predicate over a
copy of the gate in which every `cd "$WT"` has been put back to `cd "$ROOT"`, and expects red: the arm exists so
that the first one is a prediction rather than a decoration, and it is the harness witnessing itself rather than
a claim about a shell token.

MEASURED. 31 arms, 30 held, 1 missed on this tree. The miss is D188's neighbour and not this unit's: the
default-plane control arm judges the blank class in a section this tree is writing, and an uncommitted STATUS

## D190 — the committed plane is now certified three times over, and the reconciliation is arithmetic instead of a remembered number

D188 moved step 13's reader legs inside the worktree and D189 pinned that move with a regex. What was left
was a different shortfall in the same block: only 13b ran its reader twice, and 13a and 13c printed one leg
each, so the sentence "a plane knob moves the text and never the source index" was one reader's measurement
extended to three readers by a comment. Worse, even 13b's line printed two counts and asked nobody to compare
them; the numbers were derived from runs but the finding was still prose.

This unit makes all three legs answer the same question and puts the answer in the line. Each leg now runs its
reader twice: once from this directory with that step's own knob aimed at the worktree (the plane the gate's
steps 7-9 actually certify), and once from inside the worktree with no knob (the plane a clean checkout
reaches). One `reconcile` helper prints both counts and subtracts them, so the reported finding is
arithmetic — the offender count the source index alone is worth — rather than a claim about direction. Three
small helpers do the extraction, and they are the part worth reading:

  · `num` pulls the first number that a reader's own census line carries, and prints `no-count` when the text
    has no such line. It does not print 0, because 0 is a verdict and `no-count` is not.
  · `off` reads a reader's offender header (`FALSE SITES (N)`, `FILE NOT FOUND (N)`); when no header printed it
    reports 0 only if the reader printed the sentence it prints instead of a header, and `no-verdict` if it
    printed neither. A reader that crashed must not appear on this line as a clean one — the same rule D157
    wrote for an unparseable flag and D174 wrote for a checker that exits 1 on somebody else's offenders.
  · `gap` refuses to subtract words. If either leg has no verdict the line says the two legs are not
    comparable; otherwise it prints the difference, including a negative one, which would mean the knob leg is
    redder than the clean checkout — an anomaly worth seeing rather than hiding.

Measured on one commit, three pairs, all in the same direction: the jsonb reader cites 12 files with 8 false
sites when its seed comes from the worktree and its index from this directory, 10 files with 11 when both come
from the worktree; the ledger reader 77/0 against 65/41; the comment reader 21 files with 0 offenders against
21 files with 10. The `reconcile` body contains no digit, which is a checkable claim rather than a style rule.

The witnesses come in two kinds, because text predicates alone are satisfiable by a function that never
computed anything. The harness that owns step 8's seam grows five step-13 arms: the wiring arm now asks for
three knob captures, three bare captures, three calls and a digit-free helper body; and four of the arms run
that identical predicate over mutated copies — legs put back to the main tree, a count replaced by a literal,
one leg's call deleted, a knob leg repointed inside the worktree — and each went red exactly as predicted. Two
further arms cut the helper text out of the shipped gate, write it into a scratch script under the same
`set -euo pipefail` the gate runs under, and feed it synthetic reader output: one pair with headers, which has
to print 12/8 against 10/11 and a gap of 3, and one leg that printed a crash instead of a verdict, which has to
print `no-verdict` and refuse the subtraction. The harness measured 36 arms · 35 held · 1 missed, and the miss
is another lane's: an uncommitted STATUS section cites a line that is empty.

What did not change is why step 13 does not fail the gate: the committed plane's redness is other lanes'
uncommitted sources, and the remedy is their commit, not a re-aim. `check_status_citations.mjs` stays red on
