## D191 — the mode the gate runs could not see the rule it was given: `--worktree` now reads the committed plane for newness, and a blank inside a section this tree is writing reddens it

D162 wrote the rule and D163 made its red side reachable, and neither of them asked the question this unit
answers: on which plane does the gate run the reader? Gate step 8 runs `--worktree`. And in that mode the two
census calls collapsed into one object — the committed read was skipped entirely, so the predicate that was
supposed to say "is this section new?" was handed one set and asked for its difference with itself. A set
minused against itself is empty for any input, which is the whole reason the blind spot survived four units of
green: it is not a bug in a branch nobody takes, it is arithmetic that always returns zero.

MEASURED, SAME TREE, BEFORE THE CHANGE. The default plane printed fourteen blank cites counted at HEAD, one
blank inside the twenty-five sections this tree is writing, a header naming the offender, and exited 1. The
same bytes read through `--worktree` printed fifteen blank cites labelled "at HEAD", zero blanks among zero new
sections, no header, the sentence that promises every citation resolves, and exit 0. Two of those claims were
false in the same print: the count is not HEAD's (it is the working copy's fourteen plus one), and the promise
is not the reader's to make about a class it declined to judge. Both were produced by the same three lines.

WHAT CHANGED, AND WHAT IT WAS FORCED TO KEEP. The committed census now runs in every mode except `--text`,
which has no second plane by design — step 9 feeds its generated comment-plane census through it, and a plant
whose text happens to exist at HEAD would otherwise be compared with itself and judged old. `--worktree` is
strict on the working copy as before, with newness taken from the committed titles; the blank offenders print
under the run's own false-citation header instead of a special block, because under that mode they ARE the
verdict. What the change deliberately did not move: the vacuity guards follow the plane the verdict is written
on, which is what each mode already certified, and the committed backlog stays counted-not-judged on both
planes — D161's reason (an append cannot move the number an older row printed) is a property of committed
rows, not of a mode flag.

TWO READS OF THE COMMITTED PLANE MUST NOT BE QUIET, AND BOTH FAILURES ARE NOW REFUSED. An unreadable HEAD
under `--worktree` is added to the entry nobody could read list, labelled by plane, and refuses with the exit
code reserved for "this run is not a verdict" — because a committed read that comes back empty holds no
sections, and no sections means every section on disk looks like it is being written, which turns the counted
backlog into judged offenders through a sandbox that refused to spawn a process. That inversion is quieter
than a missing read, so it gets its own guard: a committed plane that opens and holds zero headings refuses too
rather than reporting a disk full of new rows. The seam arms prove both, and D163's pair of knobs combines with
`--worktree` for the first time, so the worktree mode's red is now re-runnable from a fixture instead of being
observable once in a real ledger draft.

A SECOND DEFECT, FOUND BY WIRING AN ARM FOR THE FIRST ONE. The verbose branch of this reader has been dead for
as long as its ledger read has returned a reason alongside its text: it called a splitter on that object, so
requesting a verbose run produced an uncaught TypeError and exit 1 — a crash wearing a verdict's exit code,
which is the exact shape D157 named when the argument parser stopped throwing and started refusing. Measured
on a detached worktree of the previous commit, so the claim is about the shipped bytes rather than about this
lane's half-finished file: the failure line is inside the verbose loop, and the same request without the flag
prints a verdict. Nothing had an arm for the verbose branch at all, which is how a branch stays broken quietly
for units; there is one now, and it pins the list the branch was written to produce.

WHAT THE CHANGE COSTS, AND WHO OWES IT. Step 8's mode now sees the offence the default plane has reported
since D162: a disk-only row another lane wrote cites a range in `SeoController.java` whose first line holds
nothing — verified directly, the file runs to three hundred forty-two lines and that line is empty — so the
gate's ledger step reddens on a row this lane cannot edit. Append-only ledgers mean the correction belongs to
the row's author, as a span start that names a line carrying text; it is reported, not fixed here, and this
lane's own two real-ledger arms went red exactly as predicted rather than being re-aimed at the new reality.
The falsifier went from thirty-six arms to forty (one pin of the blind spot deleted, five new: the
real-ledger print pair, the worktree seam red, its green control, the empty-committed-plane refusal, the
verbose branch), and reports thirty-eight held with the two named misses above. The self-test arm that rebuilds
the reader to prove the seam arms are predictions had to be re-anchored, because the code it anchored on moved

ONE LABEL THIS UNIT DID NOT CHANGE, AND THE MEASUREMENT THAT MAKES IT LEGIBLE. "At HEAD" is a claim about the
ledger text, not about the cited files: the same committed ledgers censised through the main tree's index

PLANE FOR THESE BYTES, AND NOTHING SHARED. This unit's code change is two files on the working-copy plane: the

## D192 — step 9's offender belt was vacuous on its own plane; the count it reads now prints in every mode, and a report without exactly one of it refuses

D191 stated the rule this unit is an instance of: a rule that cannot fire on the
plane the gate reads is not a rule the gate has. D191 found it in step 8's own mode.
Step 9, the comment-plane reader built the same week as step 8, had the same shape of
hole in a different place: it treats step 8's exit code as the verdict, and then claims a
second reader as a belt — it scrapes an offender count out of the report the child printed
and requires that count to be zero. The scraping regex was written against the wording
`N offender(s)`, and that wording is produced by exactly one line in step 8, a line guarded
by "not the worktree mode". Every run step 9 makes goes through the text mode, and the text
mode sets worktree mode internally (the assignment is near the top of the reader). So the
match list was empty on every plane step 9 actually uses.

Measured on one tree before the change, counting how many characters that regex matched per
mode: zero on the text mode step 9 calls, zero on the worktree mode the gate runs step 8 in,
one on the default plane — the only plane step 9 never asks for. An empty list passed the
belt by construction, because every over the empty set is true: whatever step 8 printed,
step 9 read zero counts, all of them equal to zero, and called that agreement. The comment
above the line asserted the opposite — that a count that is not zero is still caught there —
which is the same two-line pattern D191 recorded: the first line describes a check, the
second describes what the run declined to judge, and green units sit on the second line.

Fix, in two halves, because a belt needs a carrier before it needs a floor. Step 8 prints the
strict plane's own offender count once in every mode, worded so it is the only line carrying
that phrase, and names the plane it belongs to; the count that decides the exit code is now
visible in the report that the exit code came from. Step 9 reads exactly that number and
refuses — exit 2, its code for "this run is not a verdict" — unless it finds exactly one
carrier. Zero carriers means the producer renamed the line or died before printing it; two
means the reader is judging a report that mixes planes. Neither is cleanliness, and neither
is now read as either. The floor is taken from the same scan it protects, not from a second
loop over remembered text.

The belt is honest about what kind of check it is. Its number and the child's exit code are
produced by the same expression, so the belt is not a second observer of the citations; it is
a guard against a future refactor that decouples the report from the code. The comment says
that, instead of claiming an independence the wiring does not have — an over-claim of the kind
this lane has been paid to retract before.

To reach the floor at all, step 9 takes a checker path argument, and the harness forwards its
own copy of that argument to every arm. That seam is D165's lesson applied one unit later: a
mutant arm needs a real interface to aim at, not an edit of shipped bytes. The harness went
from thirteen arms to seventeen, and all seventeen held: the carrier prints once through the
shipped reader on a clean fixture plane; the seam refuses when given no file; the seam refuses
when given a file that does not exist; and renaming the carrier out of a copy of step 8 turns
control, the other flag spelling, the past-EOF arm, the mixed plane and the carrier arm itself
into the refusal they used to skip, while every arm that already expected a refusal stays
green. That last arm is the behavioral witness: it proves the floor fires on a runtime-
equivalent mutation, not on a crash.

Two defects arrived during the wiring, and each is now pinned by the arm that found it. First,
the brand-new seam crashed: pointing it at a nonexistent file threw out of the grammar slice
and exited 1, which in this directory is the code for "a citation is wrong" — a mistyped
request reporting a finding it never computed, D159's class re-enacted inside the minutes it
took to add a flag. It now refuses with 2 and names the file it could not open. Second, step 9
filters the child's report down to the lines worth reprinting, and that filter did not include
the offender detail's wording, so a red run printed "see the report above" above a report
whose only informative line had been filtered out. The FAIL was true; it was just unreadable.
The filter now keeps the line that says a cited line is empty.

The class this unit arms then caught the unit itself, twice, which is the strongest evidence
in it. Shifting lines inside a file that other files cite by line number moved two real cites
onto blank lines: the gate script's sentence about where the reader's root comes from, and
step 8's own header note about which flag spelling the comment-plane census uses. Both were
reported by the shipped readers, not by me — the second one reddened step 9 in the middle of
this unit — and both were repointed to line numbers derived from the call sites by grepping,
never typed by hand, which is the rule that keeps a repoint from becoming a new stale cite.

Post-change measurements, on the working tree. Step 8 default plane: seventeen blanks at HEAD
counted and not judged, two judged among the twenty-seven sections on disk that HEAD does not
have, zero strict offenders on the plane it certifies, two on the working copy, exit 1. Step 8
worktree plane: the same two halves in the same words, four hundred forty-four citations in
three hundred sixty-eight sections against three hundred forty-one at HEAD, two strict
offenders named under its own header, exit 1 — the two planes now say the same thing about the
same backlog. The carrier appears exactly once in each of the three modes. The independent blank
census agrees with the reader: seventeen of seventeen, PASS. Step 9 over the real tree:
eighty-eight comment-plane citations across twenty-seven files, all resolving, exit 0. Step 10
PASS, with fourteen STATUS sections and thirteen DECISIONS entries on disk and not at HEAD —
other lanes' unwritten rows, not this lane's. Step 8's harness: forty arms, thirty-eight held,
and the same two misses it carried through D191, both real-ledger cleanliness arms reddened by
another lane's uncommitted blank citations; this unit added none and adopted neither.

The full fresh-database gate was run twice for these bytes and stopped at step 5 both times:
two hundred sixteen rows passing, one red — the row that asks whether the reference registry
names a column the schema has lost, against a schema of fifty-eight tables and eight
migrations, sitting on top of an untracked permission-grants migration that is not this lane's
to edit or commit. Steps 6 through 13 were therefore not reached, so there is no gate-wide
number for this commit and none is quoted. That red is filed to its owner rather than fixed
here, and the committed plane keeps its known gap: at the parent of this commit the carrier
line does not exist yet, so a clean checkout reads zero carriers — D176's finding, unchanged,
closing when these bytes are on the plane being read.

Residue owned: the belt's number and the exit code come from one expression, so the belt is a
rename guard, not a second reader — recorded rather than oversold. The line-ending claim in
this unit was measured by counting carriage-return pairs in the bytes with the tool that reads
them; the shell idiom that greps for a carriage return reports the file's line count here,
because the escape arrives empty, so it is not a measurement and was not used as one.

## D193 — step 7's read census excused every miss with one bucket, and its parse failures answered in the verdict's exit code

D192's rule, one reader later: a rule that cannot fire on the plane the gate reads is not a rule the
gate has. Gate step 7 had the shape twice over. Every read its scan could not find went into one
bucket — `unseen` — which is a bucket, not a verdict: it covered the file that is not in this index,
the name two files hold, the site that cites no file at all, the file outside the roots the scan
walks, and the one case a human genuinely has to judge, and it printed nothing that told those
apart. Meanwhile the population the bucket talked about was hard-coded, so a sentence like "a
narrowed scan reports its own blind spot" could not be made false from outside the shipped bytes.

The bucket is now five named classes, each printed with its own count including the zeros:
file-not-on-this-plane, site-file-ambiguous, site-names-no-file, outside-the-census-roots,
not-read-in-the-file-where-it-should-be. Exactly one of them is fatal, and it is fatal for a
specific reason: a build that reads jsonb in a directory this scan was never told to walk makes
every answer about that directory unfalsifiable, so the fix is to widen the roots, not to be
excused for not seeing it. That one prints `CENSUS COVERAGE — N answer(s) cite a file outside the
root(s)` (scripts/check_jsonb_reads.mjs:889) and its count joins the exit term. Exactly one is left
to a human — the site resolves inside the walked roots and the key text is not in the file — and
that class is a report at exit 0, because a read through a helper is legal code and only a person
can say whether the read went through one.

The population became addressable, and two floors came with it. `--roots` narrows the read scan,
and a census that opened nothing (scripts/check_jsonb_reads.mjs:557) or opened files and found no
read at all (scripts/check_jsonb_reads.mjs:584) is refused with exit 2. The second floor is the one that matters: a scanner that
finds nothing cannot contradict an answer list, it can only agree with it, and before the floor
existed a scan aimed at a directory with no jsonb in it would have printed a green over a census
with no second reader.

What narrowing measured, on this tree. The Java root alone — services/platform/src/main/java, 130
files — reaches all 19 declared (column, key) pairs, so the second root contributes no read today.
Aimed at apps/ai/nexus_ai alone, the census opens 44 files, finds 0 reads, and is refused by the
second floor: the AI subtree is currently invisible to the read census in the strongest sense, and
the root stays because a read appearing there must be caught the day it does. Aimed at data/seed,
it opens 9 files and prints `CENSUS COVERAGE — 16 answer(s)` citing files outside the roots, and
reddens. The `scripts` root — source files that hold no jsonb key read — is the coverage case at the
other end: it reddens and the CENSUS COVERAGE number it prints is asserted by the same arm to equal
the outside-the-census-roots class count, so a census cannot report a blind spot and forget to be
stopped by it.

The three plane-fact classes each promise, in the reader's own printed text, that the FALSE SITES
block reddens the same row. That promise is now checked in-process: for every miss with a plane-fact
reason, the run requires an offender naming that row, and adds one if none does
(scripts/check_jsonb_reads.mjs:839,:840). Measured, the belt is silent on the shipped plane and on
every plant this harness files, because the site census already reddens an absent file, an ambiguous
name and a citation-free site on its own — the belt's firing side is unreachable while the rule it
polices is intact. So its witness is a mutant reader: the absent-file rule silenced in a copy of the
checker, run through the `--reader` seam against the same planted row
(scripts/falsify_quality_seam.mjs:294), which is the only arm that can make the belt speak. The
shipped-reader arms assert the opposite too — the belt's sentence must NOT print there — so a belt
that fires on a healthy plane cannot pass either. It is policed in both directions and reachable in
one, and the record says which.

The reader's five setup failures were the second instance of the rule, and the crash guard found it.
Each of them was a `throw new Error`, which prints a stack and exits 1 — this directory's code for
"a verdict about reads and sites". The harness had started flagging such a run as
"the reader died before printing a verdict or a refusal", and it was right: an arm aimed at a parse
refusal had been measuring a crash and passing on the stack's wording. All five are now refusals at
exit 2 through one helper (scripts/check_jsonb_reads.mjs:75), each naming the file it could not
parse, and each has its own plant: the read_cat loop header, its column alias, the read_answer
INSERT, the shape_answer INSERT (only the row parser reads that one, so it is the sole route to the
missing-marker refusal), and a last row that stops closing before the semicolon. The refusal arms
also require the run to be total — no header, no ANSWER SITES, no FALSE SITES, no CENSUS COVERAGE
alongside the refusal (scripts/falsify_quality_seam.mjs:404,:447) — because exit 2 alone would also pass a
run that refused and then answered anyway.

One plant was wrong before it was right, and its own red is the reason the arms name their phrase.
The first version replaced the read_cat header with `(VALUES_X`, which still contains the literal the
reader searches for as a prefix, so the run parsed, reported, and exited 0 — a green where a refusal
was predicted. The arm's failure said exactly that: expected 2, got 0.

The harness is 27 arms and all 27 held on the final bytes. Its control census is the tracked plane's
own: 22 answer rows citing 31 locations in 12 files, 38 distinct source lines read back over 41
checked spans, 174 files walked under 2 roots, 26 read sites, 19 distinct pairs against 17 declared

against 179. The first version of this entry quoted those pre-append numbers as if they described the
committed bytes and the commit message next to it invented a third pair (168 against 181) that no run
ever printed; both are corrected here, and the corrected pair is the one re-read after the commit.

Two reading steps are red on this tree for bytes this lane did not write, and they are reported, not

The residue worth keeping is a plane fact about one reader: the read scan walks 174 files under two
roots while site citations resolve against a whole-repository index of 322 files under a 21-directory

miss in the second is a stale answer — and it is why site-file-ambiguous has a witness at all:
no walked root holds a duplicate basename, yet the index holds `__init__.py` more than once. Nothing

## D194 — step 7's census could pronounce a reason and exit 0 over it, and the harness watching that census scored a death by its header line

D192 and D193 closed one rule: a rule that cannot fire on the plane the gate reads is not a rule the gate has.
This unit closes the next one, which the same two files were still carrying: **a rule that fires, prints, and
reaches no exit code is not a rule the gate has either** — and, on the harness side, a crash guard that scores the
wrong line is not a guard. Four findings, one of them in this lane's own committed record.

**(a) A verdict sentence with no exit behind it.** The census expects every declared read's answer to be filed
under one of four kinds, and it already noticed when a kind no row on the plane carries was still expected: the
sentence printed, and the run exited 0. A reader that reports a condition and then takes the same exit code it
takes for a healthy plane has not decided anything; the branch that classifies no row decides nothing, and the
record saying so in prose is not a gate. `branchlessKinds` now enters the exit term with the other reasons
(scripts/check_jsonb_reads.mjs:899-902) and the block prints `ANSWER KINDS UNUSED (N)` with the kind named and the
fix stated (scripts/check_jsonb_reads.mjs:819-827). The plant is one row whose kind word moves from `reachable`
to `dead-reader` (scripts/falsify_quality_seam.mjs:129), which is the smallest change that empties a kind:
measured on it, the census's own numbers do not move (22 rows, 31 cited sites, 12 files, 38 line spans), all five
miss classes stay at 0, and exactly one reason appears — so the reddening is this rule's and not collateral.
The witness is M1 of `.scratch/d194_meta.mjs`: put `branchlessKinds.length` back out of the exit term and 34 of 35
arms hold, the one red being the arm aimed at this sentence.

**(b) A crash guard keyed on the line a dying reader still prints.** The harness decides whether a run crashed.
It was deciding from the census's header line, and the header is the first thing the reader prints — so a reader
that announced itself and then died mid-report was scored as a finished run. The guard now keys on a terminal
sentinel the reader prints as its last act (scripts/falsify_quality_seam.mjs:264), and that sentinel declares the
exit code the process intends (scripts/check_jsonb_reads.mjs:902), so a run whose last line says `this run exits 1`
and whose process takes 0 is a crash too, not a verdict. Three witnesses, all on the shipped bytes: M3 puts the
guard back on the header line and 33 of 35 hold, with exactly the two death arms red — the reader that dies after
the header, and the reader whose declared exit code the process does not take; M4 removes the clause that refuses a
finished run for an arm that declared a death (scripts/falsify_quality_seam.mjs:459-461) and 34 of 35 hold, red
only on the arm that polices it; M5 deletes the sentinel line from the reader and the whole census goes to 20 of
35 — fifteen arms red, because a run that prints no terminal line cannot be certified as having finished. The
`expectCrash` inversion is checked by calling the same predicate the loop calls (scripts/falsify_quality_seam.mjs:456,
arm at :684-689) against the control's real result, so the flag cannot be proved by a plant that only ever dies.

**(c) The seam died where it should have refused.** D159 made a mistyped `--quality` value a legal request that
refuses; nothing between that legality and the verdict ever said the file is simply not there. Pointed at a path
with no file behind it, or at a directory, the census reached `readFileSync` about fifty lines later and ended in
`node:fs` frames at exit 1 — this directory's code for "a read or a site is wrong" (measured before the guard:
both paths exited 1 with a stack; only a file that exists and holds no answers refused at 2). Both are refusals
now, naming what was handed to it (scripts/check_jsonb_reads.mjs:99-107), and the two arms assert the sentence,
not just the code (scripts/falsify_quality_seam.mjs:625-636). Witness M2: neuter the two conditions and 33 of 35
hold, red on exactly those two arms. M2's first version was a bad witness and is kept here as the lesson: it
nulled the value the guards read instead of the conditions, which made the missing-file refusal fire for the
*shipped* path too, so the copied harness died in its own pre-flight — "the shipped plane is not green (rc 2,
control rc 2)" — and reddened zero arms. A mutation that kills the control proves nothing about the arms it aimed
at; the arm count of 0 is not a survivor count, it is the run not having happened.

**(d) My own committed citations were mis-aimed, and the gate cannot see it.** D193's edits to these two files
were insertions, so every line number its own entry cites moved — eight of them, in `docs/DECISIONS.md` at

One more defect surfaced by the same arithmetic: the sentence's second floor was a bare continuation,

**Stated limits, because a census that hides its blind spots is the thing this project keeps catching.** The

## D195 — a reader nothing runs is not a gate, and a pipe in a shell that cannot fail is not a gate either
WHAT WAS RULED. Two censuses, one per half of the same question, both measured on the shipped bytes and both FALSE
when this pass started. (A) Every first-party `scripts/check_*.mjs` must be INVOKED by a surface that runs checkers:
`scripts/db_gate_fresh.sh`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, or the `Makefile`. Ten exist; two were invoked by nothing
while both PASSED — `scripts/check_console_i18n.mjs` and `scripts/check_console_a11y.mjs` — and `docs/PLAN.md`
recorded the accessibility half of P3 as "unmeasured" while the census that measures it sat in the tree. (B) Every CI
step that pipes a checker into `tee` must declare `shell: bash`, because in GitHub Actions the default `run:` shell on
Linux is `bash -e {0}` and a pipeline reports its LAST command: three such steps could not fail, measured rather than
argued (`false | tee /dev/null` exits 0 under `bash -e`, 1 under `bash -eo pipefail`). All three declare it now. The
same census asserts that `scripts/db_gate_fresh.sh` still carries `set -euo pipefail`, because that one line is what
makes every `node ... | sed` below it able to stop the run — which is the whole of D150/D151’s proof about step 11,
and a proof about a line is only a proof while the line is there.
A COUNT IN PROSE DRIFTS, SO IT IS DERIVED. The note over the piped steps first said three steps "carried Hard-fail in
their own comments". One does; one of the other two annotates itself "Report mode for now", the opposite claim; the
third describes a verdict without that word. The count is read out of each step’s own comment and printed
(`hard-fail claims 1 of 7 piped step(s) ...`) instead of being typed anywhere. Writing it found a second defect the
reading had not: the step splitter attached each step’s comment block to the PREVIOUS step, so the one step whose
comment says "Hard-fail" was named as a different step in the offender line. Comments are carried forward to the step
they describe now.
THE NEW READER IS HELD TO ITS OWN STANDARD. `scripts/check_reader_reachability.mjs` parses its flags through
`scripts/cli_args.mjs`; its first version had a private loop, and measured on that version `--gate a --gate b` took b
in silence. `scripts/falsify_flag_dialect.mjs` counts it among the readers on the shared parser, so a revert to a
private loop reddens that census rather than being noticed by nobody.
WITNESSES. `15 arms · 15 held · 0 missed` for the reachability census (including a planted commented-out
`shell: bash` and a planted mere mention); `20 arms · 20 held · 0 missed` for the dialect census under Git Bash;
13 of 13 for the accessibility arms; gate step 14 green end-to-end under `set -euo pipefail`.
STATED LIMITS, because a census that hides its blind spots is the thing this project keeps catching. The surfaces are
read as TEXT: no YAML parsing, steps found by the indentation of `      - `, and a step’s own comment taken as the
unbroken run of `#` lines directly above it, so a blank line is what keeps a job-level note from being read as the
next step’s claim. The claim count decides nothing — a comment that overstates itself is a documentation defect,
not an offender here. Only `| tee` is censused, not `| sed`. The reachability rule covers `check_*.mjs` alone: the
`verify_*.mjs` readers, the harnesses and the `falsify_*` files are not asked who runs them, which is a wider census
than this unit takes. And the class-B population is other-lane work in flight: on HEAD’s bytes this unit started
from the workflow held no piped step at all, so the census would have REFUSED at exit 2 — the correct answer, and
why the refusal is named here rather than hidden.

## D196 — the harness scored the checker's vocabulary from three lists typed by hand, and the checker could file a miss under a class it had no sentence for and exit 0 over it

D193 established that a rule which cannot fire on the plane the gate reads is not a rule the gate has. D194
established that a rule which fires, prints, and reaches no exit code is not one either. This unit adds the third
shape the same defect takes: **a copy of another file's vocabulary is not that file's vocabulary.** It is a
snapshot, and it goes stale without leaving the report — the stale copy still prints green, because everything
scoring against it is scoring against the snapshot. Three snapshots were live in `scripts/falsify_quality_seam.mjs`
at the start of this unit, and one branch in the checker pronounced a judgement and then stepped around it.

The branch first, because the unit's own record named it. `scripts/check_jsonb_reads.mjs:815` carries the words
"D194: the second direction of vocabulary drift, and it reddens" — above the block that charges a kind no row on
this plane is filed under. A *second* direction implies a first, and the first was twenty lines earlier in the
same function: the classifier can file a row under a class the sentence table has no entry for, and the reader
printed `  <class> (N): no stated reason — this class is new and the sentence for it was not written` and joined
nothing. That is the identical defect D194 was opened for, one line further down, and finding it needed no
measurement — only reading the sentence the previous unit wrote about itself. It is now a verdict block of its own
(scripts/check_jsonb_reads.mjs:801-812) headed `NO STATED REASON (N row(s) across M class(es))`, and its row count
joins the exit term beside the other six (scripts/check_jsonb_reads.mjs:899-900). The fix line names which of the
two halves is missing — write the sentence, or retire the branch that files it — because the two remedies point at
different files.

No answer plant can reach it: a plant moves a row between classes, it cannot delete a sentence from the checker.
So the witness is a mutant reader — one `MISS_WHY` key renamed, which is the smallest change that makes a class
unnamed while leaving the row, its site and its file exactly as they were (scripts/falsify_quality_seam.mjs:313) —
and the arm pair is one measurement run twice: the same fixture over the shipped reader exits 0 and must not print
the block (scripts/falsify_quality_seam.mjs:734), the same fixture over the renamed reader exits 1 and must print
it with the sentinel declaring exactly one reason (scripts/falsify_quality_seam.mjs:745). The arm that was already
there for the hand-judged class gained the absence half, so the charge cannot leak onto a class that does have a
sentence either; it is policed in both directions and reachable in one, which is the shape D193 said a belt has to
have.

The three snapshots. `MISS_CLASSES` was five strings typed under a classifier whose names live in the checker;
`VERDICT_MARKS` was six strings typed under a checker that prints more verdict lines than six; and `TERMINAL` was
a regular expression retyped out of a sentence the checker assembles. Each has a distinct failure:

  - A hand-typed class list goes blind on a rename. `classCounts` asks the output for the five names it knows, so
    a class the checker now files under a different word counts as nothing, `onlyClass` sees its planted row
    nowhere, and the arm reports the miss it was written to catch as though it had caught it. The list is now the
    keys of the checker's own `MISS_WHY` block, read out of the file this harness instance points at, and it is
    cross-checked against the reasons that file's classifier pushes — the same two populations the checker
    compares at run time when it charges an unnamed class. They are two derivations by different means, so a
    disagreement is a fact about the reader rather than about my regex, and it refuses at import
    (scripts/falsify_quality_seam.mjs:340,:346,:356-359). A third consequence: `onlyClass(name)` now refuses to
    build an arm aimed at a class the reader never files (scripts/falsify_quality_seam.mjs:368), because an
    expectation no run can ever print is not falsifiable, it is a caption.
  - A hand-typed marks list goes blind in the other direction, and this one is a false green with teeth. The
    marks exist to check that a refusal is *total* — a census that cannot parse its input has no verdict to
    report, so an rc-2 arm requires that no answer block printed alongside it. Six marks over a checker printing
    more meant that a refusal which also answered through any of the others read as total:
    `EVERY READ THE SCAN FOUND`, `UNDECLARED`, `WRONG TABLE`, `CALLED NEVER-READ, IS READ`, `NO KIND`,
    `ANSWERS THE READ CENSUS DID NOT FIND`. The heads are now read off the checker's own `console.log` literals,
    and the single print a refusal is allowed to make is excluded by a property of the source line rather than by
    a name typed here: the line whose own statement calls `process.exit(2)` is what the refusal *says*, so it
    cannot also be what the refusal must not say (scripts/falsify_quality_seam.mjs:394-403).
  - The derivation's own first measurement was wrong, and it is recorded here because the mistake is the same one
    in a different costume: a rule stated as a shape can admit members that are not of that kind. The literal
    prefixes read thirteen "heads" out of a checker that prints twelve verdicts and one disclaimer, the thirteenth
    being `LIMITS, stated rather than implied: this is a textual scan.` — capitals, then a comma, then words. A
    mark that is prose is a false witness, not a harmless extra: any run that printed its own disclaimer would
    have read as a census that refused and answered at once. A head is now the capitals run, which ends at the
    first lower-case letter, and what survives must not end on sentence punctuation
    (scripts/falsify_quality_seam.mjs:399-402). The footer that broke the first version is the arms' plant, found
    by a property of the print that *follows* it — a quoted `console.log` opening in a lower-case letter can only
    be the second half of a sentence, so the line it continues is prose too — which keeps the plant moving with
    the reader's prose instead of becoming a fourth hand copy (scripts/falsify_quality_seam.mjs:415-432). Two
    arms score the pair: a refusal that answers through a head the six strings never carried must be seen, and a
    refusal that prints only its disclaimer must not be (scripts/falsify_quality_seam.mjs:665,:674). The check
    lives in an arm rather than in an import-time refusal deliberately: a `die` on the over-wide rule would
    preempt the arm that names the case, and an arm no run can redden is the caption D193 refuses.
  - A retyped terminal regex fails loudly, which is the least harmful of the three but not harmless: reword the
    checker's last line and the copy stops matching, `crashed` becomes true for every run including healthy ones,
    and the arms report deaths that never happened. The pattern is now the reader's last template line with each
    interpolation turned into a capture group (scripts/falsify_quality_seam.mjs:253-265), floored at three groups —
    a reason count, the report mode, and the exit code — because a reader that stopped stating the code it takes
    has removed the very thing the predicate reads.

The report prints the population it scored (`DERIVED VOCABULARY`, scripts/falsify_quality_seam.mjs:819) and lists
each class and each verdict head, because a count over a set nobody can see is a number and not a measurement —
the lesson D173 learned about remembered totals, applied to this harness's own lists. A harness copy pointed at a
mutant reader prints a different vocabulary from the shipped one, which is the point: the arms score against the
reader they ran.

This unit's own blast radius, measured before it was trusted. It inserted 12 lines into the checker and 170 into
its harness and deleted two named constants, which is enough to mis-aim citations in the sections that describe
those files — including my own. Of the 25 live citation numbers in D193, D194 and STATUS §200, 16 had moved off
their sentence, 4 named a thing this unit deleted, and 5 were already right; 16 ledger lines were rewritten to fix
them. Step 8 asks only that a cited file has the cited line, so all 16 stayed green while pointing at the wrong
sentence, which is the same invisibility D193 and D194 were opened for, this time aimed at the record rather than
at the code. The re-aiming is a derivation from the bytes: a single number must match one line's trimmed content in
the working copy and a range must match its whole block contiguously, so `scripts/check_jsonb_reads.mjs:887-890`,
whose interior this unit edited, is placed by its two ends and re-spelled as the block's new extent (899-902). Four
numbers could not be derived because their referent is gone — `VERDICT_MARKS` is now the derivation at
(scripts/falsify_quality_seam.mjs:404) and the marks array's second line is now the totality predicate at
(scripts/falsify_quality_seam.mjs:447), the hand-retyped `TERMINAL` is now built from the reader's last template
line (scripts/falsify_quality_seam.mjs:264), and one cite D194 landed four lines above its own claim, on what was
HEAD's blank line 580 and is now the `found.size === 0` refusal (scripts/check_jsonb_reads.mjs:584). That last
number is aimed by hand, and the aiming was tested: the first draft of this very sentence put the cite *on* the
blank line, naming the reader file and that empty line number as the drift example, and step 8's new-section rule
reddened it as its one offender — a citation onto an empty line cannot hold the claim, which is the rule D161
counted and D167 and D172 made chargeable, firing on the unit that relies on it. So a drift example is written here
as words, not as a number: a line the ledger cites is a line the ledger is held to. Each hand-aimed number carries
the reason printed at landing rather than assumed.

Bare continuations cannot be recognised by shape, and this unit proved it on its own text: D194 quotes drift
examples (`` `:311` at DECISIONS 5644 ``) and JSON literals (`{"rows":22,"cited":31,…}`) in exactly the spelling a

## D197 — a skip list is a hiding place until something proves nothing reaches through it, and a classifier clause that never runs is not a rule the census has

**Decided:** `.scratch` joins `VENDOR_DIRS`, and the shared list becomes the union of the two lists that had
drifted apart (`source_index.mjs` and the comment census's own `SKIP`), and the path clause of `isCitation` is
asked before the bare-dotfile clause, so a citation whose first segment is a dot directory reaches the resolver
instead of being dropped.

**Why:** two costs were paid in the same week. D196 hit the first: a lane's stale copy of `cli_args.mjs` inside
an unexcluded `.scratch` made a shipped file's basename appear twice, and the resulting AMBIGUOUS refusal at
gate step 9 stopped whichever session ran the gate next, because `db_gate_fresh.sh` is under
`set -euo pipefail`. The classifier was the larger one, because it had no symptom: ten dot-path citations in
the ledgers had never been judged by any reader since D88 wrote the clause, and a dropped token leaves no trace
in the counts. Both are the same shape — an exclusion or an early return that is invisible from the outside.

**Rule this establishes:** a directory may enter a skip list only beside a clause that charges it, and the
charge must run over the real tree: reproduce the shipped index file for file, then refuse if any file the
exclusion keeps out is tracked. An unexcluded name is a bug in the citation only if the walker can reach it,
and an excluded name is a hiding place only if nothing proves it holds no claim — the two halves are the same
test, read from opposite ends. Derived the same way as D196 decided: counts come out of the module that owns
them (the checker's own tokenizer, the shared set's own `size`), never from a hand copy — the first regex
written here by hand printed 4 against the shipped scanner's 10.

**Not decided here:** whether a duplicate basename inside the repository should be charged when the citation is
*written* rather than when it is read. The index holds 27 such names, most of them structurally legitimate, so
the population needs a predicate before it can have a gate. Recorded as the next unit.

## D198 — a reader that could not be read is not a verdict about the ledgers, and an arm whose evidence cannot hold what it predicts is a caption

**Decided:** every arm that makes a statement about a reader's output runs through `runWith`, which makes three
attempts, refuses to believe an exit code whose stdout is empty, and marks the result as a reading; the reporting
loop refuses the whole run with exit 2 (`unread N of M arms`) when any reading never spoke, instead of scoring it.
The `reading` tag scopes that refusal, so the three stub arms that aim deliberately at silent children are not
charged by it. The structural claim the guard rests on is armed against the reader's own bytes: every
`process.exit(` in `scripts/check_ledger_citations.mjs` has a `console.log(` before it, and a copy of the reader
with an exit hoisted above the first print reddens that predicate.

**Why:** the alternative was measured, and it is the failure this lane exists to keep out of the ledgers. A harness
that prints `MISSED exit 2 expected, 134 printed` has taken an abort and turned it into a finding about a census
that never ran, and everything around the number lends it the shape of evidence — the reader's name, the arm's
name, the tally, the exit code it declined to doubt. D194 established the rule one level down, in a reader that
could print a reason and exit 0 over it; this is that rule at the harness, where a child that never spoke is not a
reader that found nothing. The refusal costs the one thing a green tally is for, a number to quote, and buys the
claim that every line of that tally was read.

**Rule this establishes:** a subprocess result is a reading only if the channel that carries verdicts carried
something, and the harness must be able to say which channel that is and show the reader using it — which is why
the structural arm is asked of the reader's bytes rather than asserted in a comment. The corollary comes from this
unit's own half-written guard, which was measured before it was believed: an arm's evidence string must be able to
hold the text its prediction demands, its mutation witness must be able to redden on the mutation it plants, and a
predicate comparing two numbers must compare the two the sentence is about. Five defects of exactly those kinds
sat in the first version of this guard, and three of them were arms that could never have fired — the class D192,
D193 and D197 each found one of, arriving in the unit written to catch it.

**Not decided here:** whether a silent child and a `bash` that cannot execute deserve the same verdict or
different ones. Today only the first refuses; the second still reports three arms as MISSED, an absent instrument
wearing the shape of a wrong subject. The refusal that would fix it needs a witness in both directions, and this
host — where `bash` is the WSL stub while Git's bash sits one directory off `PATH` — is the only place one has
been seen so far. Recorded as the next unit, together with the same `run`-reads-only-the-exit-code pattern, still
unguarded, in `scripts/falsify_comment_plane.mjs`.
Plane for these bytes, working copy: the same runs that wrote the numbers in this unit's STATUS section — step 8
0 strict offender(s) over 382 section(s), step 9 0 offenders over 88 comment-plane citation(s), step 10 HEAD 171
STATUS sections and 184 decisions all present on disk with no number claimed twice, step 12 22 of 22 spelled
section citations resolving, and 56 of 56 harness arms held. That section carries the full plane; this entry is
the ruling and does not restate a count it did not measure.

The section this entry pairs with is deliberately not spelled by number anywhere above, and the reason is a
measured constraint rather than a style. The checker that reads these cites requires a spelled ledger citation to
resolve to a heading at HEAD, and that section is written by this same commit, so naming it in that form reddens
the working-copy plane until the commit lands. Read rather than reasoned: the first version of the paragraph above
spelled it, and step 12 exited 1 over the one citation with 23 citations and 22 resolving — the paragraph had moved
the population it was describing, which is this lane's recurring defect, and it is why the numbers above were
re-taken after the sentence changed.
## D199 — one question, four private answers: the fold D181 ruled reaches the last reader that kept its own
directory list, and an exclusion is only a rule when an arm runs the tree through both answers

**Decided:** `check_status_citations.mjs` imports `VENDOR_DIRS` instead of keeping a nine-name list, keeps its
dot-prefix clause as its own predicate, and gains two harness arms — one that requires the shipped reader not to
read a planted file under an excluded directory, one that requires a reader with the private list put back to read
it and redden.

**Why:** D85 made one list out of two and D181 ruled that the fold is a union; D197 shipped that union and added
`.scratch`. Step 12 had still not been asked, so the same directory answered "walked" to three readers and
"skipped" to a fourth. The cost is asymmetric in a way only an arm can show: a reader with a narrower exclusion
certifies citations into generated files, and a reader with a wider one drops citations the repository actually
owns. Measured on this tree the fold narrows by 22 files and widens by 0.

**Rule this establishes:** when a shared predicate replaces a private one, the change must come with (a) a mirror
walk that reproduces the shipped reader's printed count before its difference is quoted, so the measurement is
known to be the reader's and not an imitation of it; (b) a statement of which direction the plane moved, with the
population named; (c) an arm that puts the private answer back and requires the reader to behave differently.
A fold asserted from a comment is a preference. And: an `absent:` pattern in an arm table must be enforced by the
runner, because a mutant that dies before printing anything can still hand back the predicted exit code.

**Not decided here:** whether a line-number citation into a shipped file should be re-checked whenever that file
changes. 0418b22 moved `source_index.mjs` by ' + SHIFT + ' lines and silently invalidated STATUS §203's cite to its
`VENDOR_DIRS` declaration — in bounds, non-blank, exempt from the strict census because the citing section is
committed. Recorded as the pairing of task #126: a ledger claim about the code that nothing reconciles.

## D201 — a line-number citation names a position, and no reader asked whether the position still holds the text it was chosen for

**Decided.** `scripts/check_line_cite_drift.mjs` is that reader and CI runs it in report mode in the
contract-drift job; `scripts/falsify_line_cite_drift.mjs` is its 8-case harness and runs as a hard-fail step
beside it. Its verdict vocabulary is one counts object, printed one class per line and derived by the harness from
that declaration. Its judged population is content equality between the commit blame names for the citing line and
HEAD, over citations whose path is spelled from the repository root.

**Why.** The four classes of the existing citation reader all ask whether the cited line is there. This lane's own
STATUS §203 cited a declaration by a number that was wrong twice over — two lines at the commit that wrote it,
nineteen after a later one — and passed every reader on both planes, because the strict census exempts a section
that is already committed and a stale number is neither past EOF nor blank. A citation whose position moved is not
a rarer accident than a citation whose file is missing; it was simply the one question no reader had been given.

**Rule this establishes.** A new reader over a shared corpus must print its population and each verdict class as
its own machine-parseable line, so the harness that asserts it cannot take a digit out of the prose explaining the
class; it must state the plane on which its own predicate is meaningful and refuse any plane where the predicate is
a lie (a shallow clone blames every line to the grafted commit, so a drift census there answers confidently about
nothing); and where an arm depends on a mechanism the environment can silently decline to provide, the arm asserts
the mechanism before it asserts the verdict — this harness throws when its test repository is not shallow, because
the first version of that arm measured a full clone and called it a guard.

**Not decided here.** Whether GONE may ever redden — it cannot while a reworded comment and a deleted target are
one class, which is a meaning question and not a diff question. The 24 MOVED citations are the precondition for
`--strict MOVED` and are listed as task #129. And the 262 basename-only citations: the shipped reader resolves
those by basename against the shared index and could judge them, so this reader's population is smaller than the
corpus, which it prints instead of hiding.

## D202 — step 15 added to the gate: the ledger's line-number drift reader runs as step 15

**What the reader does.** `scripts/check_line_cite_drift.mjs` walks every `File.ext:NNN` citation in the ledgers, blames the citing line to the commit that wrote it, reads the cited file at THAT commit and at HEAD, and compares the text of line NN. It reports seven classes:

- **EXACT** — the text is identical at HEAD.
- **MOVED** — the text survives at one new line; the stale number is re-aimable.
- **NOT-UNIQUE** — the cited line was blank when written, or HEAD holds the text more than once.
- **GONE** — the text is nowhere in HEAD's file (reworded, deleted, or moved beyond recognition).
- **NO-BASE** — the line did not exist at the commit that wrote the citation.
- **UNPATHED** — basename-only cite (`File.ext:NNN` without a path); this reader resolves only rooted paths.
- **NOT-AT-HEAD** — rooted path names no file at HEAD (sibling of step 8's FILE NOT FOUND).

The `--reaim` mode prints a derived re-aim list (site, file, old number, new number) so a lane can clear MOVED citations by applying the reader's own rows. The `--strict MOVED,NOT-UNIQUE` mode exits 1 on stale numbers without failing on GONE (which is a queue for a human, not a default red).

**Why this reader.** The existing citation readers (step 8, step 9) ask four questions of a citation — file exists, basename unique, line within bounds, line not blank — but none asks whether the cited line still holds the text the sentence was written against. STATUS §203 named a line that was wrong twice over (two lines at the commit that wrote it, nineteen after a later one) and passed every reader on both planes, because the strict census exempts a committed section and a stale number is neither past EOF nor blank. That is a class, not an incident — and this script is the reader for the class.

**How it works.** For each citation: blame the ledger LINE that holds it to the commit that wrote it, read the cited file at THAT commit and at HEAD, and compare the text of line NN. Content equality is derivable from two refs; "does this sentence still describe that line" is not, so the reader never asks it. The index and blame come from `source_index.mjs` (the module step 8 already uses), so the two readers cannot drift into censusing different file sets.

**The falsify harness.** `scripts/falsify_line_cite_drift.mjs` builds a throwaway git repository for each arm, commits a code file and a one-line ledger that cites it, makes one further commit, and predicts the full verdict vector AND exit codes. It proves 12 arms covering every class (EXACT, MOVED, GONE, NO-BASE, UNPATHED, NOT-AT-HEAD, NOT-UNIQUE blank, NOT-UNIQUE duplicate, --reaim, refusals, shallow-plane refusal, NOT-UNIQUE reasons, --reaim rows) — 12/12 MATCHED.

## D204 — step 17 added: ledger numeric claims verified against the gate's own output

**What the checker does.** `scripts/check_ledger_numbers.mjs` reads every numeric claim from both ledgers, prints a census per noun (the distinct values, their counts, and which section carries the newest one), and judges exactly one thing: whether the newest claim for each expected noun matches an expectation passed in. With no expectation it prints `UNCHECKED` and exits 2 — "I have no idea what the right number is" and "the number is right" must not print the same way.

**Why this reader.** The ledger states numeric facts — "217 quality checks", "217 assertions", "217 checks", "38 arms", "216 quality checks", etc. — and these numbers must match what the gate actually files. When a check is added, the number moves and 120+ sentences go quietly stale; the failure mode this repository has met in three other shapes (a declared jsonb read whose key stopped shipping, a route no service serves, a citation aimed at a line that no longer holds its text).

**What it does.** The reader reads all numeric claims from both ledgers, prints a census per noun (every distinct value, its count, and the section carrying the newest one), and judges exactly one thing: the newest claim for each expected noun against an expectation passed in. `--expect "quality checks=217,assertions=217,checks=217"` is the only mode that produces a verdict; without it the tool prints `UNCHECKED` and exits 2. The verdict vocabulary is one counts object printed one class per line and derived by the harness from the reader's own `const counts = {...}` declaration (D196).

It prints PASS only when the newest claim for each expected noun matches the measured value. Measured: all three MATCHED, exit 0.

## D217 — the gate files a step total and no reader judges it, so this unit measured it instead of restating it

Step 17 exists because the ledger states numbers the artefacts stopped stating, and it judges three nouns.
One noun it knows but never aims at is steps, whose carrier the census itself names: the steps of the
fresh-database gate. Measured on the working copy that carrier answers three different questions at once.
Twenty-one invocations of the step function, seventeen distinct step numbers, and six denominators inside the
labels: 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17. All three are true of the same file. The invocation total is larger because a
branch files both of its legs under one number and because three sub-labels share one; the denominators
disagree because a header is written once, when its own step is the newest thing in the script, and nobody
revisits it — so the first twelve still announce themselves as one of twelve. The oldest numeric claim in the
gate is therefore a claim no reader reads, which is the same shape as the drift this lane has met in a
citation, a route and a jsonb key.

Deliberately not done: no fourth expectation. The numbers checker is a file no commit holds on this plane —
another lane is writing it live — so an expectation derived here and aimed there is only reproducible against
an uncommitted draft, and a gate red nobody else can stand up is a rumour. The spelling choice (numbered
step, invocation, or label denominator) is a convention, and a convention invented inside a commit message
has no reader to enforce it; it is owed to the lane that owns that checker, recorded rather than guessed.

What is owed next, in order: the gate derives its own total from the file rather than typing it into each
header; a step whose header disagrees with the script is the arm that proves the derivation is load-bearing;
and only then the expectation, with the noun spelled the way the derivation spells it.

## D219 — the gate derives its own step total, and the new check reddened its author before it was green

§219 measured that a step header announces a total nobody reads and that the number goes stale every time a
step is added. This unit closes it: the fresh-database gate now has a step whose only job is to read its own
file, take the highest step number present, and stop the run if any header claims a different total. Twenty-

## D226 — the drift reader credits the re-aims it lands, so a green strict pass proves a number moved, not that it is right

Step 16 now exits 0 — MOVED 0 and NOT-UNIQUE 0 across 147 judged citations — which finally lets a live gate drive
reach the step that derives its expectations from its own measurement and the step that counts its own steps. The
green needed a second reading, because it did not come from the repairs this lane filed.

Two properties, both measured on a scratch plane outside the repository with predictions written first, four arms
to four matches. First, the reader takes ledger text from HEAD and ledger blame from the working file: on a dirty
ledger the writer looked up for a citation is the writer of whichever sentence sits at that number on disk, so an
uncommitted line anywhere above shifts every verdict below it. A stale citation became NO-BASE — attributed to the
all-zero commit — when a line was inserted above it without being committed, and became MOVED again when that
insertion was committed, with the target file never touched in either arm.

Second, and this is what made four wrong citations look certified: committing a citing line makes that commit its
blame author, and the reader then compares the cited line at the author commit with the cited line at the same
number at HEAD. Those are the same bytes. A re-aim is therefore credited as EXACT by the commit that lands it,
whatever number it carries, and the reader cannot see its own wrong repair.

The consequence was found by auditing this lane's own landed sites rather than the ledger's general population:
two of the four single citations moved last unit landed on comment prose instead of the `isCitation` declaration
and the last-segment split their sentences name, and two more name the gate's census assignment while their
sentences describe the gate's in-worktree reader leg. Four repairs, each gated on the old text occurring exactly
once on its own line, with the new numbers read off the target files first. The plants-block citations were
correct.

Filed as a working rule: read the drift reader only on a plane whose ledger is committed, and audit a re-aim
against the sentence that carries it. A green step 16 is evidence that no cited line moved since its (possibly
neighbouring) writer; it is not evidence that the ledger points where it means to.

## D228 — a blame-free citation reader: one demonstrated sensitivity, two demonstrated blind spots, and a count left open

The drift reader's two properties (worktree-keyed blame against HEAD-keyed text; the landing commit being its own
baseline) cannot be fixed in place because both come from blame being the notion of "written against". So the fix
is a different question, not a patched question: does the line a citation names hold a token the sentence around
it put in backticks. That test is plane-relative and blameless, so a wrong re-aim is judged exactly as harshly on
the commit that lands it as on any other, and it can be run on any ref — which is what let this unit compare the
pre-repair and post-repair planes for the same site and watch the verdict move with the number.

Numbers over the two ledgers at one ref: 545 endpoints, 370 unresolvable paths, 98 without a referent token, 1
past EOF, 76 judged into 16 online / 11 near / 49 far / 0 absent. The 49 are mostly the reader's own grammar
accepting prose words as tokens and a block-naming citation reading as a miss, so this stays a scratch instrument
rather than a gate step, and it is honest about the cost: strict tokens shrink the judged population.

Two limits stated instead of tuned away. A line whose only content is the path gives the reader nothing to test,
so a stale and a repaired citation both pass there. And the range endpoint the reader flagged was found by hand
to be a real tee line, so that row is a false positive of the token rule, not of the number.

The finding left open on purpose: a ledger sentence cites a workflow range and claims three tee-piped steps, while
the committed workflow holds ten tee commands, nine of them inside the region that comment introduces. The next
unit decides which half is stale
by reading the original finding; a number is not edited to make a reader quiet.
## D229 — a range is decided by the commit that made the claim, not by the file the claim points at

the ledger named two twenty-four to two fifty-four, a span covering four piped steps whose last two belong to

check certified that move because it only asks whether the new line holds a token, so a wrong re-aim can be

sufficient for a citation whose sentence names a set fixed by a past change; the range must be re-derived from the
commit that made the claim, and the auditor should say which of the two it consulted.

The second site is the comment-prose class again: an early section cites the workflow's report-mode step at a line

## D230 — a ledger line is a fragment of a sentence, so a claim must be paired with a citation at clause scope

The surface reader pairs a citation with a claim verb, and the pairing scope turned out to carry the reader's whole
error rate. Pairing per LINE reddened two correct sentences, because the ledgers wrap near one hundred twenty
columns: the verb that mattered sat in an earlier clause of the same sentence ("all three declare a shell now,
under a note that says why", where the citation names the note and the note is exactly what the line holds), or in
a later clause of a later sentence, matched out of the noun "comment run". Pairing at clause scope inside a joined
paragraph releases both, and keeps the refusal this class exists for: a citation into a workflow's explanatory
comment, claimed by a verb in its own clause, is refused on the plane before the repair and matched after it, on a
workflow file that is byte-identical across the two refs.

Two masking rules are part of the scoping and not details. Inline code spans must be masked per line before
joining, because a paragraph-wide backtick toggle turns one unclosed backtick into a mask over every remaining
boundary character, and the clause then silently widens back to the paragraph — the failure is a red on a correct
row, and it is invisible in the counts. And the citation regex consumes one character before the path; using that
character as the left end of the clause walks straight past the opening parenthesis that bounds a parenthesised
reference, which is the shape most of this ledger's citations take.

The decision about the reader's status: it stays a scratch instrument. Clause scoping left six cited sites carrying
a claim verb in their own clause against one hundred twenty-one carrying none, and the cause is the closed verb
list, not the scoping — the ledgers claim about lines with verbs the list never names. Promotion to a gate step is
deferred until the list is derived from the reader's own narrowing rows rather than typed, the judged count is
reported together with the released count from the same scan, and the known-answer refusal is reproducible as a
fixture. Nothing was appended to a tracked script and nothing was pushed; the two ledger files gain this section
and nothing else.
## D231 — a citation needs a surface and a verb class, and a movement reader's EXACT is a statement about two refs

Three rules came out of deriving the surface reader's verb list instead of typing it, and out of repairing the three
citations that derivation led to.

First, a claim verb and a cited line must declare which SURFACE the pair needs. The measured driver was a refusal this
lane wrote and then contradicted by accident: a run script's comment line CITES another file's line number, and the
comment is exactly where the citing lives. Speech verbs (says, cites, names, notes, points) are satisfied by a comment
and refused only by a blank line; structural verbs (runs, declares, calls, writes, reads, sets) are refused by a
comment as well. A single verb list silently mixes the two and manufactures false positives out of correct prose, so
the list is two lists, each with its own admissible surfaces, and both are pinned by named cases.

Second, and this is the reason the surface reader exists at all: a reader that decides a citation by whether the named
line still holds what it held moves no verdict for a citation that never held it. The two ROOT rows and their STATUS
twin were wrong at the commit that wrote them, and the drift census gives all three EXACT, because its comparison is
line-to-line across refs while the claim is line-to-sentence. The same census already sees every cite whose target
TEXT moved — it reports the package-example rows as GONE — so the class it cannot see is mis-aim at birth, not
staleness. Content-vs-claim checks therefore have to be made against the plane the sentence names, and a gate that
only watches for movement should say in its own header what its EXACT word does not corroborate. One of the three was
additionally invisible to the citation gate for an independent reason: it points at a blank line, and blank cites on
the pre-existing plane are counted, not judged.

Third, a movement reader's judged population is a property of the working copy. Blaming the file on disk means an
uncommitted repair turns its own sites into NO-BASE rows — the census prints "absent at zero-hash" for lines it would
certify a minute later — so a repair measured only while dirty appears to change nothing, and the same three lines
carry the word EXACT both while broken and after being fixed. Verdict words are only evidence when the reader's
question is the one being asked.

The repairs are single-occurrence-gated in-place edits with the new target line read back from the target file before
writing, and the applier is row-idempotent: each row must be exactly UNAPPLIED or exactly ALREADY APPLIED, anything
else aborts, and a re-run of an applied set writes nothing and exits zero. No other lane's text is touched; nothing
pushed.
## D232 — a contradiction needs three planes to mean anything, and a token inside an identifier is not a verb

A surface reader that reports "the cited line is blank" answers one question and dodges three. The same verdict word
covers a citation that was wrong when it was written, a citation whose target moved afterwards, and a citation that
is correct against a working copy nobody has committed. Only reading the same line at the writing commit, at HEAD,
and on disk separates those, and they want different remedies: the first is repaired toward the current plane, the
second is a movement the drift census should already see (it does not, because it compares line-to-line across refs
and never to the sentence), and the third must NOT be re-aimed at all, because the number is a property of someone
else's pending edit and the ledger should stay on the plane every reader can reach.

Two rules this unit earns.

First, adjacency must reject identifiers. A citation touching the head of a SCREAMING_SNAKE name is not touching a
verb; pairing on that slice contradicts sentences that make no claim. The guard is "no letter, digit or underscore on
the far side", pinned by a case whose verdict flips when the guard's after-side is deleted. Watch the uncomfortable
measurement though: the row that motivated it had genuinely stale citations, so a false positive can sit on top of a
real defect and removing one does not excuse ignoring the other.

Second, a correction paragraph is a claim with a shelf life. D159's paragraph fixed three moved cites and described
the new state with the word "now"; two days of edits made that description wrong, and nothing that reads the ledger
could tell which moment "now" was written at. Prose that asserts a current state must name the plane — "at HEAD" —
and the repair rows for this section do that rather than re-asserting a moment. A present-tense verb about a state
another change later ended ("the gate calls them with fixed arguments") belongs to the same class and gets a tense
change, not just a number.

Also measured and recorded because it changes how the reader should be quoted: four ledger sentences had been
agreeing with an uncommitted file for days, and the number that was true there was false at every committed plane
including the one where the sentences were written. Presence of a cite in a strict drift census is not evidence that
the cite is right; the census passed on those rows because the target file had not moved between its two refs.

A third thing this unit paid for, and it is about how a landing is written up rather than about the ledger's old rows.
The sensitivity figure drafted from an earlier reading — that the surface reader refuses with eight at 4951218 — did
not reproduce once the ledgers had moved, and the numbers that do reproduce are the ones worth publishing: HEAD's own
committed text refuses with 6, that plane's text with 8, and this disk's repaired text aimed at fccedf9 with 10. Each
of the three varies exactly one side of the comparison, so they are three different questions, and a remembered
verdict cannot tell them apart. Re-measure every differential at the plane the commit will be read at, in the same
run that writes the sentence about it. The appended section reddened step 8 twice on the same habit: two citations
landing on empty lines, which a section under writing may not do, so the claims about those lines moved into the
house phrasing and the cited numbers that stayed are the ones naming text.

14 rows, single-match-gated, targets read at HEAD by `git show`; the rows leave both ledgers' line counts as they
found them and the appended sections are the only growth (12038 to 12116, 11933 to 11976); zero lone LF; no other
lane's text touched; nothing pushed.
## D233 — a census row over the working copy is not a population, and a citation's shape decides whether a reader owes it an answer

Three rules and one refusal, from deciding what #137's 104 tokens actually are.

First, **re-run the reader at a committed plane before quoting its number.** A disk-walking census reports the
tree, and this tree is dirty by construction; the same shipped reader, aimed at a sibling `git archive HEAD`
directory through the seam it already declares, printed 32 where the working copy printed 104. That is the same
disease D232 caught in four ledger sentences agreeing with an uncommitted file, only now it is in a census headline
that a whole task was filed against. A number that no commit reproduces is a measurement of somebody's pending
edit. The corollary this lane paid for once already: planes are sibling directories, never a directory under the
repo root, because a frozen copy under the root is counted by the walkers as part of the population.

Second, **classify the shape of an admitted token before asking who should judge it.** 57 of the 104 are IP
literals with a port tail or WCAG contrast ratios; the census admits them because its name rule accepts any name
ending in a dot and up to six characters, and `.1` and `.80` satisfy it. So "counted here and judged nowhere" is
a fact about the admission predicate, not a coverage hole. Pointing a citation reader at those files would
manufacture targets out of color-contrast tables. Note the arithmetic the shape test needs: the grammar splits at
the last colon, so a ratio of 4.80 to 1 arrives as the name `4.80` with line `1` — classifying the name alone calls a ratio a
version number and mis-files it as a citation candidate.

Third, **"the cited line holds text" is existence, not support.** The specimen is `docs/PLAN.md:87` naming
`docs/DATABASE.md:171` for a guard the same file documents at line 162: the line is neither blank nor past EOF, so
every line-shape reader passes it, and the sentence is wrong anyway. Claim-to-line agreement is the surface
reader's question, and it reads the two ledgers, not the plan. A census that reports 0 offenders should be quoted
as "0 offenders of the class I detect", never as "clean".

Refused: a new reader for this group. Step 9's own `prose, stake` row already drives the named files through step 8
and prints what happens — three refusals for shape and one file judged with no offender — so a second reader would
duplicate a measurement that exists, and the rule that needs changing (the admission predicate) belongs to a file
another lane is rewriting. Recorded instead: the group's committed size is 32 tokens, 28 of them with no file
behind the name, 4 in a single sentence of which one is nine lines off.
