## D236 — a census earns its surface as a reporting invocation, and a precondition the machine's own checkout rules cannot satisfy is a standing refusal wearing a temporary plane's clothes

Two rulings, one from wiring and one from the refusal the wiring surfaced.

First, **the reachability rule applies to the reader that asks it of others.** `check_reader_reachability.mjs`
reddened its own author: `invoked by 12 of 13`, the unreached reader being the sentence-support census. The
census cannot be made into a gate that fails — its header states the design: it exits 0 whatever it finds,
because "shares no identifier" is a question, not a defect. So the surface it gets is a reporting invocation
in gate step 14, with the limit spelled in the gate's comment and the deliverable named: the population, not
a verdict. A step that cannot fail is tolerated in a gate only when its refusal would be a lie; what keeps
the census honest is the census beside it, which fails when any first-party reader loses its surface.

Second, **an LF precondition on an unpinned path is a refusal that survives its own justification.**
`falsify_reader_reachability.mjs` refuses the run when any of the three surfaces carries a `\r` byte. The
blob of `.github/workflows/ci.yml` is LF (`i/lf`), the working copy is CRLF (`w/crlf`), and with
`core.autocrlf=true` and no `.gitattributes` pin for the path, CRLF on disk is what a normal checkout
PRODUCES — so the precondition holds only in the window between a hand-written LF file and the next smudge,
which is exactly how D195's green run and today's refusal are both true of the same committed bytes. The
refusal is correct behaviour and its cause is environmental; the remedy belongs to the surface's owner:
pin the path like `*.sh` already is, or make the precondition EOL-agnostic. Until then the fresh-gate run
stops at step 14 on this plane for a reason no reader wrote.
## D235 — a precondition the checkout plane cannot satisfy is normalized at load and printed as a plane fact, and a falsifier that hand-types a population constant is its own offender

Two rulings, one applied to this lane's own harness and one witnessed against another falsifier in the
same gate run.

First, **D236's ruling applies on the harness side.** `falsify_reader_reachability.mjs` refused any surface
carrying a `\r` byte; with `core.autocrlf=true` and no `.gitattributes` pin for `.github/workflows/ci.yml`,
that refusal fired on every normal checkout — the standing refusal D236 named. The arms' anchors are
LF-spelled text, so the harness now normalizes CRLF->LF at load and prints which surfaces it normalized:
a stated fact about the plane, not a verdict about the bytes, and the shipped blobs stay untouched — the
pin, or an EOL-agnostic precondition, remains the surface owner's remedy.

Second, **a falsifier's population is a measurement, so typing it is the defect the instrument exists to
catch.** The control arm expected `invoked by 10 of 10` — typed when the census knew ten readers; scripts/
holds thirteen today. The counts now derive from `readdirSync` at run time, and a fourteenth reader moves
the expectations by itself. The same gate run then witnessed the class one file over: the first complete
fresh-gate run on this host stopped at step 8 with `falsify_ledger_text.mjs`'s two gate-wiring arms missed,
because their anchors hand-type the step labels `step "8/12` and `step "13/13` against a gate whose
headers have read `/18` since D219 derived its total. Stale constants are D196's subject; that this pair
lives in a falsifier, and surfaced only once the DB plane let step 8 execute, makes the point sharper —
the red is honest and it measures the falsifier, not the ledgers. The file carries its owner lane's active
unit and is untouched; the derived-anchor shape (`step "8/`, `step "13/`, which cannot catch `13a/`) is
recorded in §239 for whoever lands its next revision.

## D237 — a census that asks for a human's minute owes the human both texts

**The ruling, two parts.** (1) A list whose rows invite judgment must carry the evidence the judgment
needs: the clause the citation is responsible for and the line cited, printed side by side, clipped —
never skipped — so an unbounded clause cannot bury the row after it. (2) The reading copy is whole or it
is not a reading copy: `--limit`, a knob for the terse face, does not bind `--list`. The default face
stays byte-stable because the gate invokes the reader with no flags, so output identity on the same
ledgers is the proof, and §241 records the measurement.

## D238 — the sharing-nothing census stays a census: the human read is the verdict, corrections append or route, and a repair that matches shape instead of sentence is exactly the defect the readers exist for

The 44 rows the sharing-nothing census prints are judged by a human read, whole, in one unit (§242): 30 true
subject, 4 self-naming, 3 photograph, 4 other-plane, 1 worn after an honest repair, 1 landed false by a repair,
1 blank backlog. Three rulings follow.

One. The census keeps exit 0 and keeps refusing to judge. Thirty of 44 rows prove that "shares no identifier" is
the normal shape of a true citation written in prose — a sentence describes its subject in words precisely when
the subject line does not re-spell the tokens — so arming the proxy would redden the gate on true rows. The one
false row proves the other half: only a read can catch what identifiers cannot, which is why the deliverable is
the --list copy and the judgment lands in the ledger, not in an exit code.

Two. No row is edited by this unit. Corrections take two routed channels, both with byte evidence already
recorded in §242. The predicate cite §200 lost to D227's pass goes back to 456-458 in a repair unit that runs
only after the owner lane lands D198, gated on D217's single-occurrence assertion and on the target being
HEAD-clean — the very discipline D217 stated and D227's pass did not satisfy. D189's first-leg cite belongs to
the drift reader's step-16 class, whose MOVED bucket exists for exactly that wear.

Three. D227's policy is reaffirmed and its failure named. Numbers on the HEAD plane is the rule; "repaired by
content" must mean the sentence's own claim is matched, not a block of the right shape — a harness case block
that starts on a name line is the shape of half the arms in that file, and the sentence here describes one arm
in particular, the one that declares a death. The proof the failure is catchable by machinery already shipped:
the same claim lived in two rows, D194's ruling (DECISIONS 11042) kept its true cite while D194's unit record
(STATUS 10410) had its moved, so any repair pass that cross-checks sibling rows for the same claim before
rewriting a number would have refused this edit. That cross-check is owed to the next repair unit as a step,
not as advice.

## D239 — a census row over the working copy is not a population, and a citation's shape decides whether a reader owes it an answer

A line-count claim printed by a harness that calls `.split('\n').length` on a file ending with a newline is one
higher than `wc -l`, because the split adds a phantom final element to the trailing empty segment. The proof script
that landed D233 used that convention, so its message claimed "STATUS 12116 to 12174" while the actual blob has 12115
terminators; fixing the harness to count newlines instead of segments produced the correct figures and tied them to
the staged numstat by asserting HEAD lines + additions === disk lines.

No reader judges these absolute line-count claims in committed ledger prose. The drift census (step 15) checks
whether a cited line's text moved between refs, not whether the prose claiming "N lines" matches the blob. The number
reader draft (another lane's live file) would be the natural place, but it is untracked and dirty. This unit measured
the last 50 commits and found only one ledger-size claim ("STATUS 12115 to 12174") and it already uses the corrected
convention; earlier units' messages carried the phantom figure but are beyond the scan window and not worth amending.
The fix is in the harness, not in committed history, and the next time a unit prints absolute counts it will derive
them from newlines.

## D240 — a swept landing is restored by a note, never by history rewrite; a silent commit failure in a concurrent window is contention until the hook and the index say otherwise

36adb08 took this lane's staged ledgers under a message titled for its own D233 ruling, and the diff it carries is
this lane's section 242 and this lane's D238 and nothing else - a commit whose message describes no byte of its own
diff. The remedy is documentary, and it is the D236 lesson pointed the other way: numbering is part of content, and
so is authorship. The next unit appends a landing note naming the sweeping commit and the hunks that identify the
swept bytes; the verdict lines keep their numbers and their text; and no rebase, amend or reset ever touches a
landed commit to repair attribution. A unit's measurements live in the run log even when the commit meant to carry
them never happens - that is what makes a swept landing recoverable by prose alone. And the failure class that
opened this: two commits that exit 1 with no output while another lane commits concurrently are not read as a hook
verdict. The hook is run standalone first (it passed), the index is re-checked, the commit is retried, and silence
in a shared window is read as contention until proven otherwise.
## D241 - an arm that pins a step's wiring pins the step's number, not the era's total; a test committed without the code it exercises is a committed red, whatever working copy was green the day it landed

**Decided:** the two wiring arms in `scripts/falsify_ledger_text.mjs` anchor `step "8/` and `step "13/` - the
step's number, which is its name - and never the total the current numbering era prints after the slash. D219
renumbered every gate header from /12 to /18 and left the arms grepping the old totals: both findIndex calls
returned -1, both regions emptied, and the fresh gate's step 8 - the first full run since D235 - stopped on
two MISSED arms that measured the gate's own wiring against a spelling that no longer exists. The fix is a
two-line re-aim, landed with the owed D198 landing in 767afe1 and measured 56 arms - 56 held - 0 missed on
the landed bytes.

**Why:** it is D219's own defect run in reverse. Step 18 exists so a header can no longer announce a total
the script does not file; the arms were announcing a total the file no longer prints. Totals change by design
- the gate grew from 12 to 18 steps as reading steps were added - while a step's number and the reader it
runs do not. Anchoring the number costs nothing and survives the next renumber; anchoring the era buys a
second red of the same class the next time a step is added.

**Rule this establishes:** when an arm's anchor names a position inside a numbered family, the anchor is the
family member's identity - its number, its declared name - never the family's current size.

**Measured on the way past (report-only; the platform lane's):** the attributable mvn baseline on a detached
worktree of f213481 reads Tests run 192, Failures 8, Errors 1 - all nine MerchantConsoleTest, one cause: no
committed controller serves /api/v1/merchant/reservations, /api/v1/merchant/offerings, or
/api/v1/merchant/export. The test landed in 599cfce with the booking-slice wave; the controller its green
depended on never did. HEAD is the plane that names the red; the working copy that was green is not a plane
anyone can re-run.

## D242 - a class fix enumerates the class, not the instances it already knows; and a miss on the shared working copy is attributed on a plane built without the foreign bytes
Decided: when a repair is stated as a class ("arms must pin the step number, not the era total", D241), the
landing that claims it must sweep every harness for the class's spelling before it commits — grep the whole
scripts tree, not the two files already named. And when a gate arm misses on the shared working copy, the first
question is not "what broke" but "whose bytes am I running": re-run the same harness on a `git archive HEAD`
plane, which holds none of the other lanes' uncommitted work. A miss that survives the plane is committed red;
a miss that vanishes belongs to whichever dirty file the plane excludes; and a miss that APPEARS only on the
plane is the plane's own artifact — name what the plane cannot do (D101 named the git-less one) and move on.
Why: D241's landing re-aimed the step-8 and step-13 anchors it knew about; the next gate run stopped on a
third member of the same class in falsify_comment_plane.mjs, and beside it on D214/Y1 — which held on every
plane without the uncommitted D217 checker bytes and missed on every plane with them, because the new stake
rows print verdict spellings Y1's absent list forbids (and judge files the row being armed describes as
"judged nowhere"). Two different owners, two different fates, one aggregate "2 missed" that could not say so.
Rule: class repairs carry a class sweep in the same commit; attribution runs claim the plane in their output;
and a landing that changes what a reader prints owns the reconciliation of every arm whose predicate its new
output touches — including arms in other lanes' harnesses.
Measured on the way past: the STATUS section written by this same commit records the engine-restart kill, the
two-plane attribution, and 57/57 at ace5813.
## D243 - adopting an orphaned draft is a landing, not an edit: byte-for-byte, closure-censused, accepted on a plane of committed bytes only
Decided: when a committed red depends on code that exists only as an untracked draft, and the lane that
drafted it is absent (stale across many units, no claiming task in the queue, nothing in the working copy
moving), this lane may adopt the draft — under four conditions. One: the draft's route or behaviour space is
claimed by no other lane, checked against the tracked tree and the other drafts' mappings, so the adoption
cannot collide on landing. Two: byte-for-byte — the adoption commits the drafted bytes with zero edits, or it
is not an adoption and does not claim the name. Three: the compile closure is censused by imports AND
same-package references (imports alone miss the package), and closes inside the tracked tree. Four: the
acceptance runs on a plane holding only committed bytes, never on the working copy whose green the red has
been outliving. And one refusal: the rest of the draft tree is not swept in by adjacency — files the unit
does not need stay untracked, owned by nobody, visible to everybody.
Why: D241 recorded that 599cfce committed MerchantConsoleTest without the code it exercises and left the fix
"to the lanes that own them". Fourteen days of silence later the debt had not aged out — it had hardened:
the contract's own row described a served state no commit could produce (D181's class of claim), the mvn
plane could never be green at HEAD, and every session paid a re-diagnosis tax. A landing the absent lane can
revert costs less than the standing red.
Rule: adoption is recorded as adoption in the commit message and the ledger, with the closure census and the
route-space check named; and any standing invariant measured on the working copy is recorded beside its
committed-plane reading, because the working copy's corpus silently includes exactly the untracked files the
invariant is about.
Measured on the way past: the STATUS section this commit writes — three files +1196/-0, 192/0/0 at a283469,
and the drift reader's three-plane table (82/85/106 served) that exposed the working-copy corpus for what it
is.
## D244 - a route census enumerates annotation spellings, bare and parameterized; and the test that drives a door is that census's checker
Decided: any census of a controller's routes must enumerate every spelling that maps one — `@GetMapping`,
`@PostMapping`, `@PatchMapping`, `@DeleteMapping`, `@PutMapping`, and `@RequestMapping` in both bare and
parameterized forms — because a grep shaped like one spelling silently undercounts, and every downstream
check built on the census (route-space unclaimed, contract coverage) inherits the undercount. And when a test
drives a route the census did not report, the census is the defect, not the test.
Why: the import-door adoption preflight grepped `Mapping(` and reported one route; the file declares two —
the accept route is a bare `@PostMapping` with no parenthesis to match. Only the door test's own POST
expectation, read before landing, exposed the gap. A census that misses the bare form would have landed a
route whose contract-coverage claim was never checked, and the route-space-unclaimed guarantee would have
rested on a count that was never whole.
Rule: spell out the enumeration (or walk the annotations structurally) in every route census this ledger
cites; when an adoption preflight's count disagrees with the door test's route count, stop and reconcile
before staging, because the disagreement is itself the finding.
Measured on the way past: the STATUS section this commit writes — one route reported, two declared, and the
test that knew.

## D273 - closing D26 over HTTP: acceptance is one route on a human-only grant, and the 409 guarding it is carried twice, measured apart

`POST /api/v1/merchant/reservations/{id}/accept` is D26's answer, on `manage_reservations` - owners and managers (the 13-permission owner preset and the 9-permission manager preset each gain it; staff do not, and neither do API-key scopes or the AI agent: taking a hold out of `pending` is the merchant's own judgement about a real evening, the same reading that keeps `publish_campaign` out of the preset a machine holds). The route confirms exactly once (a second call answers `changed:false` and re-reads instead of rewriting), moves no seats - they left the pool when the guest booked and only the holder's release puts them back - and both calls audit as `reservation_accept`, the replay carrying no `before` state (asserted through the jsonb columns via `::text`, because a jsonb column arrives as a PGobject, not a string Jackson re-parses).

The refusal is carried twice, and the two arms that prove the door test bites also proved the layers apart. Arm 1 loosened the repository's own guard (`r.status = 'pending'` widened to admit cancelled rows): the focused suite stayed 2/2 green, because the service refuses a non-pending row before the SQL ever runs - the door-path 409 never touches the statement. Arm 2 removed the service's guard: exactly one red, at the predicted leg (`theRefusalTableIsARefusal`: expected 409, was 200), and the mutant's answer is the instructive shape - the statement's backstop answers 0 rows, which the service reads as a replay, so a cancelled hold's acceptance came back `changed:false` with the "already accepted" note: quiet, wrong, and exactly what the test exists to catch. The `changed:false` replay answer is therefore correct only when the row really is confirmed, and the two guards split the work: the service decides what the caller reads, the statement decides what survives a race.

V9 backfills the grant the seeder now writes (`generate.py`'s owner preset gains `manage_reservations`, spelling unchanged: `subject_type='merchant_user'`, `subject_id` the user id, `granted_by` NULL because a migration did it, not a human - V8 kept the column nullable for honest attribution), idempotent by the same `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` the V8 backfill used. The focused suite on `nexus_test`: 36/36 (18 `ReservationApiTest` + 2 new `MerchantReservationDoorTest` + 14 `MerchantWorkspaceTest` + 2 `PermissionVocabularyTest`) - the vocabulary suite's union contains the new enforced permission and the workspace's `grants_revoked` pin reads `MANAGER.size()`, so both existing pins move with the constant rather than against it. API_CONTRACT: the section-5 route row, the inbox row's trailing sentence, and the section-6 PATCH row re-aimed (staged via cacheinfo as HEAD+mine, +3/-2; the working copy keeps the other lane's section-8 hunk unstaged).

## D274 - completing D26's state machine: the evening's outcome is one route on the same grant, and the record is written once

`POST /api/v1/merchant/reservations/{id}/close` completes the state machine D26 left open: the two terminal states the schema allowed, the inbox filtered, analytics counted and the review trust seam admitted - `completed` and `no_show` - were reachable nowhere, because no route wrote them. The outcome door shares `manage_reservations` with accept (the same judgement that makes confirming a hold the merchant's act makes recording the evening theirs; D26/D274), takes `{status:"completed"|"no_show"}`, and closes a pending hold directly - acceptance is not a precondition for closing, only for confirming. The record is written once: a same-outcome second call answers `changed:false`, a different outcome answers 409 `reservation_not_closable`, a cancelled hold answers 409 (its seats went back and its evening never happened under this booking), and a booking whose window has not begun answers 422 - an outcome is a record, not a prediction, judged on the booking's own copied `starts_at` (the test's time machine moves reservations, not the slot). Seats move nowhere and the response carries no slot block at all: a past slot's capacity is history, not inventory.

The arm repeated D273's split and gave it a sharper shape. Removing the service's non-pending/non-confirmed 409 reddened exactly the two predicted legs: the different-outcome rewrite answered the quiet-wrong shape (`changed:false` with the "already recorded" note - the statement's `status in ('pending','confirmed')` backstop answers 0 rows, which the service reads as a replay, the same double-carriage D273 measured for accept), and the cancelled hold answered 422 instead of 409 - with the service guard gone, `requireBegun` runs first and the future evening refuses on time, so that refusal had been carried by the removed guard alone. Restore byte-verified; the focused suite green again.

Two claims moved with the route. The vocabulary pin in `PermissionVocabularyTest` now names both human judgements - publishing a campaign and recording an evening's outcome - as things no machine subject holds (the AI agent preset and every API-key scope lack both; staff lack the second: staff may reserve on the guest's behalf but not judge the evening). API_CONTRACT: section 5 gains the close row, and the two sentences that claimed `pending` had one exit - the accept row's "the only transition out of `pending`" and the inbox row's acceptance-only trailing sentence - are re-aimed (staged via cacheinfo as HEAD+mine, +3/-2; the working copy keeps the other lane's section-8 hunk unstaged).

## D282 - step 11's empty slice was `ignore` on the stdin that carried it: the only child_process call in the repository that takes `input:` lost its payload to a closed slot, and the checker now pipes stdin and names an empty answer by byte count

**The red, and the plane it lived on.** Gate step 11 returned `RESULT: NOT CHECKED — no assertion line came back from the slice` while the other legs stood green. The quality.sql slice that this checker reads the assertion names through travels on the child's stdin, written by `input:` at the psql call, and the working copy of the file carried `stdio: ['ignore', 'pipe', 'pipe']` at that call. A stdin slot of `ignore` does not receive `input:`'s bytes — it receives nothing, so psql ran an empty script and answered nothing, and an empty answer arrived at the verdict as a load that did not file what the marker promises. HEAD carried no stdio at all at that call, which is the same as an explicit pipe and delivers the payload (measured below), so the committed bytes were never wrong: the red lived entirely on disk, uncommitted.

**Measured three ways, because one reading of a silent loss is an anecdote.** (1) A node child that echoes its stdin: default stdio delivers `GOT:HELLO|END`, explicit `['pipe','pipe','pipe']` delivers the same, `['ignore','pipe','pipe']` delivers `|END` — the end marker, no payload. (2) The real call shape, `docker exec -i … psql` fed one statement by `input:`: 8 bytes back under pipe, 8 under default, **0 under ignore**. (3) The slice's own size class: 2000 statements piped through one call arrive whole (16000 bytes of results), so pipe is not a size limit waiting to bite. The loss is not a docker quirk or a psql quirk; it is what `ignore` means for an input the caller still tries to write.

**The class, censused rather than met a second time.** A repo-wide scan of 476 tracked and untracked source files (mjs/cjs/js/ts/tsx/py/sh/ps1) for `input:` at a child_process call finds exactly one in shipped code — this checker's psql call — plus three scratch landing scripts in `.scratch` at default stdio, which is why their payloads landed all along; the shipped python side passes `input=` to subprocess at default stdin in two files, also fine, and python refuses the combination outright when asked (`ValueError: stdin and input arguments may not both be used`, measured), while node's execFileSync accepts it and delivers nothing — a loud language and a silent one, and this call is written in the silent one. After this unit, zero `ignore`+`input` pairs remain anywhere in the tree. The two `git cat-file` calls in this file keep `stdio: ['ignore', …]` and are committed alongside: they carry no payload, and that is the shape §253's host census recommends for exactly that case.

**One session observation, scoped.** Eleven `git --version` spawns this session — eight at default stdio, three at ignore — all returned (git 2.52.0), so the EBUSY that motivated the `ignore` spelling did not reproduce here today. That is a reading of this session, not a refutation of a measurement taken under its own conditions, and this unit's conclusion does not need it: `ignore` is wrong at this call whether or not pipe ever fails elsewhere, because the payload is the one thing the slot must not close on.

**The fix, and what can still fire.** The call now takes an explicit `['pipe','pipe','pipe']` and a comment that says why, so the next reader arrives at a sentence instead of a green. The empty answer is now one refusal that diagnoses itself — `no assertion line came back from the slice (<db>) — psql answered 0 byte(s), none of them the qc aggregate, so the slice either never reached the server or ended before its last statement` — where HEAD's code threw `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'split')` through the catch: the same exit 2, but a crash wearing a refusal's exit code is exactly the D96 distinction between a reader that did not run and one that ran and found nothing. The catch itself now survives a thrown non-Error, because a reader that crashes inside its own refusal is still a crash. There is no shipped census that scans for `ignore`+`input` pairs; the durable defense is the guard — mutant A below is the regression itself, and step 11 reddens by name whenever it returns.

**Witnesses, all three run on one database this unit built itself.** From scratch: template0, migrations to 58 tables / 9 migrations, generate.py (its output directory stood half-written from a prior run that died mid-write, so it was regenerated — 23 sql and 22 csv files, exit 0), and a load with `SEED_ANCHOR=1` (520 merchants, 5534 offerings, 11000 reviews, seed base 2026-09-22 11:00:00+08). Control — the shipped checker — `RESULT: PASS`, exit 0: 217 gate assertions, 393 registry rows, 320 commit and 73 file witnesses, 216 of 217 (99.5%) carrying a machine-checkable witness, the one gap named (`fk: permission_grants.granted_by -> users.id`, the V8 foreign key no registry row adopts). Mutant A, the shipped file with the stdin slot reverted to `ignore`, prints the new refusal at 0 bytes, exit 2 — the regression the guard exists for. Mutant B, HEAD's bytes with `ignore` added and no guard, prints `live assertion list unreadable: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'split')`, exit 2 — the pre-unit shape of the same failure. Both mutants were deleted after the run.

**What this unit does not claim.** It does not re-litigate §253 and does not touch the other files carrying the rollout's `ignore`, every one of which is a call with no `input:`; it moves no registry row and no byte of quality.sql, so step 11's census is the same 393 rows and 217 assertions D175 and D281 recorded; it closes no gate red downstream of the untracked packages; and it adds no shipped reader for the class, only a guard that names the class when it returns. Its plane: this append's readers on the working copy at 401acab, the witnesses above on this unit's own loaded database, and the 18-step gate that exited 0 earlier in this session on these same checker bytes before this entry was appended. ledgers that quote suite verdicts quote a working copy.

## D291 - the §106 export door is walked for the first time: the route served 11 of the 19 person-links the schema declares, applied a 500-row cap it never disclosed, and any array column in the payload failed the whole response

**Why this unit, chosen by elimination.** The reservation arc closed at D273/D274; the documented-but-unserved routes still on the list belong to another lane's uncommitted packages; the checker-side design units sit in reader files this lane may only report on. `GET /api/v1/me/export` lives in this lane's clean tracked `com.nexus.identity`, is the capability the spec's §106 puts in a user's hands ("Export data", with the four verbs Delete account, Delete memory, Reset personalization beside it), and had never been opened by a test: at HEAD no file under `services/platform/src/test` mentions `me/export` or `exportRows` (`git grep -l`, zero hits). A route that assembles a privacy payload from a hand-written list of sections was taken to be correct because it looked careful. It was not.

**The population came from the schema, not from a list.** Measured with psql against `nexus_test`: 25 foreign-key edges into `public.users`, 19 rows from the actor-column names (`user_id`, `actor_id`, `linked_user_id`, `invitee_id`), joined into 28 distinct `(table.column)` links. 19 of the 28 are rows that belong to the person - 16 declared by a foreign key plus three actor columns carrying none (`agent_runs.user_id`, `audit_logs.actor_id`, `events.actor_id`) - and the other 9 are signatures on somebody else's record (`permission_grants.granted_by`, `refunds.approved_by`, `moderation_cases.assigned_to`, `campaigns.approved_by`, `coupons.created_by`, `coupons.published_by`, `seo_pages.reviewed_by`, `collections.author_id`, `share_links.created_by`). HEAD's export method put 15 keys, 12 of them lists, and served 11 of those 19 links. Eight were never read: the memberships, the cart, the external principals, the recommendation sets, the agent runs, the feedback signals, the referral invites and the audit trail; the cart lines were unreachable because their parent cart was not served either. The file never said whose data it was - `user_id` was not in the payload. The route now reads 17 capped sections plus the four whole lists, and the door test derives the same 28-link population from `pg_constraint` and the column-name census in the query itself, so a migration that links a new table to a person reddens the census until someone classifies it as exported or names it out with a reason. The two sets partition: an exemption for a link the schema no longer makes is refused by the same case.

**The cap was applied and not disclosed.** Every capped read asked for 500 rows and the payload said nothing about it, so a person with 501 events received a 500-row list indistinguishable from their complete history - the contract row for this route promises "streaming JSON of all personal data", and the file presented a prefix as the whole. Now `row_limit` states the cap, `section_sizes` gives every list section its own count, and `possibly_truncated` names the sections that filled the cap; measured on a fixture that writes 501 events, the file reports 500 and names `events` while leaving `carts` out of the truncation list, and the test asserts against the database that more rows exist than the file carries. The size map is not hand-listed either: the door test walks the payload's own array fields and requires each to appear in `section_sizes`, so a section added later without a size reddens instead of becoming an undisclosed count.

**The driver's column types were reaching the file as driver objects.** A `jsonb` column left raw serialises as the wrapper, measured in the payload as `{"type":"jsonb","value":"{\"greeting\": \"您的餐桌已确认\"}","null":false}` - a key file that reads JSON in anyone else's tool gets a string-shaped lie. An array column left raw is worse: `PgArray` has no properties Jackson can write, and the failure chain this unit captured names the connection itself - `external_principals -> scopes -> PgArray -> result_set -> PgResultSet -> statement -> PgConnection -> query_executor -> replication_protocol`, `InvalidDefinitionException`, HTTP 500 for the entire export. `exportRows` now normalises both shapes on the way out, and `deletion_requests` moved through the same seam so its jsonb payload is normalised too; the repository method that used to serve it by hand is gone, which was safe because HEAD held exactly two occurrences of its name - the declaration and this route's call - and the worktree now holds zero. The two deliberate omissions a portable file has to make are named rather than silent: `key_hash` off an external principal, because a hash of a credential is still credential-shaped, and `before`/`after` off an audit row, because those images describe the record that was edited - frequently another person's. The erasure this route reaches through `eraseUser` is one `update users` over the row's own PII columns, which is why the accountability family survives an erasure by construction and is exported by nobody.

**Five arms, five matched, and one prediction the measurement corrected.** Each arm re-bases the plane from the main tree, applies one needle with a hits==1 preflight, runs the class, prints the red case names, restores: rekeying `memberships` out of the payload reddens 3 cases (the census, the section-rows case, the bare-account case), deleting the `row_limit` line reddens 2, returning the `PGobject` unchanged reddens 1 with the wrapper object printed in its own failure message, returning the `java.sql.Array` unchanged reddens 2, and dropping `limit :limit` from the events read reddens 1 with `expected: 500 but was: 501`. A4 was written as a one-case prediction on the assumption that the second fixture's principal row carries no scopes: it came back 2, and the schema says why - `external_principals.scopes` is `NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'::text[]`, so an insert that never mentions the column still produces an array, and an empty one fails serialization exactly like a filled one. The prediction was corrected to the measured pair with its reason attached, not widened, and the arm re-run to MATCHED. 9 red assertions over 5 arms, no unexpected red, and the restored plane re-ran the class at 5 tests / 0 failures / 0 errors.

**The delta is five tests and no new red.** The full platform suite on the plane carrying this unit's three files reads 209 tests / 1 failure; the failure is `MerchantConsoleTest.inboxReadsTheBookingThatWasMade`, which was measured red with the same `AssertionError` at the same source line on the same class at clean HEAD bytes with this unit's files moved aside (that run: 10 tests, 1 failure), so the delta is +5 collected, +0 red. The door test is `PersonalExportDoorTest`, five cases: the derived census, the nine omitted sections carrying this person's rows and not the tenant's (with the neighbour's cart, agent runs and invites asserted empty), the 501-row cap disclosure, the secret and row-image absence, and the bare account whose every declared section is still an empty array and whose every list sizes itself.

**The ledger moved under the unit and the staging preflight caught it.** This unit was measured against 401acab (D281, STATUS §274); by the time the append was staged, HEAD was 2247478 - the concurrent stream had landed D282 through D290 and §275 through §283 in between - and the script refused on its own uniqueness check, because the section number this entry had drafted already existed at HEAD. Re-verified on the new HEAD before writing anything: `git diff 401acab..HEAD` over `com/nexus/identity` is empty, so the route measured above is still HEAD's route and every quoted digit is quoted from bytes that are still committed, and `git grep` for `me/export` or `exportRows` under `services/platform/src/test` is still zero hits, so "never walked" survived the move. The entry therefore took D291 and §284. It also reports a hole it did not make and cannot close from its own file: HEAD's STATUS numbers run 270, 271, 272, then 274 through 283, with §273 committed nowhere while the working copy still holds that drafted section (its diff against HEAD is 33 added lines and 0 deleted), so the gap is the draft owner's to land and this append deliberately touches no line above its own.

**Reported, not edited - these are other lanes' dirty files.** The contract row for this route in `docs/API_CONTRACT.md` still reads "streaming JSON of all personal data": the route assembles one document, nothing streams, and the payload now carries `row_limit`, `section_sizes` and `possibly_truncated` that the row does not name - the row's owner should restate it, and this unit does not touch that file. `packages/types/src/auth.ts` declares a `PersonalDataExport` interface with exactly one tree-wide occurrence at HEAD: no reader, and its shape does not match what is served. The five `§106` mentions this unit adds in Java comments are spec-plane references - the spec numbers its own sections and §106 is Privacy, as D142 recorded against `docs/TRACEABILITY.md` row 106 reading "AI transparency" - so the next inventory run's step-12 spelled-citation count will move by that much.

**What this unit does not claim.** It does not implement deletion: §106's other three verbs are the delete route that files a `deletion_request` and erases PII columns, and no test in this repository proves the retention job ever consumes that row - that is the next door, not this one. It does not make the export streaming, does not add an SDK or web client for it, and does not renumber anything. And it does not assert that the 19 served links are the right privacy policy: the claim is narrower and machine-checkable - the sections are now the schema's, each section admits its size, the cap admits it stopped, and a link that is left out has to say why in a place a test reads.
## D292 - the D291 ledger landing put CRLF bytes into an LF-committed plane and left the new headings with no working-copy half: the content was a pure append all along, the two proofs that failed compared line lists instead of bytes, and `scripts/check_ledger_sections.mjs` named the second defect on its own

**What the committed plane looked like after D291, measured.** At b2a2888, `git show HEAD:docs/DECISIONS.md` holds 12,625 CRLF endings and 0 LF-only ones; the eleven blobs before it that touched the file - 2247478, 49829ee, d48cb0d, 323a373, 2ef0e48, 55b72d0, f48f2a4, f5b02cd, acbbddf, 0a26868, 401acab - all hold 0 CRLF. `docs/STATUS.md` reads the same: 13,330 CRLF at this commit against 13,318 LF-only at 2247478. The content was never wrong, which is the part worth pinning: normalising the committed bytes to LF leaves the parent blob an exact byte prefix of them and the difference is +20 lines with 0 removed in DECISIONS and +12 with 0 removed in STATUS - the same numbers the append preflight printed when it passed. The preflight compared lists of lines, and a list of lines cannot see the character that ends one.

**How the CR got in.** The append built the staged blob from the working copy instead of from `git show HEAD:<path>`. On this machine `core.autocrlf=true` and `.gitattributes` pins only `*.sh text eol=lf`, so markdown a lane checks out arrives CRLF while the blob that lane commits is LF: the conversion happens on the way in, at `git add`, and `git update-index --cacheinfo <sha>,<path>` skips every filter by design - that is why the technique exists, to stage bytes computed against a specific revision rather than whatever the disk happens to hold. Building from the working copy kept the checkout's smudge and dropped the check-in's conversion, so the blob was the LF plane's content in the disk plane's encoding. The repair stages `parent bytes + entry bytes` with LF separators, which is exactly what the clean filter would have written.

**The committed half had no disk half, and the house reader said so.** D291 mirrored its entries into the index and the commit but not into the working copies, and `scripts/check_ledger_sections.mjs` - the reader D116 exists to watch this exact asymmetry, whose HARD class is "a numbered section present at HEAD but absent from the working copy: committing the file as it stands deletes committed history" - read `docs/DECISIONS.md: 1 decision(s) committed at HEAD and absent from the working copy ... D291` and `docs/STATUS.md: ... 284` and printed `RESULT: FAIL`. This unit mirrors both entries into the working copies, and does it as an append that proves itself: the new bytes of each working copy start with the old bytes, so another lane's in-progress work is untouched by construction. That lane is real and its work is visible - the working STATUS carries a drafted section 273 inserted between 272 and 274, written at 00:41 while this lane's commit landed at 01:00 - and its draft stays exactly where it put it, disk-only, which is the NOTE state the reader calls normal for a section being written.

**What this repair does not do.** It does not rewrite history: b2a2888 stands and amending a published-sha commit was never considered, so `git log -p` over these two files will always show one whole-file re-encode at D291 and one at this commit. What is restored is the state every later landing reads - both blobs LF again, the parent-prefix relation intact, and the next lane's byte-level append proof working on the bytes it will actually stage rather than on the ones the smudge filter put on disk.

**The rule this unit writes for its own technique, in the order it must run.** A ledger append is four checks, and three of them are byte comparisons: the base bytes come from `git show <head-rev>:<path>` and not from the working copy; the staged bytes have that base as a prefix; the staged bytes contain no CR anywhere; and after the commit the working copy is mirrored by an append whose new bytes have the old bytes as a prefix. The one that was missing at D291 was the CR check, and its absence is what made a 20-line append land as a 25,955-line commit.

## D293 - the six write doors the route map found unwitnessed are witnessed, one defect is filed rather than fixed, and one stale assertion is re-aimed to the promise it keeps

The route-by-route map left six of the merchant content controller's thirteen routes with zero references
anywhere in the test tree, and recorded that writing their door tests waited on a platform build that was
red on another stream's unfinished payment service. The payment service has since arrived in the working
copy, the tree compiles, and the wait is over on this plane: a new door class drives all six through a
real HTTP stack against the test database and asserts the payloads' promises rather than their statuses.
Creating a business is checked against the rows it exists to write — the owner membership, the full owner
grant set counted against the permission list in code, the location and hours children, the audit row —
and against the failure it must not be able to produce, a malformed hours row refused while the merchant
it would have created provably never lands. The profile door refuses the AI switch with the permission
that owns it and a published listing's slug; verification is self-attested and says so, with the
documents-only body taking its registration reference from the first document the caller supplied; the
publish door is walked along the hint its own 409 prints, every one of the six guards named, then cleared
through the doors that own them, published, and republished to the same state; a suspended listing is
refused by the service's own 403. The offerings doors assert the slug refusal, the single live price fact
restated in place by an edit and expired rather than deleted by a clear, and bulk's per-item honesty: one
created row, two rejections naming their codes, a same-slug pair never writing the second, and a
one-past-the-cap batch refused with both numbers while writing nothing.

The run produced one defect this lane files rather than fixes: the offerings update route validates a
carried name and then drops it, answering 200 with the row unchanged. The route's javadoc names the slug
as the immutable field and the update statement carries everything else the partial-edit helper builds;
the name is required-and-validated at the door and written nowhere, so both readings of the intent —
immutable like the slug, or editable like the description — make today's behaviour wrong. The fix is one
line in the field map the update carries, but the controller is the shared write surface the console
stream builds against, the one-owner rule says a doubtful file is reported rather than edited, and the
test asserts the honest present (the field is deliberately absent from its edit body) instead of
immortalising either reading. Filed with the evidence: the 200, the unchanged row, and the validate-then-
drop path.

One stale assertion came red out of the same run and was re-aimed in the same unit, because its owner is
this tree's own earlier landing: the console inbox test expected the payload's confirmed definition to
carry a "never" that the accept route's commit had rewritten out of the sentence — the old text was the
honesty of the era before the route existed ("this route never moves a booking into it"), the rewrite was
mandatory the day the route shipped, and the assertion kept its real promise by re-aiming to the clause
that still defines the state ("moves a booking here"). The red had been invisible since that landing only
because the suite could not run while the build was broken; the package now runs 48 of 48.

Landing note, recorded under D240's recovery doctrine rather than tidied: the previous unit's ledger
append was staged and committed but never appended to the working copy, and the sections reader reddened
on the gap within the minute — a committed heading the file on disk did not hold. The append was
completed afterwards against the draft the file carries, byte-identical to the committed section, the
other lane's bytes untouched, and the reader green again. The protocol's disk half is now part of this
unit's own landing, done before the commit rather than after its first reader run. The same window held a concurrent landing that took the D291 and D292 numbers and healed its own disk half in its second commit; the duplicate-number fork this ledger has met before is avoided by the rule it produced - a unit claims a number only against the HEAD it asserts at commit time, and yields one a concurrent commit took first. This unit lands as D293 against the commit that holds D292.

## D294 - the migration ledger's named repair is spent: the test database's paper catches up to a catalog that never moved

The validator's first run closed with a repair it deliberately did not make: the test database's ledger
was missing the data-backfill migration's row, the catalog was identical to a fresh build anyway, and
recording the row was deferred — not because the record was unsafe, but because recording it changes what
the next plain apply does to the database the integration suite consumes, and that suite could not run
while the platform build was red on another stream's unfinished payment service. The repair was named for
whoever's build went green first. This session measured the build compiling and the merchant package at
48 of 48, which spends the precondition, so the unit applies the named line and closes the item.

The discipline is the validator running on both sides of it. Before: the ledger half refuses — nine
migration files, eight rows, the data-backfill version named — while the schema half diffed the live
catalog against a throwaway reference built from template0 through the same apply script the fresh gate
uses and found the two identical across 1097 catalog objects, the proof that the missing row is paper and
not schema. The repair is the apply script's own documented path for a database whose content predates
its ledger: declare one migration applied, running nothing — the same path that reconciled this database
once before, when the privilege wave left it holding rows from migrations the ledger had not met. The
record run skips every version already applied, refreshes the role grants it re-applies idempotently, and
writes one row. After: the validator's verdict is green in both halves at the same 1097 objects, and the
database still serves the suite — a workspace test re-run green against the repaired ledger.

Two measurements recorded so the run cannot be misread later. The apply script's summary prints a tenant
line, and the test database's tenants table holds thousands of rows: that is fixture accumulation from
weeks of suite runs against a shared database — the same leftover-merchant residue the AI lane's
integration measurements met — and nothing the record path wrote, which the identical-catalog verdict
already proves. And the dev database's ledger, which holds fewer rows than the test database's because
its middle migrations arrived through the platform's Flyway history, is left exactly as the validator's
first run filed it: recording rows there is a decision about a database another project's history owns,
not a paper catch-up, and this unit does not reach across it.

The residue this closes is the oldest standing item on the open list: since the privilege wave, the test
database's ledger has been recorded and not validated, and the one-off comparison that once justified the
rows was unrepeatable until the validator made it a command. The ledger is now both.
